--- Page 12 ---
Franc. Bacon, Book 3, Chapter 4, on the Advancement of Learning.

One is moved to wonder at Aristotle's boldness, who, driven by a certain impulse of contradiction, and declaring war on all Antiquity, not only usurped the liberty of coining new terms of art at will; but also strove to extinguish and destroy all ancient wisdom. So much so that he nowhere names ancient authors, nor makes any mention of their doctrines, except where he might censure men or refute their tenets.

A little after.

Concerning a man so excellent indeed, and admirable for the sharpness of his intellect, Aristotle, I would readily believe that he received this ambition from his disciple, whom perhaps he emulated; so that if the former subdued all Nations, the latter might subdue all Opinions, and establish for himself a kind of Monarchy in Contemplations,
A fortunate plunderer of doctrine, not a useful example given to the world. ———

Nobiliſſime Domine,

[Large decorative initial A] It is not my intention
to crown with ivy your ancestral
virtues, which, derived through a lineage
celebrated for its achievements and honors,
have settled upon you with augmented
splendor. To your benevolence towards us,
and to the testimony of your most sincere
affection, shown not just once, some
expression of a grateful mind was due.
And while that awaits an opportunity
to be rendered more fully, by this, as it
were, a public pledge, I offer...
        * 3                ob-

--- Page 14 ---
**DEDICATION.**
...publicly to acknowledge myself bound. A trifle, I confess, is what I offer, and it bears only the title of a translation; but it hopes for some splendor from the author and your patronage; who both love all kinds of studies, and are accustomed to benignly embrace the efforts of rising genius. More worthy things and things equal to your Name to be extolled did not occur from the meager assessment of our progress. Therefore, while I strive even thus to prove my diligence and faithfulness to readers, I also wished this to stand as a pledge of our veneration for you. Farewell, Most Noble Lord, and may you long survive for the praises of your family and your own, from the hereditary clientage of the Muses. Middelburg, Zeeland. Kalends of September, 1648.

THE INTERPRETER
TO THE READER.

[Decorative initial F]RANCIS BACON of Verulam's *Natural History* has long been a work desired in Latin. Printers have more than once earnestly solicited its translation, even with payment. Hitherto, the variety of the subject, entangled with many difficulties, has deterred everyone; it would also weary Englishmen and scholars. No confidence in my studies, the harvest of which is scarcely in the blade, nor a deeper knowledge of the English language, but fortune, impelled me here; whether it will turn out well or ill, rests with you, kind Reader;

---

TO THE READER.
Reader, if you would allow my efforts, conscious of their own slightness, and never destined for the press, yet brought here by the gentle importunity of friends, from which I cannot now withdraw, to find safety in the hope of your pardon; while I am unwilling that Latin philosophical audiences should longer be without the work of that Illustrious Man, a work most useful for constructing the rules of Physics, which brings it into line with Nature. For after I decided to devote the leisure, cut off from occupations and relaxations, to the exercises of the pen, seeking real things, so to speak, and somewhat removed from the incorporeal noise of words, I stumbled upon these, indeed most pleasant, and opportune for fostering my medical studies; but elsewhere not rarely intricate to one translating, indeed even desperate, unless most learned—

--- Page 17 ---
L E C T O R I .

*of very learned men (whose names are too*

*struggled through the whole course of difficulties, when the*
*papers, now reduced to a volume, came*
*into the hands of those whom it would be a matter*
*of conscience for me not to obey, I immediately*
*felt measures being taken, until it was no longer*
*permitted for the fruits of my diligence to be*

perhaps it might render a varied likeness of our former reading. Nor yet do I dare to promise that I have completely achieved what I diligently pursued. Indeed, some things will be found which will easily testify how I have not everywhere satisfied myself. Thus you will see some English additions on the pages, even where Latin is not lacking; sometimes even where I despaired of being able to express it. But here and there, kind Reader, I expect from you a remedy for the faulty passages; if perchance, through the benevolence of the learned age, the hope of a second and more improved edition will not have been unreasonable, and in a difficult work and in rendering into Latin matters of nature so remote, some ignorance is beyond blame, indeed, if even a slumbering attention errs within the hope of pardon.

W. RAWLEY
PREFACE
*translated from English.*

[Decorative initial C]Since my Lord author has not dis-
dained my humble effort in this
collection, I feel publicly obliged,
so that (with his assent) I may pre-
pare the way for the Reader, by in-
dicating those things which concern
both the form of the work and its
publication. I remember it often
being said by him in conversations,
that if he had consulted only his
own reputation, it would have been
better to consign the *Natural Histo-*
*ry* to private obscurity, than to pub-
lish it *to be worn out by individual
public use*. For it seems merely an
undigested mass of particulars, lack-
ing that splendor which a precisely
observed *Method* usually bestows
upon books. But that the concern
for his own honor has prevailed over
whatever of man-
                                      kind

--- Page 21 ---
P R E F A C E.
might serve the advantages and security of mankind. Nor was he unaware that no other way remained by which human intellect might be brought into freedom, bound and enchanted by the fallacies of notions and speculations, which utterly destroy the good fruit of operations; but that above all, deference must be paid to sense and experiments, at least at the beginning. Moreover, he was obliged to provide an example of Natural History, as if it were the designated third part of his Instauration. My Lord repeatedly stated that many of the things which he would include in this writing, men would consider to be base, unworthy, merely curious, and feigning utility. Therefore it is to be wished that they should constantly keep in mind what is now to be done, and what difference there is between this Natural History and the scholarly works of others in this field. For whatever of this subject

--- Page 22 ---
P R A E F A T I O.
Whatever indeed is read on this subject indulges in the pleasantness of descriptions and showy treatises, affectedly peddling miracles that rarely occur and secrets. But our hero composed a Natural History, from whose foundation true philosophy may be awakened, which may both illuminate the intellect with a torch, favor the construction of axioms, and play the principal role in the direction of works. For thus he believes he has discharged his bounden duty, by extending the boundaries of the sciences and faithfully attending to their growth. Since he has here gathered material suited for the structure, and in the New Organon (whose second part shortly awaits the public Reader) has suggested instruments and rules, men will have been unjust to themselves, unless they raise the arts to that pinnacle of perfection to which human ingenuity can attain. And hence sometimes arose my Lord's complaints, when he had dis-
charged

--- Page 23 ---
P R E F A C E.
he thought himself soon also to be driven to the lowest labors of a workman, indeed (following the example of the Israelites after their exodus from Egypt) to collect straw through the fields and burn bricks. For he was convinced that it was in vain to hope for anything from others, men being hardened in their stubborn contempt for what they had received that would be beneficial. As for the fact that the dignity of experiments is not everywhere established according to the opinion of some, indeed becoming worthless elsewhere, it must be considered that they are honorable enough insofar as they acknowledge God as their author. If they are criticized as if they were obvious, it must be known that clear experiments, free from all doubts, provide illumination for the solid structure of axioms. It was also customary for our Hero to render what presents itself as admirable most clearly explained, and not to arrange things of this kind so that they might appear admirable. Moreover, experiments into minute

--- Page 24 ---
P R E F A C E.
te details should be broken down, he used to say, lest
they remain whole, and such as they were at their ori-
gin. Regarding their use; the distinction of experi-
ments, often repeated by my Lord, whereby some are
called fruit-bearing, others light-bearing; and he
thought that whoever acknowledged no use of light, because it is diffused
immate-rially, did not have a sound mind. Furthermore, expe-
riments elsewhere have reasons appended, so that the work of inter-
preting Nature, which is being undertaken, and the axioms to be elicited,
might be more readily available. He considered the causes given by himself
to be more soli-
d than those usually given by others: not
because he boasted of any excellence of intellect above others (as he used
to say), but because of his familiarity with Nature and experi-
ments. More-over, by scattering causes, he did not want men
(who impatiently bear being stopped by ignorance of causes as if by an obstacle)
to wander endlessly in a vast forest, but to dwell on them for a little while

that he interrupted the series of his

If he had arranged his material more meticulously,

such an endeavor. How scrupulously
indeed he urges method, the book
"On the Advancement of the Sciences" will prove,
following that thread of order (if
I am not mistaken), which scarcely anyone else could have ren-
dered more exact, or I am greatly mistaken.
My Lord's saying will close the preface,
that the world is exhibited here as it
is in itself and as the work of God, with all
rashness and license of imagination pro-
scribed.

I also wished the Reader to be advised, that in this translation I have not exactly followed the order which the English original presents,

--- Page 28 ---
L E C T O R I.
TO THE READER.
...the order which the English exemplar presents, because it has manifest confusion in the arrangement of things, scattered in various places, more by chance than from a certain reason. Moreover, having been aided by the greater part of the papers which the author left in manuscript, I judged it necessary to add or remove several things, omitted or added by Bacon's Almoner, who, after the death of his Lord, confusedly subjected to the press whatever he found of this subject in his study. This I attest here, lest those who understand the English language accuse my fidelity, if they find more things in my version which the autograph entirely lacks.

TO JACOB GRUTER,
His Brother,
ISAAC GRUTER
Sends Greetings.

[Decorative initial R] EM, my Brother, you have undertaken a task which, while easily to be approved by fair judges of things, will nevertheless be troubled by harsher judgments when you encounter ill-disposed censors, who form a large part of our age. From this crowd, those who will receive you most mildly will declare this whole kind of translation useless, which bestows upon the Latin world writers so far removed from Antiquity by their origins, as much as they differ in spirit from the genius that makes books enduring. But there was no reason why malice, scrutinizing every hidden fault, should deter you from your undertakings, even if you are erring (if perchance) by following greater examples, whose authority in literature is bene-

--- Page 30 ---
will charitably defend the expenditure of your leisure. For, eager to temper your pauses from reading with writing, you drew the lines of your pen, and (as the saying goes) furrows in fertile dust, choosing the field of your Physical and Medical studies, establishing a union of charm and rigor, and an interplay of content and style. Thus you took a holiday from poring over authors, with a subtle shift in your literary diligence, so that an account of your studies in another genre might be established for you; and yet reading does not complain that anything has been withheld from it, for it finds its own place even in writing. I am a witness that the hope of glory – which perhaps by others here would be contended for more boastfully, or at least pursued more ambitiously – was not your aim, if in a brother's business a brother is to be heard as a fitting witness (οἰκεῖος μάρτυς). Offered to the public, and not merely privately inspected by foolish judges, these works seemed unlikely to be unwelcome to the schools of philosophers; yet you refused publication, which others would eagerly press for—

--- Page 31 ---
...you refusing publication, which others
urged. I joined those who, from their retreats,
fleeing the cares of the world, and establishing
them, deemed it necessary to bring you forth,
since everything of that Man, to whom you have
now rendered the service of a Latin interpreter,
had always pleased me with a very widespread,
as it were, applause. Here, the method of refined
discussion pleased me, in its selected variety of
argument diffused through many subjects. It was
far removed from the narrow confines of the modern
Peripatetics, who fabricate notions rarely in
agreement with Nature. Nor, however, do I think
*Verulamium* surpassed the mists of human
intellect, so that, established in clarity, he always
had things he could present as certain. He led
the way, for the aroused industry of others to
follow, which will pay tribute to diligence, wherever
either explored novelty will expand the boundaries
of knowledge, or doubts inextricable to predecessors
will receive light from the good fortune of a
succeeding age. But this is the subject matter of
your dissertation, into which, lightly touched upon
in brief words, I feel I have strayed by a subtle
digression, while con-

--- Page 32 ---
...while other matters, offered by the urgency of writing, take pre-
cedence over the congratulation I had conceived. To bring this let-
ter to a close – a letter not to be sent from these confines, had
my initial thoughts corresponded to the outcome into which I am
rashly carried by the dictate of occasion – know that nothing could
have happened more pleasing to me than to see the fresh sheets from
the press, with the added brief announcement of the work being com-
pleted. May God grant that he whom we now diligently praise for
another's work, may soon, attempting some work of his own, be ad-
vanced by fame with kindly auspices.
Farewell. August 8,
1648.

FIRST CENTURY.

Various Experiments concerning the percolation
and penetration of one body through another.

[Decorative initial E]IG a well, a little above
where the outermost sea wave
runs out, with a depth
that corresponds to the last decrease
of the ebbing sea; the surging sea
will fill this with fresh water suitable for drinking.
That is popular on the coasts of Mauretania.

--- Page 46 ---
2 FRANCIS BACON
popular experience, where it alone compensates for the lack of fresh water. Julius Caesar understood this well when he was besieged at Alexandria. For by digging wells on the shore, he frustrated the laborious efforts of the enemy, who had diverted seawater into Alexandria's spring; and then saved his army unharmed, when the hope of salvation seemed to have been cut off. Caesar, however, ignorant of the cause, thought that a spring of fresh water was inherent in the sea sands, but it is clear that it must be attributed to the seawater, which fills the well according to the measure and increase of its tide, and having entered beneath the sands, and been filtered, deposits its saltiness.
	2. I remember reading of an experiment in filtering salt water through earth, with ten vessels placed one upon another, yet it did not shed its saltiness so as to be suitable for drinking. The same Author relates from the account of others, that salt water drawn through twenty vessels became fresh. This experiment seems to contradict the other one about wells dug on the shore; yet he says that when repeated twenty times, it is not without effect. But it is worthy of note how miserable our imitations are found to be, as we commonly apply ourselves to experiments, unless they are guided by great judgment and a certain light of axioms. For, first
			A

--- Page 47 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 3
for, there is no small difference between
the passage of water through twenty small vessels, and
the distance, such as appears in rising and falling water.
Secondly, there is a great difference between sand and earth. For
all earth contains a certain kind of nitrous salt,
of which sand is generally devoid.
Moreover, earth does not filter water as exquisitely as sand.
But a third reason now remains, which is as
suspect to me as the other two. This is, however,
that in the experiment of the transmission of seawater into
wells, the water rises, and in the experiment of the
transmission of water through vessels, it descends.
Now it is established that the more saline parts of water
(if once thoroughly imbued with salt) penetrate to the bottom.
And therefore it is not surprising if the derivation
of water by descent does not render it fresh. Furthermore,
I doubt whether the impact of water driven from the sea
is more suitable for shaking out the saline parts
than when water flows by its own motion.
3. Percolation or transmission seems to be a
certain kind of separation, which not only separates
the coarse from the fine, and the dregs from other parts,
but also much more subtle natures; and it is varied
according to the bodies through which the transmission is carried out;
A 2 as if

--- Page 48 ---
4 FRANCIS BACON
just as if a liquid deposits fat through a woolen sack, if through sand, saltiness. They report concerning the separation of wine from water, transmitted through ivy wood, or a similar porous body, but it is not confirmed.

4. The gum of trees (which usually appears to us translucent and clear) is only a thin transmission or percolation of the tree's sap through the wood and bark; and likewise, diamonds endowed with angles, and carbuncles collected from rocks (which also shine more than gum) are subtle exudations of stone.

5. Aristotle gives an inept reason why the feathers of birds are of more vivid color than the hairs of animals; for no beast has green hairs representing the color of lapis lazuli and living flesh. The reason is, he says, that birds are more frequently in the sun's rays than beasts. But that is manifestly false: for cattle spend more time in the sun than birds, which generally live in forests or shade. The truest reason is that the excrementitious humor of living things, which equally constitutes feathers in birds and hairs in beasts, is transmitted in birds by a thinner and more delicate filtration than in beasts; for feathers pass through quills, but hairs through the skin.

--- Page 49 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 5
6. Clarification of liquids by adhesion is like an internal percolation, and it occurs when some glutinous body, mixed into the liquids, is agitated along with them. This motion causes the coarser particles to adhere to the glutinous body; and in this way, the finer particles are separated from the coarser ones. Thus pharmacists clarify syrups with egg white, mixed and agitated in the liquids to be clarified, because the egg white collects all the dregs and coarser parts, and after the syrup is placed on the fire, the egg whites harden and are removed. In this way, Hippocratic wine becomes clear if it is mixed with milk and thoroughly agitated, and then passed through a woolen sack, which they call Hippocrates' sleeve. And what is glutinous in the milk draws the aromatic powder and the coarser parts of the liquids to itself.
7. The clarification of water is a practice conducive to health; besides the fact that crystalline and clear water delights the eyes; but it is done

*Various Experiments concerning the motion*
*of a body from pressure.*

9. Take a glass filled with water, and
           move a moistened finger around the rim of the
           glass, pressing it rather firmly. The finger,
           moved around for a short space of time, will
           cause the water to ripple and leap up in fine
           sprays. This instance excellently demonstrates
           the force of compression in solid bodies. For
           whenever a solid body (such as wood, stone,
           metal, etc.) is pressed, an internal commotion
           of its parts arises to free itself from the
           compression; and this is the cause of all
           violent motion. And it is worthy of the greatest
           admiration, that this motion has never been
           observed, though it is most obvious among all
           motions, and the principal root of all mechanical
                                                               operations.

--- Page 51 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR: Centur. I. 7
root. This motion first operates in a circle, as if trying, seeking a way to free itself, and in its progress explores where an easier liberation might be found. This motion is manifest in liquids. For all liquids form circles, and cause them to collide with each other; but in solid bodies (which are not broken) it is so subtle that it escapes sight. Nevertheless, it reveals itself through various effects: as in this example which we have in hand. For the pressure, facilitated by the moistening of the finger (since it adheres so much more easily to the rim of the glass), after some time excites all the particles of the glass to action, so that they strike the water sharply; which striking generates a splashing of the waters.

10. If you strike or pierce a fragile solid body, such as glass or sugar, it is not only broken in the part where the force was most directly applied, but it is torn apart all around into segments and fragments. The motion from pressure, exploring all ways, breaks where it finds the body weakest.

11. Gunpowder, expanded into such a flame that it does not suffer compression, moves circularly (for flame consists of the nature of a liquid body) sometimes receding, sometimes bursting the engine, but generally expelling the ball with an explosion.

Various experiments concerning the separations of bodies by weight.

14. Take a glass with a capacious belly and a long neck. Fill the belly partly with water. Take also another glass, into which you pour red wine mixed with water. Invert the first, with its belly turned upwards, and stop up its neck with your finger. Then insert its opening into the other glass, and remove your finger. Kept in this state for some time, it will separate the wine from the water; the wine will ascend and cling to the top of the upper glass, the water will descend and settle at the bottom of the lower glass. The passage is visible to the eyes; for you will see the wine emerge upwards in a slender (so to speak) vein. Therefore, for convenience (since the experiment requires a little time), it is advisable to suspend the upper glass by a nail. For as soon as so much pure and unmixed water has been collected at the bottom of the lower glass that the opening of the upper one is immersed in it, the movement will cease.
15. If there is wine in the upper glass and water in the lower, you will be able to experience no movement at all. If there is pure water in the upper, and colored water in the lower, or vice versa, no movement will exist. But experience shows.
A 5

--- Page 54 ---
10          OF FRANCIS BACON
it is established, even if the mixture of wine and water in the
lower (vessel) consists of three parts water, one (part)
wine, no impediment to motion arises.
This separation of wine and water is recognized to
exist from weight. For an unequal weight of
bodies is required, otherwise the operation is
thwarted. And the heavier body should always
be in the upper glass. But note,
that the water is made suspended, and a great
weight of water in the belly of the glass is as if sup-
ported by a small column of water in the neck of the glass.
For this cause excites the motion; for even a longer
delay scarcely separates water and glass in one glass.
     16. This experiment can be trans-

simple bodies, which consist of various and
similar parts. Therefore, use in the
experiment brine or salt and sweet water,
pouring the salty (which is heavier) into the
upper glass, and see if the sweet ascends. Try the same with
sugar and pure water, and observe whether the
water that ascends deposits its sweetness:
for which purpose it would be necessary to have a small
siphon in the belly of the upper glass.

*Various experiments pertaining to accurate*
*infusion both in liquids*
*and in air.*

17. In bodies that are more subtle, easily dissipated, and contain spirits, when you prepare an infusion, observe the following. A short stay of the body in liquids extracts the spirit; a longer one spoils it, because it simultaneously draws out earthy parts and corrupts the more subtle ones. And therefore it is an error in physicians if they rely only on a longer stay as if it strengthens the virtue. But if you require a strong infusion in bodies which consist of more subtle spirits, let the rule be that a longer stay is not allowed, but that the infusion of the body is repeated often. Take violets, and infuse a proper handful of them in two pints of vinegar. Let them stand for three quarters of an hour, and then remove them, and renew the infusion seven times with a similar quantity of violets; it will make the vinegar so fragrant with the smell of flowers that, if after twelve months it is brought forth in a vinegar cruet, you will perceive the scent before it is offered to you. *Note, that it smells more perfectly of the flower's fragrance after a longer period than the first time.*
          A 6               18. These

--- Page 56 ---
12 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; OF FRANCIS BACON
18. This rule, which we have prescribed, is of excellent use for the preparations of medicines and other infusions. For example, borage leaves are strong with an excellent spirit for dispelling the vapors of melancholy, and thus cure madness; nevertheless, if the leaves remain infused too long, they only provide a crude substance, devoid of all virtue; therefore, I suppose that if borage is steeped for a short space of time in must or dregs of beer, while it ferments and before it is decanted, with new leaves being added repeatedly, I would make a most efficacious potion against melancholic passion. I also hold the same opinion concerning orange tree flowers.
19. Rhubarb clearly contains parts of contrary operation to each other, namely, purgative and astringent to the body. The former are easily separated, the latter adhere more firmly. So that if rhubarb is infused for an hour and thoroughly pounded, it will purge better and astringe the body less after purgation, than if it is steeped for 24 hours; as experience has taught. I also conceive that, by repeated infusion of rhubarb (as was said concerning violets), with only a short delay allowed each time, an equally strong purgative can be made, as by

--- Page 57 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 13
Scammony. And it would be no small aid in medicine to be able to make Rhubarb and milder medicines as effective as those which are not without harmfulness.

20. The most purgative part of purgative medicines resides in a more subtle spirit, as appears from the fact that they suffer no ebullition without great loss of potency. And therefore it would be of good use in medicine to be able to retain the purgative power and remove the harsh taste of the purgative. And it seems that this can be done by observing a series of infusions, frequently repeated for a short space of time. For it is probable that the horrid and harsh taste adheres to the coarser particles.

21. In general, operation by infusions is crude and blind, unless it is observed which parts (of the substance) are extracted more quickly, and which more slowly, so that with a time proportioned to each, you may remove what you desire, and leave the quality. To know this, one must proceed by a twofold path. The first is, that you try what a long or short delay effects, as already said; the other, that you observe in order infusions of one and the same body in various liquids succeeding one another. For example, take orange peels, or rosemary,

--- Page 58 ---

rosemary, or cinnamon, whatever you wish,

      22. Infusions into the air (if it be permitted to call smells thus) have the same differences

      23. Just as sometimes we desire to extract

by the manner of wine, or by some similar process. Decocted Senna leaves reduce some flatulence, and generally, subtle and flatulent spirits are removed by burning or evaporation. Therefore, in infusions of substances that have vehement spirits, it will be preferable to reject the first infusion after a short time and use the subsequent one.

    *Experiment concerning the desire for continuity in liquids.*

    24. Bubbles have the form of a hemisphere, with air inside and a thin membrane of water outside. Nor is it unworthy of admiration that air, when enclosed by water, can swell up so suddenly, and then, having gathered itself into a peak, be contained by such a fragile covering as a bubble. As for the swift ascent of air enclosed by water, it is a motion of percussion from the water, which itself, descending, propels the air upwards, not a motion from lightness in the air. Democritus calls this a motion of impact. In this obvious experiment, the cause of the bubble closing itself on all sides is that an appetite resisting separation and discontinuation (which is strong in solid bodies) is also found in liquids, although weaker and more relaxed;

--- Page 60 ---
16        FRANCIS BACON'S
and weaker; as can be seen in this movement of a bubble.
This can also be observed in small glass-like bubbles made from
saliva, which boys make from reeds; and
in bubble castles, which they prepare by blowing
into water that has acquired some degree
of tenacity from soap. The same is evident
in drops of water, which, having obtained enough
to flow down, are drawn out into a thin thread
lest they separate; if that is lacking, they contract
into round drops; this shape most strongly
preventing the discontinuation of the body. The cause
of roundness in a bubble is the same both regarding
the membrane of water and regarding the internal
air. For air likewise flees separation,
and therefore rolls itself into a round shape.
The persistence and brief stay of the air in a small
space shows that air, by its own nature, has a slow or
no tendency to rise.

A solitary experiment regarding artificial
fountains.

25. The rejection of experiments, which
I occasionally employ, even if it is not apparent, is varied.
But if an experiment proves to have been used in practice,
I accept it, but I present it as of doubtful
credibility. An unknown man describes a method
of preparing an artificial fountain. Seek out
sloping ground, where conveniently a swift
flow—

--- Page 61 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I.      17
...course for rainwater. Arrange a channel
half-full of stones of suitable size to a depth
of three or four feet in the same ground. Let
one part be placed on the ascent, the other on
the descent. Fill the channel with ferns in
suitable abundance, spread sand on the surface.
You will see (he says) after several repeated
showers, the lower part of the channel gushing
forth like a spring. Nor is it surprising if this
happens while rainwater is in its course. But he
adds that it will last for a long time after the
rain has drained away; as if the water is
multiplied, aided by the air, by the coldness, by
the condensation of the earth, and by the
association of the previous water.

A solitary experiment concerning
  the poisonous quality of human
             flesh.

  26. The French (from whom the Neapolitan
disease received its name) relate that during
the Neapolitan siege there were wicked
merchants who sold the flesh of men recently
killed in Mauritania, preserved in vessels, in
place of tuna; and that the origin of this
disease is ascribed to such foul and grave
nourishment. Nor does it deviate from the
truth; for it is known that cannibals in the
                                         West

--- Page 62 ---
18 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;OF FRANCIS BACON
to eat human flesh; and that India,
when it was first discovered, greatly
suffered from this disease. Also in our
time, poisons, which are most potent for the
West Indians, consist of a mixture of human blood, fat,
or flesh. Many witches and sorceresses also,
both among heathens and Christians, feed
on human flesh, for strengthening (as it seems)
the imagination with foul and acrid vapors.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*the conversion and transmutations*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*of air into water.*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;27. These seem the most likely true
reasons for changing vapors or air into
water. The first is cold, which condenses,
as is shown by the condensation of air in a calendar
glass, where to some extent it becomes more
like water. We also see in the generation
of springs, to which the ancients assigned their origin
(very probably) from the
conversion of air into water, facilitated by
the stillness which the air enjoys in these parts of the
earth, so that it cannot be dispersed, and by the
coldness of the rocks; for springs are generated
most abundantly in those places. The same is evident from the effe-

--- Page 63 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I.      19
[...by the effe]cts of cold in the middle (as they call it) region of the air, which produces dews and rains; and by the experiment of the change of water into ice with the help of snow, nitre, and salt (about which we will speak later), which can be transferred to this conversion of air into water. The second reason is compression, as in Alembics, in which vapor is repelled back into itself by the opposing sides of the Alembic; in the dew adhering to the lids of a boiling pot, in the dew, in in time of rain, on marble and panelled work. But these contribute little, unless a thicker air is present in the vapors, and which is already in the next degree to water. The third reason is (still to be explored and not yet sufficiently manifest) the mixture of humid vapors with air. Let an experiment be made whether a greater quantity of water comes forth from the return than there had been before. If this happens, the increase is from the conversion of air. Fill the bottom of the Alembic with water, the neck being stopped, but first having ascertained the weight of the water. Suspend a sponge in the middle of the alembic, and see how much water you can squeeze from it. Whatever more or less there may be should be compared with the water consumed. For it must be known, if any change can occur, it happens most easily where the pores are small; and this is the reason why a sponge is prescribed to be used.

The fourth probable reason is also,
although not yet discovered; and it is
when air enters the tiny pores of bodies.
Indeed (as we have already heard) every
thing is more prone to conversion with a small
quantity of itself. Tangible bodies do not
delight in the company of air, but try to subdue
it into a denser body. In whole bodies
this is prevented, because there is nothing
to succeed the condensed air. Therefore
it must happen in loose bodies, like sand and
dust; which, if kept stored, collect
moisture.

*A solitary experiment on how a good*
*bodily habitus and stature*
*may be produced.*

28. Some of the Ancients relate that puppies
or other animals, if, when tender, they are enclosed
in such a cage or box, so that they cannot fill the just
measure of their kind, but grow in breadth
or height, grow to the form of their place. If
we are not deceived by the report of the ancients,
and if it can happen that tender offspring
compressed in this manner and kept more tightly
do not die, a method has been found
which produces dwarfs of monstrous and exorbitant
figure. That is beyond controversy

--- Page 65 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 21
...that, beyond controversy, long-time observation has established, that by pressing, the formed parts of a tender fetus deviate considerably from their shape. Thus the foreheads of infants, handled by hands (which was noted by the ancients), produce macrocephali; which head shape was then prized. A moderate elevation of the bridge of the nose prevents the deformity of a flat nose. This observation, thoroughly examined, reveals the means by which men and women may become in many ways more graceful and comely than the infancy of their native conformation would allow. Thus the retraction of the calves upwards prevents them from falling, but rather makes them support themselves. Likewise, the retraction of the forehead upwards renders it spacious and not low. The common custom of wrapping infants in swaddling clothes makes them grow up more slender and with a better shape. For we see young women use tighter constriction of their bodies against stoutness.

*A solitary experiment concerning the con-*
*densation of air so that it can be weighed*
*and provide nourishment.*

29. Suspended onions spontaneously germinate, and also pennyroyal, and a certain herb called Or-pinagria by the Latins, with which houses in the fields are adorned, tied to a small plank or stick and to

--- Page 66 ---
22 FRANCIS BACON
and set up against a wall, does something similar. But we see this more clearly in the greater houseleek, which bears leaves for two or three years. But it is known that its root is wrapped in oiled linen, which is renewed every six months. Nor is this inconsistent with what the ancients relate about the stem of Lilies. The cause is a strong, dense, and succulent moisture in these parts, which does not easily evaporate, and therefore suffices for germination to its former abundance, even if no nourishment from the earth is added; which happens in late spring or early summer, at times suitable for germination. We also see tree trunks fallen to the ground sprouting for a time. But there is a noble experiment, and one which consequently hints at more things, if it is investigated whether these, while germinating, increase in weight; which should be inquired into by weighing them before they are suspended, and after they have put forth shoots. If they do not increase in weight, nothing else is concluded from this, than that something departs from some parts, which in germination accrues to others. But if they do increase in weight, then it is one of the great wonders of nature. For it shows that air can thus thicken, so that it can be converted into a dense body; since the cycle of all things that are above the earth ends in attenuation, and pneumatic things...

A solitary experiment concerning
the commingling of flame and air,
and its great force.

30. Flame and air are not easily mixed unless instantaneously, or in the vital spirits and living creatures. In gunpowder, its vehemence was ascribed to the rarefaction of the earthy substance in the flame. So far true, and then (indeed) another element emerges, whose form occupies a larger space, whence necessarily expansion follows, and, lest two bodies fill one place, the necessary expulsion of the ball, or the blowing up of tunnels. But these speculations have something crude and dull. For flame, if nothing else were present, nor if it prevailed in the greatest quantity, can be suffocated by another hard body, such as an iron ball or the barrel of a gun. So that flame by a hard body

--- Page 68 ---
24      OF FRANCIS BACON
is not sufficient for expelling the body, but a hard body extinguishes the flame, and does not allow it to ignite or disperse. But the cause of such violent motion is in saltpeter (which we also call niter), because, containing within itself a crude and flatulent spirit, it first expands with the heat of the fire (nor are we unaware that simple air, thinned by heat beyond its nature, will prepare a place for itself, dissolving and expelling obstacles with its blast); secondly, when the saltpeter has expanded, it propels the flame outwards with a blast, like an internal bellows. And therefore we observe that sulfur, pitch, camphor, Greek fire, and other flammable materials besides, although they burn with a vehement and scarcely extinguishable flame, yet do not excite such fiery blasts as gunpowder. On the contrary, we see that Mercury (a most crude and watery body), when heated and tightly enclosed, possesses the same power as gunpowder. As for living beings, it is most certain that their vital spirits are a substance composed of airy and fiery matter. And although air and flame do not easily mix by themselves, they do not refuse to be coupled in a fixed body, which is evident in two bodies (which are their nourishment): water and oil. For these also of their own accord

they do not easily combine, but in the bodies of plants and animals, they allow mixing. It is not surprising, therefore, if a small quantity of spirits in the ventricles of the brain and the ducts of the nerves can move a body of such great mass with such vehemence, as in wrestling, running, and with such agility, as in the trembling play of a tortoise. Such indeed is the power of air and flame when they are incorporated.

A solitary experiment regarding the hidden nature of flame.

31. Take a wax candle and place it in an iron or bronze tube. Afterwards, place it upright in a saucer full of heated spirit of wine. Then, with the candle and spirit of wine simultaneously set on fire, you will see the flame of the candle expand, and swell four or five times more than it usually did before; and it appears in a round, not pyramidal, shape. Moreover, you will observe the internal flame of the candle with its color preserved, nor will it take on any blueness towards the color of the external flame in the spirit of wine. This is an excellent instance, supplying two things worthy of note. First is, that a flame enveloped by a flame is not extinguished, but is a fixed and continuous body, like air or water. Therefore, the flame will continuously ascend with equal magnitude,
                                B

--- Page 70 ---

magnitude, unless it is extinguished by being repressed from the sides;

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the differing force of the flame in*
*the Middle and at the Sides.*

32. Hold an arrow placed in a flame for the space of ten pulses. Then, having removed it, you will find the outer parts of the arrow towards the flame more scorched and blackened, and for the most part turned into charcoal; while that which was in the middle appears only to have been touched by fire. This instance leads to many observations concerning the elucidation of the flame's shape; and clearly demonstrates that the flame burns more intensely around the sides than in the middle, and what is of greater importance, that violent or fierce heat or fire does not exist, except where, being more compressed, it thins itself. And therefore the Peripatetics (although their opinion concerning the element or fire above the air has deservedly been refuted) acquit themselves very well here. For to those who object that if a fiery sphere were given, which would envelop the world in such a close embrace, it would be impossible for all things not to be exposed to be consumed by fire,
B 2

--- Page 72 ---
28          FRANCIS BACON
exposed to be consumed by fire, they respond that purely elemental fire in its natural place, not irritated, is only of moderate heat.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the di-*
*minution of the natural motion of gravity*
*at a great distance and a certain*
*depth of the earth.*

33. It is a constant assertion of many,
confirmed by obvious experiment, that in the bottom
of a mine shaft a mass of crude metal can be moved
and rolled by the labor of two men, which,
if transferred to the surface of the earth, would require the combined strength of six
men at least, to be moved from its place.
It is a noble instance, and it is expedient that a more exact account be had
of this experiment. For it is very probable
that the motion of gravity operates slowly
both at a great distance from the earth and in
the interior of the earth. The former occurs because the appetite
for union of dense and compact bodies
with the earth is weaker at a distance.
The latter, because the body has in some measure
obtained its own nature, from being under
the earth at a certain depth. But
as for motion towards a certain point or place
(which is the opinion of the ancients), it is
utterly vain.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*the contraction of a mass or bulk of a*
*body from the mixture of liquid*
*bodies with solid ones.*

34. It is strange that, when the ancients admitted experiments on the faith of others, they were able to build things of great importance upon them. This is one of their most trustworthy observations: They boldly assert that a vessel filled with ashes receives the same quantity of water as if it were empty. But it is plainly false: for it does not absorb a fifth part of the water. I attribute this difference to the ashes being placed more loosely or more tightly; as we see that ashes by themselves and unmixed, if compressed, occupy less space; so also ashes with air are held in a looser space, with water, in a tighter one. I have not yet ascertained whether water itself, with ash or powder mixed in, contracts into a narrower space.

     *Various experiments concerning*
          *purgative medicines.*

   36. The operation of purgative medicines
and their causes have hitherto been reckoned among
the secrets of nature; and therefore the profound
ignorance of men attributes them to an occult
property, a specific virtue, and a fourth quality,
and to similar hiding places of ignorance. The causes
of purgatives are various, all open
and clear, and thoroughly proven by
experience. The first is, whatever
cannot be concocted and digested by the heat of the
stomach, the stomach expels either by
vomiting, or casts down to the intestines, and
the expulsive motion of the stomach and intestines
provokes other parts of the body (such as the orifices
of veins and similar parts) to expulsion
by consent. For nothing in the human
                                                       human

--- Page 75 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 31
human body is a more familiar and more frequent motion than that by consent. A heaviness of the stomach is caused either by the quality or the quantity of the medicine. Quality is of a threefold difference: either it is extreme bitterness, as in Aloe, Colocynth, etc.; or nausea from a most unpleasant and acrid taste, as in Agaric, Black Hellebore, etc.; or a hidden and hostile malignancy to the human body, often not manifesting itself by taste, as in Scammony, Mechoacan, Antimony, etc. It must be observed that if any purgative medicine reveals none of these qualities, a just suspicion of poison is aroused. For it either effects it by corrosion, or by a latent malignancy, and a certain repugnance with nature; and therefore caution must be exercised both in preparing and taking medicines of this kind. Also, the quantity of what is taken excites purgation, as we see in a large quantity of freshly drawn milk, indeed, even in excessively consumed foods; for too eager ingestion of foods often turns into purgation, both through the upper and through the lower parts. Therefore, we generally observe the operation of purgatives to succeed after two or three hours from when the medicines were taken, because the stomach first attempts to digest them.
               B 4               Simi-

--- Page 76 ---
32 FRANCIS BACON
We experience something similar with a stomach too overloaded, or with milk excessively taken.

37. The second cause is a sharp and biting irritation of the orifices in the parts, especially in the mesenteric veins, as it is known that salt or something similar, pricking and biting, inserted into the anus, provokes that part to expulsion; mustard excites sneezing, and whatever is hostile to the eyes with sharpness, moves tears. Therefore, we see all purgatives to be effective by a certain kind of irritation, besides the biting sensation which flatulence causes. And if this irritation exists in the highest degree, it slightly prevails over corrosion from poisons; and this sometimes happens with Antimony, especially if it has been administered to those whose bodies are not filled with humors. For wherever humors abound, there they (the humors) look out for the parts.

38. The third cause is attraction; for I do not deny that there is a power in purgatives which is directed by itself towards attraction, as with attractive plasters in Surgery; as we see crushed sage and betony, sternutatory powder, and other powders or liquids (which Physicians call errhines) taken through the nostrils, draw out phlegm and humors from the head. So also in Apophlegmatisms

--- Page 77 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 33
tisms and gargles are used, which draw out catarrh through the mouth. And this, without a doubt, is the power by which some purgatives draw out this humor, and some another, according to common opinion; as Rhubarb draws out bile, Senna leaves melancholy, Agaric phlegm, etc. Nevertheless, some draw more, others less, indiscriminately. Note also, that besides the sympathy between purgatives and humor, there is another cause why certain medicines draw out a humor agreeable to them more than another. That is, because certain medicines act more quickly than others, and those which act quickly draw out only the thinner and more fluid humors, but those which draw slowly exert their power on the more tenacious and viscous humors. Therefore, caution must be used as to how rhubarb and similar substances should be used, not by themselves, nor without any admixtures, nor habitually. For it quickly carries away the thinner part of the humor, leaving behind a more stubborn mass of humors. Something similar can be said about absinthe, so greatly celebrated.

39. The fourth cause is flatulence; for excited flatulence causes expulsion. And indeed it is found that all purgatives contain within themselves a crude spirit

Various experiments concerning food and drink, especially the most nutritious.

45. We have dealt with the evacuation of the body; now we pass to its repletion from restoratives in consumptions and emaciating diseases. In plants, one part surpasses another in nutritive power. Thus, grains and roots nourish more fully than leaves, so that the order of the Folianati was rejected by the Roman Pope, inasmuch as he considered foliage unsuitable for the nutrition of the human body. Whether the flesh of animals also differs in this way has not yet been duly explored; for example, whether livers and other internal organs nourish more than external parts. Among the Romans, I find that goose liver was a delicacy, to such an extent that they even had means by art to make it both more elegant and larger; but whether it nourishes more fully does not appear. It is known that marrow nourishes more abundantly with fat, and I believe that a decoction from crushed and properly strained bones and sinews is a very nourishing broth. Thus it is also observed that Scotch-
                                        ham

of beef cooked for a long time; also gelatin,

made from the bones of veal. The pulp
in a crab, which is cooked sprinkled with spices and butter,
is more suitable for nourishment

Let them macerate in it for three days and nights, with the opening left open for the process. Then let it be closed, and so let it remain for a day and a half. Afterwards pour it into bottles, and on the third day after pouring, it is drinkable, and it will last for six weeks (experience has taught) and will be drunk lively and flowery and frothy, and it will not be musty. A draught is very beneficial to those wasting away, either by itself or mixed with other beer. It quenches thirst, and is not flatulent. Note, it can hardly happen that food and bread taken in broth or drink (as is customary) immediately reach the veins and extremities as finely and easily as that incorporated in this way, or almost turned into chyle.

     51. It is known that freshly drawn milk possesses great nourishing power; likewise a good remedy for treating emaciation. But, while the cow is being milked, two small bags should be placed in it, one with powdered Mint, the other with powdered red roses. For the milk, in some way, prevents coagulation in the stomach: Add sugar also for the same reason, partly also for the sake of flavor. But it should be taken in a moderate draught, lest it remain long in the stomach and coagulate. Place the cup in which you receive the milk into a larger cup with hot water, so that you may consume it warm. I judge cow's milk, prepared in this way, to be preferable to ass's milk, because (without doubt) the latter is not so easily transformed/digested, but rather acidulous. Mare's milk is more effective against acrimony of the urine, and ulceration of the bladder, and also for all soothing purposes. Woman's milk is also prescribed for other debilitated persons; but I do not consider it among good foods, as it is somewhat too close to the juice of the human body, except for infants, for whom it is natural.

Therefore, if for a consumption which the weakness of the stomach causes, the use of wine must be indulged, it should always be presented burnt (distilled/heated), so that the more volatile spirits may evaporate, or at least be extinguished by two small masses of gold repeated seven times.

A Solitary Experiment concerning
cure by custom.

61. There is also a certain hidden method of treatment, not yet brought into use, derived from habituation to a thing harmful in itself. Poisons have been rendered familiar to some, as has been said. Those who commonly tend to people suffering from the plague are rarely infected by contagion. The toleration of torments from habit renders them lighter. The digestion of immoderate food or wine, when turned into a habit, prevents indigestion and drunkenness. In general, chronic diseases, such as coughs, consumptions, certain types of paralysis, lunacy, etc., are most dangerous in the beginning. And therefore it is for a prudent physician to consider whether the disease is incurable, and whether its exact cure is free from danger. If there is danger, let him resort to palliation, let him alleviate the symptoms, not being too much occupied with a perfect cure: but often this method (provided the patient only has patience) achieves more than opinion would have promised itself; as also if the patient's disposition can overcome the symptoms during a paroxysm, and turn patience into a natural habit.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the cure*
*of diseases which are contrary to the*
*predisposition of the body.*

64. Hippocrates' aphorism, namely 'in diseases less,' etc., contains a good and profound speculation. For it indicates that diseases contrary to the constitution of the body, age, sex, season of the year, and diet are more dangerous than those which are agreeable to these. Someone might, on the contrary, be of the opinion that where the symptom of the disease and the natural disposition, as it were, lend mutual aid, the disease will be more vehement; and there is no doubt about this, assuming a similar quantity of matter. But what the Aphorism asserts is that such diseases indicate a more abundant collection of matter, and thereby can turn natural inclinations to the contrary. Therefore, in such a state of diseases, the physician should aim more for purgation than alteration, since the fault lies in quantity, and the qualities spontaneously return to order.

A solitary experiment concerning pre-
paration before purgation, and the complete

65. It is a wise observation of physicians to
employ preparations before proper purgations;
for it is indeed true that the body is often greatly
harmed if both the things preceding purgation
and those following it are neglected. The harm
from a lack of preparation is the tenacity of
non-fluid humors, and their inconvenient exit;
which causes great disturbances in the body and
adverse accidents while the purgative is at work;
whence the strength of the medicine is dulled and
diminished, so that it does not purge sufficiently.
Therefore, the twofold office of preparation is
to render the humors mature and fluid, and the
ducts more pervious; for both facilitate the exit
of humors. As for the former (rendering humors
mature and fluid), syrups are most beneficial;
for the latter (making ducts more pervious),
decoctions or preparatory broths. Clysters also
ensure that medicines do not stick in the intestines,
and that they do not operate by tearing. But it
is true that bodies full of humors and fatty, and
a clear and serene atmospheric condition are in
themselves preparative, and render humors more
fluid. But let the physician attend to purgations
to be administered during frost,
            C 3

administered in frost, and to lean bodies, unprepared. For whatever harm exists after purging, arises from humors badly obstructed elsewhere; but it is indeed true that some humors fixed in certain parts of the body may rest without harm, while to other parts (especially the ducts) they bring much damage. Therefore, it will be advisable after purging to use decoctions and broths, not so much opening ones, as before purging, but to resort to cleansing and purifying clysters, so that the remnants of humors which could descend to the lower region of the body may be removed.

	*A Solitary Experiment concerning Diet.*

68. Experience dictates that diets strictly instituted from Guaiacum, Sarsaparilla, and similar substances afflict the patient more at the beginning than in the later stages. Hence, most of the more delicate patients stopped in the middle, deceived by the opinion that they would not be able to endure them until the end if the beginnings aroused such great disturbances. But the reason is that such diets dry out humors, catarrhs, and similar things, and they cannot dry them out unless they first attenuate them. And while the humor is attenuated, it becomes more fluid than before, and disturbs the body, until it has been dried out and consumed. Therefore, patients ought to wait a proper space of time, and not be put off by the initial effects.

	*Various Experiments concerning the Pro-*
		*duction of Cold.*

The production of cold is most worthy of inquiry, both on account of its use and the knowledge of its causes. For heat and cold are two hands by which nature principally operates. We have heat readily available, with respect to fire. Cold must be waited for until it ar-
					rives,

--- Page 101 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 57
it arrives, or must be sought in caverns, or on high

we cannot obtain it in the highest degree.
For furnaces heated by fire far surpass the heat of the Sun;
but vaulted places and hills do not greatly excel in the cold of winter frost.

69. The first cause of producing cold
is that which nature supplies to us, namely
a cold exhalation from the inner parts of the earth in
winter, when the Sun is unable to overcome it.
For the Earth (as has been well noted by some)
is primarily cold. Both ancient and modern
Philosophers assert this. Parmenides was of this opinion,
and the author of that discourse in Plutarch
(for I do not acknowledge Plutarch as its author)
concerning the primary cold. Telesius held the same view,
who revived the philosophy of Parmenides,
and among moderns is commended above all.

70. The second cause of cold is the con-
tact of a cold body. For cold is active,
and passes into adjacent bodies, like heat;
which is evident in those things which snow and cold
things touch. Therefore, whoever has devoted himself to the
scrutiny of nature, let him turn his eyes and mind to the conservatories of
snow and ice; such as are held in delight for cooling

in summer time, but that use is not so significant, and should be rejected in preference to others which such conservatories provide.
    71. The third cause is the primary nature of all tangible bodies. For it must be accurately noted that every tangible thing is cold by its nature, unless it has adventitious heat from fire, life, or motion; for even the spirits of wine, or chemical oils, whose power in operation is significant, are cold to the touch, and compressed and condensed air gathers some cold by the breath of the mouth.
    72. The fourth cause is the density of a body; for all dense bodies are colder than most others, such as metals, stones, glass, and they retain heat longer than softer ones. And it is most certain that earth, being dense and tangible, participates in the nature of cold. The reason is that since all material tangible things are cold, necessarily more compact matter imparts cold more intensely.
    73. The fifth cause of cold, or rather that which increases it and renders it more intense, are active and swifter spirits enclosed in a cold body; as various instances will prove to one carefully considering nature. Thus nitre (endowed with an active spirit) is cold, and colder to the tongue than a stone.

But if you wish to achieve hardening with a certain tenacity and less fragility, the method of the physician must be chosen; which Aristotle well noted, but did not approve, namely, that bodies be boiled in water for three or four days. However, it is necessary that the bodies be minimally permeable to penetrating water, such as stones and metals. For if such bodies are those into which water can insinuate itself, prolonged boiling will soften rather than harden, as has been proven in eggs, etc. Therefore, softer bodies must be placed in flasks, and the flasks suspended in boiling water with their openings outside the water, so that water cannot enter. For in this way, the potential heat of the water will enter, and indeed of such a kind that it will by no means render the bodies fragile or burnt, but the substance of the water will remain enclosed. This experiment was once performed by us with such a result. It was found that a fragment of cut stone and tin, placed in abundant water, had absorbed a little water.     *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
        *the Conversion of Water into Air.*

    91. The eye of the intellect is similar
to the eye of sense. For just as large objects

                                                                 nature from

--- Page 115 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I.      71
are clearly visible from humble and lowly instances. The sudden consumption of watery moisture by air, and its conversion into air, is not more conspicuous in any visible things than in the swift resolution and evanescence of a thin cloudlet of exhalation or vapor from glass, and the blade of a sword, and a body polished in that manner, which by no means retains or absorbs moisture; for the misty haze is suddenly dispersed and dissipated. But a similar cloudlet, applied to oily or greasy things, is not dissolved, not because it adheres more tenaciously, but because air consumes water, and flame and fire consume oil. Therefore, for removing spots from grease, they apply charcoal wrapped in blotting paper, because fire acts on fat or oil, as air acts on water. We also see that paper smeared with oil, or wood coated with oil, or something similar, preserves moisture for a very long time, but when moistened with water, dries out or rots more quickly. The cause is, that air mixes with difficulty with oily moisture.

Therefore, perform an experiment, anointing doves or other birds when they are still covered only with down, or even puppies, trimming their hairs as much as possible, or other animals, with an ointment least harmful to the flesh, which may harden and firmly adhere, and see whether the colors of the feathers or hairs are changed. It is also certain that white color results from scarcity and lack of moisture. Thus blue violets and other flowers, when they wither, become pale and white. Age and a scar make birds and horses gray, and the same cause produces gray hairs in man. Therefore it is very likely that the feathers which first emerge in birds are often of diverse color according to the nature of the birds, just as the skin is more porous; but where it is firmer, the feathers come forth white. *A Solitary Experiment concerning the*
     *nourishment of living creatures before*
          *they are brought forth into the light.*
   94. It is a work of providence, most truly observed by some, that the yolk of an egg contributes little to the generation of the bird, but only to its nourishment. For if a newly hatched chick is dissected, you will find many remnants of the yolk; and it is necessary that birds, which are generated outside the womb of females, have in the egg both the material for nourishment and that from which the body is generated. For after the egg is hatched, and separated from the body of the hen, it receives no further nourishment from the hen, but only the vivifying warmth from her incubating. But beasts and man need no internal nourishment, because they are generated within the womb of the female, and are continuously nourished from her body.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the hidden processes of nature.*

98. Human knowledge has hitherto been limited by speculation and sight, so that whatever the eye might perceive, whether because of the thinness of the body, or minute parts, or the subtlety of movement, has been little explored. These things, however, especially govern nature, and with these disregarded, a true analysis cannot be instituted, nor can the processes of nature be indicated. Spirits or pneumatic bodies, which are present in all tangible things, are scarcely known. Sometimes the name of void is given to them, although they are most active in the body. Sometimes they are taken for air, from which they differ wonderfully, as wine from water, [or] wood from earth. Sometimes they suppose them to be natural fire, or a portion of the elemental,

--- Page 121 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 77
...elemental, since some of them exist crude and cold. Sometimes they call them the virtues and qualities of tangible parts, which are known by sight, although they subsist by themselves; when it is a question of plants and animals, they call them souls. They indulge in such superficial speculations, as if a perspective drawing exhibited things in recession, when they are only depicted. Nor does this question rest merely within words, but it has a subject matter infinitely solidified in nature. For spirits are nothing other than natural bodies, proportionally rarefied, enclosed within the tangible parts of bodies as if by a covering. Nor do they differ less among themselves than dense and tangible parts, and they are present in all tangible bodies more or less, and for the most part never cease. From these and their motions principally proceed desiccation, liquefaction, concoction, maturation, putrefaction, vivification, and the principal effects of nature. For as we have described them in the wisdom of the ancients in the fable of Proserpina, in the infernal kingdom you will find few acts of Pluto, but many of Proserpina; since the tangible parts of the body are inert, and the spirits accomplish everything. Regarding the differences of tangible parts in bodies, the industry of chemists has contributed some light, while to separa-

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the Efficacy of Fire.*

99. It is certain that heat is the chief of all faculties, both in the fabric of nature and in the works of art. It is also clear that the effects of heat are most promoted when it exerts its force upon bodies without dissipation or detriment of matter, which confounds theories. And therefore it is true that efficacy can best be perceived in distillations, which are performed in closed vessels and receptacles. But there is nevertheless a certain higher degree: for although distillations preserve bodies in

A Solitary Experiment: Annihilation does not occur.

100. Nothing is more certain in nature than that it is
not possible for any body to be utterly reduced to
nothing: but just as it was the work of God's Omnipotence
to create something out of nothing, so too it is entirely
within omnipotence to destroy. And therefore it was
well said by a certain obscure writer among the
Chemists, that there is no other way of producing
wonderful transmutations of bodies than if in all ways
the reduction to nothing is urged and attempted.
Here is a great secret for preserving a body from
change. For if you can prevent them from turning
into air, because no air can enter, nor from passing
into adjacent bodies, since they are entirely heterogeneous,
nor from completing a circuit within themselves,
they will never change, even if by their nature they are
most perishable and mutable. For we see how flies
or spiders find a more lasting tomb in amber than
the preservation afforded to a royal corpse by balsam.
I feel the same about bodies placed in Mercury. But
then those must be thin, like leaves, and a particle
of paper or membrane. For if they are of greater
thickness, they will alter in their own body—

--- Page 127 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. II. 83
altered, even if they are not consumed. But
more on these things in the section on the conservation
of bodies.

	102. Sounds which constitute tones are
generated by such bodies as consist of
equal parts and pores, so that the
sounds themselves are also equal. Such are produced
by the percussion of metals, as in bells, or

and held in high esteem by Nero, now

is not produced between the plectrum and the
string, but between the string and the air,
just as it is not usually produced between the finger
or a quill and the string in other instruments.

     104. It is worthy of note (and the more so,

106. It is worthy of observation, namely that whatever power is finally ascribed to the number for tempering the notes of a harmony, that power should rather be attributed to the preceding whole number than to the whole number itself; that is, because the sound recurs after six or twelve (notes), so that the seventh or thirteenth accomplishes nothing, but the sixth or twelfth (does); while the seventh and thirteenth are merely the limits and boundaries of the recurrence.

107. In musical harmonies, which are called perfect or semi-perfect, between the unison and the octaves, the fifth is the most perfect of all, then the third; the sixth is more harsh; and in the judgment of the ancients, as well as my own, and others, the fourth, which they call diatessaron. But the tenth, twelfth, or thirteenth, and so on to infinity, are merely recurrences of the preceding ones, namely the third, fifth, and sixth, being distinguished from each other by an octave.

occurs, of which the former immediately precedes the unison, but the latter immediately follows the octave in descent; whence it appears that Harmony requires a just distance of notes.

   109. In musical compositions, if dissonance is not felt with the bass, an intervening dissonance with other parts generates no disturbance, provided that the dissonance of two (notes) is absent, which is most disagreeable. Therefore, the common harmony of four parts consists of an octave, a fifth, and a third with the bass. But that fifth, if you consider the upper voice, is a fourth, and the third, a sixth. The reason is, because the bass strikes more air; but the upper voice overcomes and suppresses (unless the dissonance is very harsh) and obscures a small error. For we see that some of the lower strings of a lute produce no upper sound, nor a mixed one; but only the sound of the bass.

   110. No harmony consists of quarter tones, because perhaps they admit no harmony. For we experience that semitones only sometimes recur. Nevertheless, there are tremulous [*a*] variations and certain gradations of voice and strings in a continuous series from one (note to another).

   111. The causes of sound, whether pleasing or unpleasing to the ears, can be illustrated from those things which either delight or offend the sight. Two things are pleasing to the sight (setting aside the representations of forms, which are only secondary objects, and which only please or displease the memory): colors and order. The delight from colors symbolizes or has agreement with the pleasure which we perceive from one and a simple tone; but the delight from order symbolizes with harmony. Hence we see how much garden-knots in gardens and [a] frets of houses, and any figures rightly proportioned by equality please (such as spheres, pyramids, cones, cylinders), since in unequal things there is only deformity. Both these pleasures, pertaining to the ears as much as to the sight, arise from rightly observed proportion; so that it is certain that Harmony is produced from equality and symmetry. But the proportion of symmetry is difficult and obscure. We will nevertheless attempt something when we deal with tones, in the general inquiry into sounds.

113. In Music, certain figures and tropes occur, very similar to those of Rhetoric; and which correspond to the affections of the mind and other senses. Firstly, division, and the vibration of the voice, of such delight in Music, agrees with the scintillation of light, like the rays of the Moon, while playing and wandering in the waves. Next, the transition from dissonance to consonance, a cause of the greatest sweetness, agrees with those affections which, after certain disturbances, are brought back into order. It is also akin to taste, for which the continuous use of sweetness creates satiety. A slip from a close or cadence exists not unlike the rhetorical figure which is called "beyond expectation"; for it is pleasing to be thus deceived. Repetitions and fugues agree with the rhetorical figure, repetition or traductio of words.

SYLV. SYLVAR. Centur. I. 91
Music's modes cause a great alteration in character. Thus, for a man to be filled with a warlike spirit, to become soft, to be made effeminate, to be rendered serious, lively, and inclined to mercy, etc. The reason is that hearing, by striking, affects more immediately than the other senses, and more incorporeally than smell. For sight and touch have organs which do not afford such obvious and immediate access to the spirits as hearing does. As for smell (which certainly impresses its force immediately upon the spirits, and remains vehement while the object persists), that is a certain communication of breath or vapor from the object emitting the odor. But to harmony, an easy entrance is open, so that, approaching without any mixture and manifest motion, it frequently affects the spirits; and when these have been reduced to an equal order of position, there follows in them no small alteration and motion, even from an object remote at a distance. All these things show that there exists between tones and modulated melodies a certain affinity by their nature with the emotions. For some tones are cheerful, sad, [a] solemn, inclining the mind to mercy and to war; so that it is no wonder that the spirits are altered,

It has been observed, however, that although varied tones variously dispose spirits and from these generate affections conformable to themselves, yet generally, Music nourishes and fosters the primary disposition of the spirits, that which existed before any alteration. It is also known that diverse tones, and songs derived from them, please different nations and people, as experiments show they have a sympathy with their spirits.

_Various experiments concerning tones;_
_and first, the nullity and entity_
_of sounds._

Perspective has been diligently treated up to now, and the nature of sounds has not lacked similar success concerning Music; however, when generally observed, it yields only perfunctory and superficial observations. It is reckoned among the most subtle secrets of nature. My intention is, as I previously mentioned, to add to the inquiry of things immersed in matter, either immaterial things or things participating less in matter; such as that

--- Page 137 ---

Concerning noise. The sky is rotated very rapidly, yet no sound is perceived; although in the dreams of some, it is said to excite the sweetest music. Likewise, the movement of comets and fiery meteors (like a falling star, etc.) produce no sound. If anyone thinks great distance is the reason why sound does not penetrate all the way to us, let him consider that lightning and flashes generated in a space not very distant from us are seen without any sound at all, although they do not occur without percussion and a tearing apart of the air. Winds in the uppermost region of the air move clouds with a movement imperceptible here to us, and pass without sound. Winds blowing lower down on the plain, unless they are violent, produce no sound; these winds, however, are perceived among trees. In general, when winds produce sound, they always do so unevenly, with waxing and waning intensity; sometimes, when they are fiercer, they tremble at their greatest force.
Rain and hail falling even with great force do not make a sound by passing through the air, unless striking the ground, water, houses, or something similar. The rapid course of a river through its channel, if it is deeper, does not affect the hearing, but flows silently.

--- Page 138 ---

the slipping of water in shallow, sandy, or stony places, is heard.
Water dashed against the shore, or compressed in narrow places
(as in its flow under bridges), or dashed by winds, produces
a resounding sound. A beam or any solid body propelled by another
contiguous one without collision, lacks sound. So also, balanced
bodies placed mutually upon each other, even if the upper depresses
the lower, produce no sound. Thus, the movement of minute
particles in solid bodies (the principal cause of violent motion,
hitherto unobserved) is accomplished without sound. For that
sound sometimes noted is produced only by the breaking of the air,
not truly by the impulse of the particles. It is also clear that
wherever the front body yields, with the rear one succeeding,
no sound is rendered, even if the motion is very great and very swift.

But wherever air is enclosed and compressed, there a breath,
producing only a light percussion by exciting, suffices for sound;
as in pipes and pneumatic instruments.
