120. It is rumored in popular discourse that a certain white powder is found for exploding weapons without sound. It is certainly a dangerous thing, if it be true, since it would be useful for secret murders. But it seems to me that it cannot happen that air, expelled and compressed, should rush into the open without sound. As for the white powder (provided a means of extinguishing and removing sound is found), it seems to consist of a certain mixture of saltpeter and sulfur without charcoal; for saltpeter catches fire by itself. If anyone thinks that sound can be abolished and extinguished by the air exploded while enclosed, before it reaches the mouth of the cannon and the open air, he conceives things that reason escapes, since they ought to produce sounds all the more distinct. Just as if a transverse tube were hollowed out in the barrel of a gun, it could emit various sounds, both through the front opening and from the sides. But my mind dictates to me, if such a thing could be brought about, that the air around the mouth of the cannon would not be compressed, and the ball would fly out with little or no sound.

Secondly, if there is no enclosed air from which an impact into the open air might occur, the cause of sound is lacking; nor, nevertheless, will the ball cease from its forward motion; since that motion (which has been repeated several times) inheres in the parts of the ball, not of the air; which we are taught by experiment, if a small hollow metal object is taken, to be filled with gunpowder, and a ball is placed on its opening, with half of itself standing out into the open air.

So far, these things are undoubtedly true, if that efficacy can be reconciled to mirrors, which the burning of the fleet made famous among the ancients. The mere percussion of air from such mirrors will produce no sound; no differently than flashes of lightning and sheet lightning without thunder.

125. It is acknowledged that no motion is initially produced, unless a local motion of air or flame, or some such intervening medium, intervenes, and that with a certain resistance, whether in the air or in the body. For if there is mere yielding, no sound is produced, as we said before, and in that, sounds differ from light and colors, which pass through the air, or another body, without local motion of air, whether at the beginning or afterwards. But it must be accurately distinguished between the local motion of air (merely the vehicle of the cause) and the sounds themselves carried through the air. As for the former, it is clear that no sound is generated (not even from the impulse of air into air, as in organs, etc.) unless with a perceptible blast of air, and some resistance of the air struck; just as all speech (which is the gentlest motion of air) occurs by a slight expulsion of breath; and pipes produce both a blast and a sound. We also perceive that sounds are carried by the wind, which, being favorable, allows them to be heard at a longer distance than when adverse, and likewise they are raised and lowered with the intensity and remission of the wind.

But the impression of sound is entirely different,
which plainly lacks a perceptible local motion of air,
and in that respect is not unlike visible species.
For after the ringing [a] of something and the sound
of a bell, local motion in the air cannot be discerned
as long as the sound is heard, but only at the beginning.
Nor does the wind (however far it may carry the voice)
confuse any delicate, tender, and articulated figurations
of the air, in such a variety of words, with its own motion.
And if someone speaks with a loud voice against
a candle flame, it will not excite a great tremor in it;
but most of all, when letters are pronounced for which
the mouth is contracted, such as f and s, or certain others.
But a gentle breath and an inarticulate puff will
move the candle much more; which more easily proves
that sound occurs without any local motion of the air,
since just as it differs from sight in that sight requires
local motion of the air at the beginning; so sound in
many other respects agrees with sight and the radiation
of visible things, which undoubtedly impart no local
motion to the air, as already stated.

127. The ancients recorded, and it gained belief among others, that very great applause and acclamations of people gathered in a dense crowd so rarefied and disrupted the air that birds flying overhead fell down, and the air was not able to sustain them. It was also believed by many that violent sounds of bells in populous cities repelled thunder, and by that means dispersed pestilential air; all of which a concussion, not sound, can effect.

128. A huge sound, carried from nearby, made many deaf, who at that very moment felt a membrane as if ruptured in their ears. To me also, while I was standing near something ringing loudly and sharply, sudden harm was inflicted, as if some rupture or dislocation had occurred in my ears; and a little later, a sonorous ringing arose (not a common singing or whistling, but much clearer and different) so that I feared deafness. But after a quarter of an hour it vanished. This effect can most truly be attributed to sound.

  131. Just as a completely round receptacle preserves sound, so too does a semi-concave one, but to a lesser degree, that is, proportionally less.     134. Take some silver vessel, and another of wood, both full of water; then strike the arms of the tongs, as before, a hand's breadth from the bottom; you will find the sound from the silver vessel clearer than from the wooden one. Hence, besides that observation of great importance, that no sound is produced from air, two things can be gathered from this: first, that sound is communicated to the bottom of the vessel, and second, that such communication passes better through water than through air.

      137. His ignorance would not be excusable, who would think (as we partly said before) that the sounds of strings are produced between the hand and the strings, or the plectrum and the strings, or the bow and the strings, since these are only vehicles of motion, by which sound is created; the sound otherwise truly arising between the string and the air, not however from the impulse of air made by the first motion of the string, but from the return or rebound of the string to its original place, after being tensed by the touch of a finger. That rebound motion is swift and sharp, while the former [motion] is soft and dull; thus the plectrum continuously strains the string, and for that reason makes it vibrate perpetually.

Various experiments concerning the magni-

   138. If someone blows a whistle into one end of a pipe, and an ear is applied to the other end, such a sharp impact of sound will be felt that it can scarcely be tolerated. The cause is the circular diffusion of sound, which, though otherwise dispersed through the air, if confined by a channel, will necessarily generate a greater sound. In this experiment, it is to be noted that by confining receptacles, sounds are not only preserved, but also increased and sharpened.
   139. A hunting horn, wider at one end, will intensify the sound more than if the opening were entirely uniform. The reason is that the air, having first entered narrower spaces, is compressed, then, having reached larger ones, it pours itself into a wider exit and expands itself. And in its exit, striking more air, consequently it becomes more powerful and deeper. Therefore, hunting horns, which are sometimes made straight and not curved, always open wider towards the lower parts. An experiment could be made with pipes wider below, or with some chamber, then tapering into a straight cavity.

141. The bells of hawks, with openings open at the sides,

penetrates more, the same (air) being denser at night, it is contained.

     144. Sounds are reflected in two ways,
either at a distance, which is called Echo, where
the original voice and its reflection are distinctly
perceived, about which we will speak later;
or in concurrence, when the reflecting sound
(for the reflection arises from nearby) returns
immediately after the original, and therefore
is not repeated, but rendered ampler.
Hence Music is found to be more sonorous in waters,
and in rooms having panelled rather than draped

     145. The strings of a lute or a pandura, or

communication of the upper air with the lower,
which by closing prevents the diminution or
dispersion of both.

    149. When the string of a bow is struck, with the horns (of the bow) applied closer to the ear, it increases the sound and raises the pitch of the tone. The reason is, because the sensory organ is struck by the compression, before the air is dispersed. The same also happens if a horn is held by the teeth. But this is a manifest transmission of sound from the teeth to the organ of hearing, on account of the great communication between these two; which is evident even from this, that a harsh and rough tone dulls the teeth. The same happens if the horn of the bow is applied to the temples. But here it is only a slipping of sound from there to the ear.
    150. An iron or brass rod, with one part applied to the ear and the other struck, will produce a much greater sound than if a similar impulse were given to a rod not so contiguous to the ear. From these and certain other instances, partly already mentioned, it appears that sounds are not only conveyed along the surface of a smooth body, but are also communicated to the spirits residing in the pores of the body.

**156.** In a lyre and other musical instruments, if the strings are pressed with fingers placed high [a] (whereby it happens that [b] less space is left for them to vibrate), a sharper sound is produced, but one that fades more quickly.

**157.** Take two cups, and strike the rim of one against the bottom of the other in a jar containing water, and by experiment it will be established that the deeper you immerse them in water, the duller the sound produced, even if part of the other remains out of the water. If the whole is submerged in water, it will produce a clearer sound, but lower and more muffled, as if carried from a distance.

162. If bellows inserted into the mouth of a drum are inflated, and then the drum is struck, it renders the sound a little more obscure, without any manifest alteration. The cause is clear, because it both impedes the exit of the sound, and renders the air compressed by the blast unfit for motion.

Therefore, the vehemence of percussion generates clarity and fineness of sounds, as in a stronger and gentler percussion, in a more intense and more relaxed blowing of horns, in a stronger or gentler striking of a bell, etc. The vehemence or intensity of percussion depends more or less on the hardness of the body struck, or on the strength of the striking body. For a cloth struck sounds less, wood more, metal so much more strongly; and among metals, the sound of gold, as being more flexible, if struck, is duller, silver or bronze more ringing; but air, if strongly compressed anywhere, equals a hard body, which the sound excited by the explosion of a cannon proves. *Solitary Experiments concerning sharper and graver sounds, and Musical ones.*

178. It is evident that when a greater quantity of air
is struck, the sound is grave; when a lesser, acute.
The striking of a greater quantity is due to the
magnitude of the striking body, the width of the
hollow space which the sound passes through, and its
length. Hence hypate is graver than nete; flutes for
grave sounds have larger holes than those for acute
sounds. And these flutes and similar instruments
produce a graver sound, the further the holes are
removed downwards, and the further they are from the
opening; and the nearer to the opening, the more acute.
Moreover, a solid body, such as [a] an andiron struck
at the top will produce a more acute sound; in the
lower parts, a graver one.
179. It is also clear that the sound is more acute,

a] as an Andiron of Brass.

sound, the sharper and faster the percussion of air is; and the graver, the slower it is. We observe the same in strings, which, the more taut and twisted (whence a faster vibration), the sharper the sound that arises. Thus, a thicker string more taut, and a thinner string less taut, produce the same sound.

180. Boys, women, and eunuchs emit thinner and sharper voices than men: the reason is, not because these (men) have a larger head, whence a stronger voice might emerge (for the effectiveness of voice or sound matters for differences in clarity or softness, but very little for differences in pitch), but a more dilated organ; heat also contributing to the dilation, as is certainly established. But the reason why the years of puberty change the voice, more escapes us. It seems that this happens because, with much of the body's fluid, by which parts were previously more fully irrigated, being driven to the seminal vessels, heat begins to abound in the body, which renders the passages more dilated; since all the effects of heat occur, such as hairiness, roughness of the skin, and hardness of the skin.

Various experiments concerning inner and outer sound.

Moreover, there is another difference of sound, which
we call inner and outer, which is neither
low nor clear; neither deep nor high-pitched;
neither musical nor unmu-
sical; although it is true that the in-
ner sound does not possess the power of
generating a tone; but on the contrary,
the outer sound may or may not be musical.
And therefore we will rather devote our effort
to enumeration than to exact distinction;
even if (to some extent to outline our
opinion) the inner sound is for us more truly
an impulse, or a bruising of air, than
an elision or cutting of the same; so that percussion
differs less with respect to the other, just as a blow
[differs] from a cut.
188. In human speech, a whisper, whether

Various experiments concerning articulated sounds.

192. It is evident, and also reckoned among the most admirable secrets of sounds, that sound, undiminished in any part of itself, is dispersed through the entire air, and adheres whole even to the smallest particles of air; so much so that the skillfully articulated diversity of sounds, both from humans and from birds, passes unconfused even through the narrowest crack.

193. Unequal agitation of winds, and similar things, even if, by carrying it to more or less distant places, they provide a vehicle for sound, nevertheless disturb the distinctions of sounds very little within that space where they can be perceived; although perhaps they are the cause why they are heard less far than in a calm sky; as partly said before.

194. Excessive distance confuses articulated sounds, as is evident from the fact that, perceiving the voice of a preacher or similar, you cannot distinguish the speech, and one articulated sound is confused with another, as happens when many speak at once.

195. In that experiment, if someone under

water emits a voice, a faint voice is rendered; but so that articulated sounds of words may be distinguished, as we said before.
   196. Thus I conclude that a sound extremely faint, or extremely deep, cannot be articulated; but the articulation of words requires a moderate sound; because both excessive thinness of sound confuses articulation by contraction, and excessive intensity by dispersion. And although (as said in the preceding sections) articulated sound can entirely be contracted after production in the passage through a narrow fissure, nevertheless, prior articulation requires a greater dimension.
   197. Observation has taught that a preacher in a place or chapel vaulted above and below cannot be heard as conveniently as in other places. The reason is, because subsequent sounds arrive before preceding sounds vanish; and therefore articulated sounds are more confused, even if the quantity of sound is greater.
   198. The movements of the tongue, lips, throat, palate, etc., which serve for the varied pronunciation of the letters of the alphabet, are worthy of inquiry, and pertain to the present investigation of sounds. But since they are subtle and require a long description, we deem them to be omitted, and
                                       among

among the experiments of speech to be recounted.
The Hebrews showed diligence, designating which letters were labial, dental, guttural, etc. But the Latins and Greeks applied a distinction between semivowels and mutes, and among the mutes they made others slender, middle, and aspirated; nor in vain, but not precisely enough. For the special movements and impulses, from which the formation of these sounds arises, were investigated too little diligently; as for instance, that the letters B, P, F, M cannot be expressed except by contraction of the mouth or by closing the mouth; that the letters N and B cannot be pronounced without the letter N being changed into M, as Hecatonba becomes Hecatomba; that M and T cannot be uttered unless P intervenes, as emtus is pronounced emptus, and many similar cases. So much so that by applying themselves more deeply to this investigation, they will discover that fewer movements are required for the formation of the entire alphabet than there are letters.
   199. The lungs, of all parts of the body, are most spongy, and therefore are most suitable for contraction and dilation. When contracted, they expel air, which, passing through the trachea, throat, and mouth, forms the voice; but articulation requires the aid of the tongue, palate, etc., which are called instruments of voice.

    200. A certain kinship has been observed

animate bodies, and to attend to the cause of the conformity
of that similarity; and thus the
notion of that effect will become clear.

Various experiments concerning the movements
of sounds in any line, circular,
oblique, straight, upwards, downwards,
forwards, backwards.

201. All sounds, whatever kind
they may be, move in a circle;
that is, in all directions, up-
wards, downwards, forwards, backwards;
which all instances demonstrate.
202. Sounds do not require to be conveyed in a straight
line to the sense, as
visible things do, but it can be curved; although
it is true that they move most strongly through a straight
line. Yet this is not due
to the straightness of the line, but to the shorter
interval; for a straight line is the shortest.
Hence if someone from the other side of an intervening wall's
part

--- Page 180 ---
136          OF FRANCIS BACON
side utters a voice, it can be heard from the other; not because the voice penetrates by passing through the wall, but because, being arched, it ascends beyond the wall.
     203. A sound stopped and reflected will reach the other side along an oblique line. Thus, if a curtain is lowered on one side of a carriage and raised on the other, if someone begging speaks to the closed side, he will seem to be standing at the open, not the covered, side. Also, a small bell or a large bell, for example, placed on the northern side of a room, and a window on the southern, he who is in the room will perceive the sound as if from the south.
     204. Although the movement of sounds is in a circle (for indeed a circle or spherical area is given to them), it is nevertheless most vehement, and is carried furthest along the front lines, and by the first local impulse of air. And therefore the voice of a preacher is more conveniently perceived from directly in front of the pulpit than behind or at the sides, even if it is open. So also a musket or a cannon will be heard further forward from the region of its muzzle than backward, or to the sides.
     205. It might be questioned whether sounds move better upwards than downwards. Pulpits are erected and stand out; and Empero-

--- Page 181 ---

Emperors of old, when about to address the army, would ascend a platform made of turf, because a voice from [a] the level ground would encounter obstacles for listeners and for the speaker, who was equally low. But something of greater moment seems to be at play. For it might be that the spiritual species (or forms) of both visible things and sounds are moved more easily downwards than upwards. It is strange that a person standing on the ground sees those who are on the top of St. Paul's as of smaller stature, and cannot distinguish them; whereas the contrary happens to one looking down from the summit, where neither is the stature so much contracted, nor does all distinction entirely vanish. It is certain, however, that to one standing on high, the objects below appear diminished in appearance and in a more compact form; just as topiaries offer themselves more pleasingly to one looking down from above.

Various Experiments concerning the Duration
and Evanescence of Sounds, and the Time
necessary for their Generation and Transmission.

207. The production of sound is momentary,
between which and its decay a short space of time intervenes.
And here a strange error of men is detected,
of those who consider that to be a continuation of sound, which
is nothing other than a renewal. For the percussion of the body
imparts a vibration to its minute parts, and thus
renews the percussion of the air. You may clearly infer
this from the fact that the dying sound of a struck bell
or string, which is considered a continuation, completely
ceases, as soon as the bell or string feels a hand
laid upon it, as in harpsichords, where the damper
falls and touches the string, the sound ceases. Also, if a
small bell is touched after being struck, the sound ceases.
Here a twofold vibration must be distinguished:
one manifest and local, as in a hanging bell; the other
hidden, of minute parts, such as is described in the 9th
instance. But it is true that from the local [vibration] there
                                                              accrues

--- Page 183 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. III. 139
aid comes to the occult. We also see in
pipes and other wind instruments, the sound dying with the blast. Nor are we
ignorant that, where there is an illusion, a confused murmur wanders in the
organs for a time, while the bellows, namely, previously inflated, subside.

208. It is certain that the sound of a war engine, which has laid low many,
can be carried over at least twenty miles on land; much farther on sea; which
will reach the ears, not at the very moment of the explosion, but after an hour
or much later. Necessarily this is a continuation of the former sound, since no
vibration is detected from which it could be renewed, nor will contact with the
engine extinguish the sound more quickly; so that in greater sounds the
continuation is more than momentary.

209. However, in order that the time in which sound is carried may be
exactly observed, let someone ascend a pyramid or a lighthouse, having taken a
torch, to which a veil may be held before it; let another stand at the distance
of a mile. Then let him strike a bell, and at the same moment of percussion let
the veil be removed. The other, standing in the field, let him determine the
interval of time from the counted pulses of the artery, between the shining
light and the perception of the sound; since it is certain that light is carried
in a moment.

--- Page 184 ---
140          FRANCIS BACON'S
carried instantaneously. The same experiment could be tried at a longer distance, with the magnitude of light and sound proportioned to it.
     210. It is known to all from observation that an object of sight moves faster than one of hearing; since the flash of a cannon is perceived sooner by the eyes than its sound by the ears; which also usually happens in splitting wood, where, standing a little distance away, one will see the hand raised for the second blow before one has heard the sound from the first; and the greater the distance, the greater the anticipation; just as the flash of thunder, very far removed from us, precedes the crash by a considerable interval.
     211. When colors present themselves to the eyes, they are not accustomed to fading or diminishing gradually and by degrees, but a continuous vigor and efficacy persists, while sounds gradually perish: the reason is that colors do not participate as much as sounds do with the motion of the air; and that sound communicates somewhat with its local motion (as a necessary condition) is also evidenced by the fact that it perishes so quickly; since the cut and impelled air is continuously restored and reunites itself, which also happens in water, but not with equal speed.

Various experiments concerning the passages and interceptions of sounds.

In exploring the passages of sounds, or conversely, you must observe lest in any body an exit to the side deceive you for a straight passage through. Therefore, the intercepting body must be closed very tightly, since sound escapes even through the narrowest crack.

212. Wherever sound passes through a solid and well-closed body (such as water, a wall, metal, as in stopped bells, etc.), it is necessary that that solid body be thin and slender, lest it completely extinguish the sound. Likewise, when someone speaks underwater with the help of air, the voice must not be too suppressed underwater, so that it can penetrate. So also if a voice is uttered towards the other side of a closed wall, excessive thickness will prevent it from being heard on the other side of it. Imagine a barrel to be empty, with sides two feet thick, and its opening closed; I conceive that the resonance from the communication of the exterior air with the interior will be faint, or no sound at all; with only the perceptible noise of the exterior percussion, as if the vessel were full.

213. It is certain that for sounds passing through solid bodies, the spirit or parts cooperate...

--- Page 186 ---

pneumatic parts of that body. But
this will be observed much more accurately if the sides of a hard
body are struck, than if they are struck from within, without an impact on the sides.
Therefore, take a bell, whose holes are stopped up,
and let it be suspended in a glass flask, the mouth of the glass being very tightly closed with wax.
Then, shaking the glass, observe whether the sound of the

Various experiments as to how much the shapes of pipes or cavities, or of the bodies conveying [sound], contribute to the production of sounds.

   How much the shapes of pipes, or of the cavity through which sound passes, or of the bodies conveying [sound], contribute to the variety and alteration of sounds; whether a greater or lesser quantity of air received in the cavity is considered; or the space through which sound is conveyed more briefly or more lengthily, or other circumstances, we have treated under other headings. Here, a place is due to examining shapes, which I conceive as lines through which sounds pass. Such are straight, oblique, angular, circular, etc.
   221. The shape of a bell is not unlike a pyramid, except that its outline and expansion, as it were, slope down and expand more quickly. The shape of hunting horns and flutes is oblique. Straight horns are also found with as many oblique holes, but with a moderate difference in sound; except that straight ones are blown more forcefully. The shapes of flutes and pipes are straight; but these consist of a smaller and larger hole above and below. The trumpet has the shape of the letter S, by which that shrill sound is produced. In general, a straight shape

Furthermore, solid bodies of various shapes should be tested by their percussions, such as spherical, flat, cubic, cross-shaped, triangular, etc. Let there also be a combination of them; flat against flat; convex against convex; and convex against flat; and let the differences in sounds be accurately noted. Also to be explored are sounds produced by hard bodies of various thicknesses. I have experienced that the sound of a golden bell is excellent, not inferior to silver or bronze, indeed better. **Various Experiments concerning the Reflection of Sounds.**

There are three kinds of reflections in sounds: concurrent reflection, iterative reflection (which is Echo), and super-reflection (an Echo from a previous Echo). The former having been discussed under the title of the magnitude of sounds, the two latter are now to be treated.
242. The reflection of emanations from visible objects can be directed by means of mirrors, inasmuch as these, having emanated and advanced in straight lines, can be brought to some point; but the reflection of sounds hardly allows itself to be governed, because sound more loosely occupies space in curved lines.

--- Page 201 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. III. 157
...filling space with curved lines, does not admit such a control, hence the method of preparing artificial echoes has not yet come into use; and whatever Echo has hitherto become known does not admit a reflection in a narrow place.
   243. Natural Echo is generated in walls, wood, rocks, hills, and banks. Water, however, where it is nearby, creates a concurrent Echo; where it is far distant, it produces an iterative one. For concurrent and iterative Echo are distinguished in no other way than by the swiftness or slowness of the reflection. But it is beyond controversy that just as water promotes the transmission of the original sound, so it serves for the Echo to be carried further.
   244. It has been said in previous [sections] that when a voice is uttered through a body permeable to sounds, with one end of it stopped, the return of a breath can be felt at the mouth, but not a sound: the reason is that the preservation of the original sound by means of the obstruction does nothing for the preservation of the reflected [sound]; moreover, the generation of echoes, unless from clear sounds, is altogether rare.

--- Page 202 ---
**158 OF FRANCIS BACON**
It should be tested whether speech sent into hollows, with no other return path than that by which the voice descends, generates an Echo just as in wells.

245. Echo travels circularly in the air, like the primary sound; whence it would be expedient to explore whether repercussion from a body about to form an angle would create an Echo, like the return towards a wall, etc. as we see in mirrors a similar angle of incidence is given from the object to the glass, and from the glass to the eye, and if you strike a ball transversely, not on the surface, an equal rebound will occur. Whether Echo also produces this effect (that is, whether someone standing at the side of the reflecting body hears better, or indeed where the voice is uttered, or anywhere in a straight line) could be tested; likewise if he stands closer to the place of repercussion than the speaker, or vice versa. At the same time, it would come to be known whether Echo, like the original and primary sound, is stronger nearby.

246. There are many places creating various forms of echo, of which one follows another and is received. That happens where various hills or shrubs exist, dissimilar to each other, whether nearby or distant; so that the very last return also happens to be perceived by the ears.

Various experiments concerning the agreement and disagreement between those things which are perceived by sight and hearing.

255. Both spread themselves circularly, and fill a whole orb, but not beyond certain and determined limits of progression; they languish and gradually die out according to the proportionate distance of objects from the sensory organs.

256. Both sustain an entire and undiminished species/form, and insinuate themselves into any minute parts of the air and the medium; and just as species/images introduce themselves unconfusedly through narrow cracks and pass through, as is evident, in the indicator of the instrument of equilibrium as regards sight; and in fissures and cracks as regards sounds.

257. Of both, the sudden and easy generation and propagation, with equal swiftness of vanishing, namely, when light is removed, and bodies emitting sound (are removed).

258. Both receive and carry with them exquisite and accurate differences, such as colors, figures, motions, distances in visible things; the tones of articulate voices, songs, vibrations in audible things.

259. Both seem to pour forth nothing of a corporeal effluvium into the medium, by which it might complete the sphere of its activity, nor is there eviden-

--- Page 208 ---
164      OF FRANCIS BACON
nor evidently to impress a local motion upon the medium through which it passes, but merely to carry away spiritual propagations with them. The cause of this phenomenon, since the diligence of investigators has not hitherto fully applied itself to it, will deserve examination in its proper place.
   260. Both appear to be generative of no effect, except for that which is appropriated to their object and sense; and apart from that, everything else seems sterile.
   261. But both, by their own proper action, manifestly produce three effects: the first, that a species more (so to speak) quantitative and of greater impression subdues a lesser and weaker one, as sunlight subdues the light of a glow-worm, or the roar of a cannon subdues a voice. The second, that any object in excess and overwhelming destroys the sense, as sunlight destroys the eye, or a violent sound near the ear destroys hearing. The third, that both admit repercussion, as in mirrors and Echo.
   262. Neither destroys or hinders the species of the other, even if encountered in the same medium, just as light or color does not remove sound, or vice versa.
   263. Both affect living beings by objects moving the senses in diverse ways, depending on whether they have been pleasing or displeasing; which however,

--- Page 209 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. III. 165
which however, if rightly attended to, also affect inanimate things, namely having a certain conformity with the organs of both senses. Thus visible objects operate in mirrors, which are not unlike the pupil in the eye; and audible objects in echo-generating places, which resemble the concavity and structure of the ear.

   264. The actions of both vary according to the varied disposition of the medium. Thus a trembling medium (such as smoke) imparts trembling to the object; and, being capable of intensity and remission, it raises and lowers sound.

   265. Air is a most convenient and favorable vehicle for both; for water or glass cannot compare with it.

   266. *Differences of those things which are perceived by sight and hearing.*

268. The species (images/forms) emanating from visible objects seem to be certain emissions of the rays constituting them; such as something that happens in widely propagated odors; except that those (species) are carried more separated from the body, and the species striking the hearing (ear) communicate more with local motion, as if impressions made in the air, and its percussions; thus whatever is corporeal, when it exerts its action in a twofold manner, either by really communicating its nature, or motion, the former diffusion is to be assigned to visible things, the latter to audible things.

269. The conveyance through the air is more manifest for audible things than for visible things, since the barrier of a struggling wind does not greatly (in my opinion) impede the perception of these (visible things), while in those (audible things) the contrary happens in their conveyance.

270. This above all must be noted, the diffe-

--- Page 211 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. III. 167
difference between the objects of sight and hearing, from which other differences of lesser importance flow; namely, that those (with the exception of light) are carried in straight lines, these in curves; which mode of diffusion least incurs the inconveniences of mixture or confusion, as we said before that sounds are subject to these. Hence the solidity of bodies hardly creates an impediment to vision, provided they are transparent, with pores turned towards straight lines, as in glass, crystal, diamond, water, etc. However, a thin veil or handkerchief, although less solid bodies, obstruct sight, while on the contrary porous [materials] offer little impediment to hearing, but solid ones either stop or rather attenuate [sound]. Hence also, for reflecting the rays of visible things, small mirrors suffice, but for the reverberation of sounds, larger spaces are required; which was not omitted by us in the preceding [sections].

271. Visible things present themselves to the sense at a longer distance than sounds, with the proportion of magnitude preserved, whereas to a more remote interval a more intense sound may spread than a tiny body can be seen.

Various experiments concerning the sym-

   278. All consonance and dissonance in music is nothing other than the antipathy and sympathy of sounds, also in that music which they call broken, or associated. From the blending sounds of certain instruments, the combination of these exists more pleasingly, one with another (a matter hitherto not sufficiently diligently observed), as the Irish lyre is best joined with a barbiton of a deeper tone, and the pipe with music to be played on strings; organs do not reject accompanying singing voices, etc. But harpsichords and the lute, or the Welsh-British lyre and the Irish lyre, deny that a solo voice can properly blend with pipes. But many things remain to be brought back to experiment regarding the refined conjunction of instruments, from which a great addition would be made to the grace of more refined music.

Various experiments concerning impediments and aids to hearing.

283. Yawning impedes the sense of hearing, because of the stretching of the membrane in the ear, which repels sound rather than admits it.
284. Retention of breath makes for more exact hearing, than if the contrary happens; and

The reason is that every exhalation is a movement repelling outwards rather than attracting sound; and whenever we apply ourselves more diligently to a task, and with a vehement intensity of effort, we, as it were, hold the breath drawn inwards; and every more difficult capture of a sound escaping the hearing is a kind of effort.

285. For the aid of hearing, let an instrument be made in the manner of a funnel, concerning whose good success I do not despair. I have understood that something similar has been devised by the Spanish, which, applied to the ears, facilitates hearing for the hard of hearing.

Various experiments concerning the spiritual and subtle nature of sounds.
287. The repercussion of sounds (called Echo) strongly demonstrates the spiritual essence of sound. For if it were corporeal, the generation of the secondary sound or repercussion would be the same, as regards the manner and instruments, as that of the primary: But the pronunciation of words requires various and exquisite instruments, which no structure of a similar kind recognizes for their return; but a mere impediment, whence repercussion arises.
288. For seals serve impressions excellently, to which the first generation of sounds exhibits something analogous, but their transmission and continuation, without a distinct imprint, exclude them from the category of impressions.

A Solitary Experiment concerning
Splendid Colors in the Dissolution
of Metals.

291. The dissolutions of metals exhibit vivid and pure colors; gold a remarkable yellow, mercury an exceedingly green, tin an intense blue. The same is observed in their putrefactions or rust, such as minium, green color, Bise, cissus, etc., and also in vitrifications. The reason is that their hardness is due to enduring fire or strong acids, and they can be held in a uniform arrangement; they also retain part of their principal spirit. These two, namely, uniform arrangement and agile spirit, are primary in rendering colors bright.

A Solitary Experiment concerning
the Prolongation of Life.

292. If such liberty shall have been established for human actions, that they undertake nothing *invita Minerva* (against their natural genius), but are urged on by their genius, the prolongation of life will rely on the best aids. To this contributes a gentler motion of the spirits, so that, being less predatory, they do not so much consume the body's vital fluid. Then actions are to be circumscribed by rules and moderation, exercised in

For victory and a not vain opinion of command generate the best disposition for the spirits, especially when a gradual process is instituted, where the sense of victory is more vigorous. The former example is provided by rustic life; the latter, by the institutions of Monks, and those who have wholly applied themselves to cultivating Philosophy, and who continually master themselves.

*A solitary experiment regarding the ap-petite for union in bodies.*

293. All bodies have an appetite for uniting themselves, and avoid the solution of continuity; and of this appetite, various degrees are given, but the three most worthy of observation, and which can be distinctly noted, are: The first in liquids, the second in solids, the third in glutinous and tenacious bodies. Of these, liquids exhibit this appetite but faintly, conspicuous in the connection as if by threads in dripping water, where they conglomerate into round drops (this is a kind of union), and where they persist for some time in bubbles and foam. The appetite of the second degree is more ardent in iron, stone, wood, etc. The third remains in the middle, on the border of both the former, where bodies partly adhere, being compliant to the contact of another; partly H 6 len-

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the diverse operations of Fire and Time.*

295. Some things, having undergone fire, first soften, then harden, as the crumb of bread; some things fire hardens, afterwards softens, as the crust of bread, biscuit, sweet-meats, salt, etc. The reason is, that in those things which are hardened by time, the operation of fire is a certain kind of liquefaction. But in those things which are softened by time, the operation of fire is a certain kind of concoction, and all things thoroughly cooked by fire, time in some way dissolves.

*A solitary experiment concerning the*
*incorporation of powders and*
*liquids.*

298. You would see most powders cohere more tightly when water is mixed in than with oil, although oil is a thicker body, like flour, etc. The reason is from the affinity of bodies, which, the greater it is, makes for a more perfect imbibition and incorporation. And this (affinity) exists more greatly in most powders with water than with oil: however, painters' colors and ashes are better incorporated with oil.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*bodily exercise.*

299. Frequent movement and exercise is beneficial to some bodies, to others, rest or gentler movement. To a warm body which does not abound in humors, excessive agitation causes harm; and in this, physicians err—

--- Page 228 ---
184        FRANCIS BACON
Physicians [err], that they encourage men of such a bodily constitution to exercises, which will be harmful to them, living on a stricter diet. But with increasing exercises, a fuller diet should correspond; and for those more sparing in food, such should also be the exercise; whose advantages are these: First, that it transmits nourishment more to the parts to be nourished; then, through sweats, it facilitates excretion, whence a more perfect assimilation in the parts; third, that it renders the body more solid and compact, and less subject to predatory spirits. The opposite evils are: that it inflames the spirits, makes them predatory; that it absorbs and too much attenuates the body's humidity; that it too much shakes the internal parts, especially violent exercise, which rather enjoy quiet. In general, if exercise is too much, it is adverse to the prolongation of life; whence women are longer-lived than men, because they move less.

Various experiments pertaining to the clarifi-
cation of liquids, and the
acceleration thereof.

[Large decorative initial V] It is observed that to anticipate by art the time of nature working in accelerating its effects, is deservedly to be reckoned among the Great Works of Nature. Moreover, and indeed, after the creation of matter from nothing, that retraction, as it were, of time in advance, approaches divinity in the second place. Therefore, to explore these inner recesses, the labor of our inquiry proceeds; setting aside for another place the acceleration of germination, for which we reserve a general treatise on Plants. Now we will pursue accelerations engaged in other matters.

301. Very many liquids, permeating their whole
substance, at first exhibit dregs, being turbid,
such as must, beer not sufficiently boiled,
or

SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IV. 187
or chyle of beer, expressed juices of shrubs and herbs, etc. Waters, over time, when they have settled, are allowed to clarify. To achieve this more quickly than usual, however, is among those things which most commend themselves by their own significance. For by applying stimuli, we impel nature, into whose order we thus invade, perverting it. That thing also has an excellent use in drink, in the speedy preparation of potables and condiments, and other things pertaining to the same. But it is necessary to preface the productive causes of clarification before understanding the aids promoting it. Separation provides the first cause, by which the somewhat thicker parts of the liquid are separated from the thinner ones. The second is the equal distribution of spirits in liquids along with their tangible parts; which, by itself, is also effective in making bodies appear non-turbid. The third is the attenuation of the spirits themselves, from which transparency is brought to the liquid.

302. This pertains to separation.

     312. The maturation of drink is accomplished by the gathering of spirits, where the coarser parts are more perfectly digested. This consists of the same aids as clarification (of which we spoke before); but it must be noted that through the ultimate efforts of clarification, the spirits are rendered so smooth that they become sluggish, and the drink becomes flat, which ought to moderately effloresce. Hence, drink from amber is served as if dying.
     313. The degrees of maturation can be observed in must, in wine [a] suitable for drinking, and in vinegar. Among these, must does not have spirits well-gathered; wine obtains them well-united, so that they render the parts more oily; Omphacium indeed has them gathered, but more meager and in a smaller quantity, with the thinnest parts for the most part dissipated by exhalation. For we see vinegar prepared when a wine vessel is exposed to the warm sun, nor is that burned, because exhalation has drawn out and dispersed very many of the thinner parts.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the making of gold.*

Up until now, the hope of making gold has disgracefully deluded the world, which hope I declare not to be vain, nor to exceed the limits of human faculty. But the means destined for this effect labor under fallacies and errors, as far as practice is concerned, and embrace nothing sound in their concepts, as far as Theory is concerned. For that which nature is said to intend, namely the conversion of all metals into gold, and not to deviate from its goal if freed from bonds and impediments; and that metals, once their crudities and impurities are purged, and their roughness removed, will turn into gold; and that a moderate quantity of Medicine injected into base metals is sufficient for changing a great quantity into gold and for multiplying it – these are mere dreams; to which the remaining foundations of Alchemy are consonant.

In order that this fable may be handsomely adorned, Alchemists call upon many vanities from Astrology for help, and have other subsidiary aids from natural magic, from superstitious interpretations of scripture, from oral traditions, and from fabricated testimonies of the ancients, and other things of this kind. On the other hand, it cannot be denied that not a few useful things

--- Page 243 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IV. 199
useful experiments, and a certain
restoration of the world. But we, about to treat of the
transmutations of bodies and experiments
pertaining to metals, will show the true and
well-trodden paths of nature, and certain footsteps
leading, whence light may shine forth upon so notable a work.
We praise the industry of the Chinese, who, having
despaired of the making of gold, toil in preparing
silver, diligent even to madness. For that former
(gold), certainly most weighty and among metals most
endowed with matter, has difficulties not easily
explained, such as you would not find in others,
by no means equaling the weight and matter of gold;
and it would be of lighter labor to prepare silver
from lead or mercury, even though these exceed the
weight of silver, since rather a greater degree of
fixation is required than any condensation. Meanwhile,
while we encounter axioms pertaining to maturation,
we will provide an experiment for maturing metals
by a method of change, by which some of them may
turn into gold. For thus I am convinced, that if
metals have been properly concocted, digested, and
matured, easy paths for producing gold lie open.
And here it occurs to me, that a German became
known to me, whom, by his boasted knowledge of
preparing gold, more closely to a distinguished man and an intimate
          I 4               familiar-

intimate familiarity. I was present at his discourses, when he said that such a thing could be done, but that common Alchemists spoil their attempts with too little intense fire. For the making of gold, he said, requires a justly tempered heat, as it is a subterranean work of nature, into which a moderate heat emanates, but more precisely regulated than in other metals. And so he would accomplish it by the use of a large lamp, whose heat would be regulated and equal, and it would be the work of several months. The device of the lamp savors of foolishness, but what concerns too vehement heat, the ruin of the whole undertaking, and reducing it to equality, and a just space of time, is not entirely to be rejected.
	Therefore we return to our axioms concerning maturation, previously designated by us. Let the first be, that heat be applied within moderation, which indeed is that sufficient for digestion and complete concoction. The legitimate temperature of heat, however, is estimated from the fact that it is accommodated to the nature of the subject; while it is suitable for fruits and liquids, in metals it is considered ineffectual. Secondly, that the spirits of the metal be quickened, and the tangible parts be opened; for without these two aids, whatever you attempt with the metallic spirits will be useless for the digestion of the parts.

--- Page 245 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IV. 201

...parts. Third, that the spirits may disperse themselves equally, and not move by leaps, which will render the parts tightly closed and flexible. Here heat is required, not varied in intensity and remission, but as much as possible, continu-ously equal. Fourth, that no passage may lie open for the spirits, which must be retained, since with them emitted, the body becomes hard and rough. That will be effected by a temperate fire and careful closing of the vessel. Fifth, that the most suitable metals for transmutation may be chosen and optimally prepared, whereby the work will be facilitated. Sixth, that a just space of time may be granted to the operation; not that hope may be prolonged (as is customary among Alchemists), but that nature may unfold itself in a suitably determined interval. These principles are most certain and most true, from which now the rule of experiment is to be derived, which perhaps a longer meditation might disapprove.
      327. For gold, as is well known, is the most compact and the heaviest of all metals, and most flexible and extensible. *Note*, no one should hope to make gold from quicksilver, for the reason that it is weighty; for mercury is in no way [a] equal to resisting the testing flames; in my judgment, copper should merit the second place after silver, being a material approaching most closely to the aptitude of the former.

*Various Experiments concerning the Pro-*
*duction and Acceleration*
*of Putrefaction.*

To overcome the delays in hastening putrefaction has something most worthy of universal and most widely diffused inquiry, since corruption corresponds conversely to generation, and those two are, as it were, the circumscribing boundaries and confines of operating nature, by which it entirely encloses itself; a twofold guide to life and death. Putrefaction is the action of spirits which attempt to depart from the body, so that dispersed into the air they may enjoy the free Sun. That attempt of spirits to be gathered into the body of the air (which, in its egress, takes a step) has five indications of diverse effects. If a more vehement movement agitates spirits detained in the body, liquefaction follows, as in metals, etc.; if a gentler one, digestion or maturation, as in drink and fruits. If spirits are not entirely detained, but are moderately pushed forth by a confused and disorderly movement,
I 6 exi-

--- Page 248 ---
204 FRANCIS BACON
putrefaction occurs, whose nature is to very unevenly dissolve the body's consistency, as in flesh, rotten apples, phosphorescent wood, etc., and also appears in the rust of metals. But if that motion proceeds in a certain order, it is vivification and formation, as shown by living things generated from putrefaction, and those of that kind which are more perfect. If an exit is open to the departing spirits, drying, hardening, consumption, etc., follow, as bricks show, and the evaporation of a liquid body.
     329. The aids which contain the causes of putrefaction and accelerate it are what the following text describes. First, if a raw or watery humor is added, as witnessed by the moistening of any flesh, apple, wood in water, etc., whereas preservation is due to somewhat oily and fatty substances.
     330. Second is invitation and excitation, as if a rotten apple is applied to a whole one; or if dung (a substance that has undergone total putrefaction) is added to other bodies. Cemeteries, in which burials are made daily, provide a clear indication of this, where the earth consumes any recently placed corpse much more quickly than pure earth.

332. Fourth, is the solution of continuity, as we see in apples, which, when cut or pierced, experience more rapid corruption, and also wood, etc., and animated flesh from a wound inflicted somewhere.

Their governance being disturbed by dissolution, any part withdraws into its own sphere to be aggregated with homogeneous parts. Thus urine and blood, when cooled, dissolve.    Those things have a most worthy use in inquiry,

   341. The first thing that prevents putrefaction

342. Secondly, astringency, which resists dissolution, since generally astringent medicines ward off putrefaction. The same principle of astringency causes a small quantity of oil of vitriol to prevent water from putrefying. This astringency inheres in the substance, whose virtual cold it is, and which operates almost in the same way as cold (substances).
343. Thirdly, the exclusion of air, and its admission, which, though opposite in nature, nevertheless produce the same effect (as often happens), depending on the condition of the subject matter. Thus wine or beer from accurately closed bottles acquire a certain durability. Underground granaries preserve grain longer than above-ground ones. Fruits enclosed in wax do not lose their freshness, bodies immersed in honey or flour remain fresh, and the liquids of drinks and juices, with oil poured over their surface, do not cease to be fresh. On the contrary, if clothes are not exposed to air, moths breed in them and they become moldy. Flowing water lacks putrefaction; and the human body also expels it with frequent exercises. A solitary experiment concerning luminous
wood in the dark.

352. We have certainly given no small effort to properly
investigate the experiment of wood luminous in the dark;
and the more willingly, because it excels in its greatest
durability, compared to other things emitting light among
us, with a movement scarcely perceptible to the senses.
Fire and flame are a continuous consumption. Sugar
shines only while it is grated, seawater while it is
agitated, glow-worms while they live,
or a little after, fish scales only when putrefying
seem to be of the same nature with shining wood.
Nor are we ignorant that there is an internal motion
in all putrefaction, no differently than in fire, or
light. Such was the outcome of that experiment.

Perhaps the same may be found in others.
3. Roots and bodies shine; but that roots

   353. The acceleration of birth in living creatures

in animals has a double respect; if either

from truth, this reason is given: if the birth
anticipates the ordinary time by so great a space,
it is to be ascribed to the vigor of the infant;
but if by a lesser space, it is a defect of maternal
weakness.

*Solitary Experiment concerning the ac-*
     *celeration of growth and stature.*

354. Rapid increases in human stature are
either from a fuller diet, or from the nature
of the nourishment, or from a more vigorous
and excited heat which nature confers.
As to the former, excess in food is harmful,
as it rather distends the body and makes it broad,

--- Page 261 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IV. 217
rather than long, progressing. An image of this in plants is seen, which rarely attain height when, while tender, they begin to spread out widely. As for the nature of nourishment, let it not be too dry, because infants fed with milk, in regions where its use is frequent, surpass in height those for whom nourishment from bread and meat is more common. It is also a common saying among the people that daisy roots [a] boiled in milk (which have a remarkable drying property) make dogs small. Nor is it disputed that excessively dry food causes a retardation of stature. Furthermore, let the food possess an opening power, whereby the humor is thinned, and spirits are promoted upwards. Nor is it without reason that Xenophon so highly commends the use of cardamom in raising Persian infants, as it contributes to growth and a more agile bodily habit. Cardamom is called nasturtium in Latin, which herb, when tender, is pleasant to eat. The excitation of native heat occurs most effectively through exercises, so that consequently in frequented schools, the sedentary life of boys detracts from their growth, whereas country people, not sent to similar gymnasia, are generally of better stature. *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*Chameleons.*

360. A chameleon is almost the size of a common lizard, with a head not proportionate to its size, and huge eyes. It moves its head with its neck unmoved; its neck, I know not how, does not bend, as happens to pigs. Its back is curved, its skin sprinkled with tubercles, which are less prominent towards the abdomen. Its tail is slender and long.
K 3

--- Page 266 ---
222 OF FRANCIS BACON
long. On each foot there are five toes, three extended outwards, two drawn inwards; its tongue, of admirable length compared to the rest of its body, having a cavity at its tip, is put forth for catching flies. Its color is green and yellowish, shining more with whiteness towards the abdomen, yet interspersed with blue, white, and red spots. Placed on things colored green, it becomes green, the other colors as if extinguished. It becomes yellow when brought near yellow; but near blue, red, or white, only the spots shine with a deep green. From contact with black, it becomes black, with a mixture of green intervening. It is not fed by air alone (though it is its principal food), since it also feeds on captured flies (as we have said). There were some, however, who, having kept it for a whole year, denied they had been able to perceive what had served as nourishment for it besides air. It is to be noted that when air is drawn in, its belly swells and its jaws close, which the rays of the sun, when turned towards it, usually open. It is a foolish tradition of magic that storms will arise from a chameleon burned on the tops of houses (these things are fashioned from dreams of sympathy), for since it feeds on air, it is believed to possess great power for generating an impression in the air.

361. Some ancient writer relates that in a certain region of Media, flames erupt from the plain, which he denies are pure, or enveloped in an abundance of belched smoke, ashes, or pumice, such as mountain caverns vomit forth. The definite reason is that the flames lack compression, as in mountains, or in earthquakes that become fiery even to the ejection of flames. And hidden fires manifest themselves, unaware how to flame up, and finally bursting forth when oil is poured on them. The reason is that the fire seems so suffocated that it cannot remove a stone, and it is heat rather than flame, yet sufficient for igniting oil.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
           *the congelation of air.*

   363. Take the largest bladder you can, fill it with air, bind it around the neck with a waxed silk thread, and moreover, seal it very tightly with a thick wax stopper, so that even if the neck of the bladder dries out, air is prevented from entering and exiting. Then bury it four or five feet deep in the earth, in a vault or a snow cellar, so that snow is excavated around the bladder: and after a period of fourteen days, see if it has contracted. If this happens, it appears from the surrounding cold of the earth or snow that the air has condensed, and has become more like water. The efficacy of this experiment is wide.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
        *Summer and Winter Diseases.*

   382. It is commonly known that more people sicken in summer, and more die in winter; unless a plague is raging, which usually invades summer or autumn. The reason is, because heat, for the most part, gives origin to diseases, which are mostly cured by sweats and purges, the summer season being conducive to this; and they are more easily provoked. As for pestilential diseases, the reason why most die in summer is this: because that season of the year is most fertile for generating them. Otherwise, for those seized by such a plague in winter, the fear of immediate danger is not lacking.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
        *Pestilential Seasons.*

   383. It is a popular opinion that in hot and humid years—

...and humid years usually contain something from which they are suspected of generating plague, this with the weak argument that putrefaction draws its origin from heat and humidity. In England, this belief struggles, since through many summers remarkable for dryness, that plague has reigned with the greatest destruction. The reason perhaps is that dryness in the bodies of Islanders, accustomed to a humid air, exasperates the humors and inclines them more to putrefaction or inflammation. Besides, it usually infects waters and renders them less healthy. Add that in Mauritania plagues rage in the summer months, with a hot and dry climate.

Therefore Hippocrates in his prognostics has good observations of diseases which testify to the nature of past time.

Experimentum solitarium spectans
[a] Hæsitantiam.

386. It is known that many are stutterers. The cause perhaps could be a cooling of the tongue, from which comes a slowness of natural movement. And therefore we observe that delirious people usually stammer, and stutterers also, after drinking a moderate amount of wine, stammer less, because it warms them up. Nor is it hidden from us that stutterers stumble more with hesitation at the beginning of speech than in its progress, the tongue, of course, warming up a little through movement. In some, however, the cause may perhaps have been (though rarely) dryness of the tongue, an equal impediment to movement, with coldness, a common affliction for wise and distinguished men, such as Moses, a man of impeded tongue. Very many stutterers are found to be very choleric, with choler inducing dryness of the tongue.

*Various Experiments concerning Odors.*

389. The fragrance of odors is greater in free air and
from a moderate distance than
if they are brought to the nose, as previous [experiments] elsewhere
have shown; the reason is twofold: first, a more
subtle mixture or incorporation of the odor.
Thus, sounds are most pleasing to the ears if
any part, being separate and distinct, does not strike the
sense. Second, because all fragrance consists of and is
carried by crude and earthy odors mixed in.
From a distance, a sweetness is achieved,
which comes from a greater spirituality, abandoning
whatever earthy [elements] it carried in its company.
388. Crushing reduces the sweetness of odor
latent in dry substances to its maximum
vigor. Thus, pricked rinds of
oranges and lemons render them more fragrant.
In general, motion and agitation elicit
fragrance from bodies, even those not crushed,
as when a perfumed sachet is shaken.
The reason is twofold: first, a more copious
effluvium of spirits, their exit being facilitated
by crushing, pricking, compression, and to some extent, by
movement; the latter includes the other,
namely the impulse of air, thence a bent vehicle of odor.
389. Plants produce the greatest delights
of odors in flowers, whose [other parts are] entirely

And it will be entirely permissible to conclude that the water is more concocted and nutritious from which a more generous drink is made; although for medicinal uses, that water will be rejected. Such water is usually supplied by large rivers accustomed to navigation, and also by large and pure ponds; the efficacy of the sun reigns more here than in narrower springs and rivers. I would assign the next place in goodness after this to chalky water, for preparing a drink from it. It also benefits concoction if it is drawn from a deep well, specifically for removing the crudities of the water. But chalky water near the surface of the earth is too corrosive, as appears in the washing of clothes, which the use of such water gradually eats away.

    *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
        *temperate heat under the Equi-*
                *noctial.*

    398. In Peru, and other parts of the West
Indies, although under the line (equator), the heat
is not so intolerable as in Mauritania
and regions subject to the Torrid Zone.
The cause is *the great Brizes* which movement
of air in larger circles (such as are in
the zones of the world) produces, whence cooling.
Nor therefore is the midday heat so great
when *the Brizes are great*, as around
the ninth or tenth hour before noon.
Another cause is, the longi-
                                            tude

--- Page 289 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IV. 245
length of nights, by which the dew is accustomed to compensate for the inconveniences of daily heat. A third cause is the Sun's stay, not with respect to day and night (for I have spoken of these before), but to the season of the year. For the Sun's passage in its oblique course along the line doubles summer and winter, whereas in the regions of the Torrid Zone it doubles and recedes, and thus makes one long summer.

  *A Solitary Observation concerning*
    *the dark color in Ethiopians.*

  399. The heat of the Sun dyes men in certain places with a blackish color, as in Ethiopia, Guinea, etc. That this is not an effect of fire, glassmakers show, who are constantly occupied with fire. The reason perhaps is that fire acts upon the spirits and blood, so that they evaporate, and thus renders men pale and swarthy. But the more benign heat of the Sun only draws the blood to the outermost parts of the body, and rather digests it than liquefies it. Hence all Ethiopians are of a fleshy indeed but ill-proportioned bodily build, and with thick lips, which indicate moisture retained, not drawn out. We also see them born in regions abundant in water because of rivers and other causes. For Meroë, the metro-

*Solitary Experiment concerning mo-*
*tion a very few moments after death.*

400. Certain animals, decapitated,
move for some time, like birds; for a
very short time, man, and all beasts.
Certain creatures show motion when their body is cut into various
parts, like snakes, eels,
worms, flies, etc. Firstly, therefore, it is established
that the immediate cause of death is the dis-
solution or extinction of the spirits, the destruction
or corruption of the organs being mediate.
However, certain organs are so absolutely
necessary that their destruction is immediately
followed by the extinction of the spirits, with the
intervention of the shortest possible time. A certain
classical writer among the ancients, neither
                                        suspect-

of doubtful credibility reports that a bellowing was heard from a beast slaughtered for sacrifice, even after its heart was removed. Of similar authority is this account, that with a piglet's head opened, its brain, removed and placed on someone's palm, palpitated, with no part of the brain injured, and without separation from the spinal cord. Throughout this entire period, the piglet appeared dead and was devoid of all movement. A little later, with the brain replaced and the piglet's skull closed, it walked about a little. Nor is it unknown that when an eye is gouged out by the law of retaliation, it may hang for some time by the optic nerve, deprived of the power of sight during that time, but a little later, by restoration, the act of seeing returned. Therefore, the spirits are contained primarily in the head and ventricles of the brain, which both man and beast have large and capacious, so that when the head is dissected, they move little or not at all. But the heads of birds are very small, and therefore the spirits are more dispersed through the nerves, whence movement in them is a little more prolonged. So much so that Histories have recorded that a Roman Emperor, to demonstrate his skill in shooting, aimed a huge bifurcated arrow at an Ostrich as it swiftly crossed the Theater, and took off its head; and with the head removed, it nevertheless

403. Strawberries irrigated (with irrigation intervals spaced by three days) with water that has macerated sheep and pigeon dung will anticipate maturity. It seems probable that the same effect will occur in other berries, herbs, flowers, grains, and trees. Therefore, although the experiment with strawberries was taken from common practice, it has not yet come into general use and is to be applied to many things. For it is common to correct the soil with manure, as well as to restore it by applying dung to the roots. But water that has macerated manure, which seems to be of greater efficacy, has not yet been received into popular use.

405. What we have premised concerning growth has as its cause either good and effective nourishment, or spirits in plants strengthened and excited by attracting better nourishment. For strengthening the spirits in them, we mention the following, which are not, however, to be applied to the roots of trees or to seed. Trees planted in a warm place on a mound, and exposed to the South and East-South-East winds, produce ripe fruits with accelerated growth; and the East-South-East wind is preferred to the South-West wind, although the latter is hotter. But the primary reason is that nocturnal cold succeeds the antemeridian heat; partly also because the Sun radiating from the South-West quarter errs by excess of heat. The planting of them near the outer part of a chimney, which is frequently heated by a fire, promotes the whole work of growth and maturation. Also, to draw back branches to the interior of a place where fire is frequently used, produces the same efficacy.      413. It is a pleasure to give a slower

                                                            not

There is not one [method]; the first is, if the apex is cut off immediately after it has germinated, from which, around November of the same year, with the flower restored, it will bloom; but not exactly at the apex which suffered the iron, but from shoots which were like stolons. The reason is, because the sap, which would otherwise be the nourishment of the apex (even after germination), due to its cutting, by making a diversion to the surrounding lateral shoots, will bear the bloom of a later rose.

414. The second, if you pluck the rose buds where they have swelled into the first nodes. Then the lateral shoots are fruitful. The cause is the same as the preceding one, that the cutting of the apex and the plucking of the buds produce a similar effect, both by retaining the sap for a time, and by diverting it to the shoots which were not growing so much.

415. The third, the removal of certain buds at the top in springtime, leaving the lower ones to grow. The reason is, that branches help to draw the sap more vigorously; for leading it to the top, when trees are pruned, two or three branches should be left there. 421. Some cherish a specious opinion, namely, that if you graft a late-ripening fruit onto the trunk of an early-ripening tree, the fruit will anticipate in ripeness; as if a peach were grafted onto a cherry tree. And conversely, if a notable shoot bearing early-ripening fruit is grafted onto a stock that ripens later, the adopted shoot will retain its native character, as if a cherry were grafted onto a peach tree. But the authors of this opinion are deluded by empty notions. The reason is that the shoots have dominance over the stock, which behaves passively, neither providing nourishment nor impulse to the shoot.

the root's nourishment. This is of great use for onions,

452. It is not doubted that fruit is generally better from grafting. The reason suggests itself, that the nourishment is prepared in the stock rather than in the raw earth. It must be observed, however, what they say, that some trees grow more successfully from the seed than from grafting, such as quinces and the Persian apple. I state the cause to be that the nourishment which these plants require is more humid. And although that (nourishment from the stock) excels in fineness and preparation, nevertheless, in humidity and abundance, it cannot compete with nourishment from the earth, since we see that these fruits are by their nature very cold.

Various experiments concerning the compo-
     sition of fruits and flowers.
Among living things that distinguish sexes, we observe various results from various coition, and as it were a certain composition in creatures. Thus a mule is generated from a horse and a she-ass; and other changes in species are given, which are called monsters, but are rarer. That proverb
too, 'Africa always produces something monstrous,' is not thought to have flowed from any other origin than that the scarcity of spring water in a parched region gathers various beasts from all sides to a watering place, which, refreshed after slaking their thirst, very frequently mix with a species not their own. The variety of composition and coition in plant genera has not yet been thoroughly investigated by experiments; yet, if it can be attempted, it is more subject to our control than that of animals, where the itch of pleasure creeps in, and they rush spontaneously into Venus. Therefore, that composition of plants, if it can be achieved, will be most noble,
inasmuch as it promises diverse and new names of fruits and unknown flowers. Inoculation (grafting) does nothing towards this, merely improving fruit, duplicating flowers, etc., but it is ineffective for generating a new species; the scions predominating over the stock.

--- Page 327 ---
SYLVA SYLVARUM. Century V. 283

477. Some of the ancients recorded that the sprouts of fruit-bearing trees of various species, having their sides joined and very tightly bound, when placed in the earth, would form a single trunk from which they would sprout, with the fruits unmixed, testifying to the unconfused nature of their own species. Hence it is to be noted in passing, that the unity of continuation is an easier task than that of species. They also report that if vines accustomed to bearing red and white grapes are planted in the earth, their uppermost parts being gathered and tied together, there will be grapes of various colors on the same branch, and similarly distinct grape seeds of the same grape; but this occurs where the course of one and another year has perfected the unity (as it seems) more through germination. It would be useful after the first rudiments, as it were, of the union, to irrigate frequently; since in any moisture there is an inherent power of uniting. They also advise tying the bud as soon as it swells; at least for a time.

478. They record that various seeds, wrapped in a small linen cloth, and placed in well-manured earth, will produce contiguous plants, whose shoots are to be incorporated later if they are gathered. A similar account concerns kernels, to be placed in a narrow-mouthed flask filled with earth.

*Various experiments concerning the sym-*
*pathy and antipathy of plants.*

Many traditions and observations have flowed
down to us from deep antiquity, accepted by public belief, concerning
the sympathy and antipathy of plants;
namely, that some rejoice in the vicinity of others, growing more
vigorously from sympathy, while others shrink away, faring
ill from antipathy. But these concepts betray igno-
rance, lacking true knowledge of causes, as many expe-
riments concerning sympathy and antipathy
teach. In plants there is no such agreement from friendship or from
enmity disagreement, such as people fabri-
cate for themselves with vain imagination, and which they designate with the utterly erroneous
nomenclature of sympathy and antipathy. On the contrary, here all
things happen, with sympathy declining into antipathy,
and vice versa, when in this
                                            manner

--- Page 329 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. V. 285
it happens in this way. If a plant draws its own peculiar sap, [a] such as imbues the earth (as it qualifieth the Earth), so that what is left behind by the former becomes unsuitable for another plant, then proximity is beneficial, because the nourishment is of a contrary nature and not of the same kind. But if two plants are nourished by the same sap, even if it is sufficiently abundant, proximity is harmful, one defrauding the other.

480. Therefore, any plant that feeds largely from the earth, and thus [b] by drying it out (soaking the Earth) exhausts it, harms all those placed near it; such as large trees (especially the ash) and all those that send their roots not far from the earth's surface. Thus, not only is there discord between the cabbage and the vine, though not unknown to the ancients, but also the cabbage does not agree well with other trees, inasmuch as it preys most greedily on the richest saps of the earth. And, if it be true that a vine creeping near a cabbage turns its path elsewhere, the reason might be the poorer nourishment it encounters; and although the root may be in the same place as the cabbage, nevertheless (I somewhat doubt it) the plant to be nourished will turn itself away.

481. Plants of different natures, and to be nourished by different sap, thrive in friendly conjunction.

484. Plant lettuce or Pompeian cabbage, or an improved thistle, next to wormwood or rue, and observe if the sweetness increases in the lettuce and the others.
