      489. Conversely, you ought to avoid the proximity of herbs that share the same sap. In this way, I think, Rosemary will suffer a loss of sweetness if placed near lavender, laurel, or similar plants. But if one wishes to diminish the efficacy of a herb, it is advisable to join other such plants nearby, so that its virtue may become weak. Mugwort placed near Angelica will perhaps become more languid and more suitable for a mixture in fumigation, and rue from the proximity of common wormwood may degenerate more towards Roman wormwood.
      490. The meaning of this axiom embraces many things, and therefore selection is necessary so that a more exact method of experiment may be adopted; nor is variety so much to be regarded here as further perfection.
      491. It may be permitted to make an experiment with poisonous and purgative herbs, which might allow their native malignity to be removed or broken by applying to them the temperament of a more efficacious poison or purgative.
      492. It is reported that the shrub called smooth or black bryony, which is a species of bryony, and cabbage, when brought very close to each other, have a harmful conjunction either for one or for both; for they are twin preda-

493. Ancient and modern writers, some from the school of natural magic, observed a sympathy between the Sun, Moon, and principal Stars, and herbs and plants. Hence, names derived from the Sun and Moon arose, and other things which, ostentatiously adorned from the storehouse of absurdities, were sold. It is established that certain herbs have a twofold relation to the Sun, so that they either open themselves or close, or bend or incline their head. For marigold, tulips, pimpernel, and most flowers expand their leaves at the splendor of the Sun; partly they contract in response to the approach of evening or a cloudy sky. Nor should the reason be assigned so pompously, that they rejoice at the Sun's presence and are saddened by its absence, since the closing is nothing else than the weighing down of the leaves and swelling around the lowest parts from moist air, which, when dry, extends them. And they consider it a kind of miracle that garden clover hides its stem when the Sun is shining, when it is merely the fullest expansion of the leaves.

     494. What a little moisture can do in vegetables, even dead and separated from the earth, conjurers demonstrate, for whom an oat awn is sometimes used, which, if you pay close attention, is twisted in the lower part, but at the top is a whole and light straw. They take the twisted part, cutting off the rest, and leaving the awn the length of a finger. Then they form a small cross from a reed, selecting the part of it that consists of pith and is oriented lengthwise, and another part that is transverse with respect to the part of the reed that lacks pith, so that the entire cross equals the height of an upright finger. Afterwards they pinch the bottom part which contains the pith, and insert the awn into it, with half of the reed (cross) sticking out. Then they take a small white wooden box, as if an auxiliary device for the trick, into which a hole is pressed with a feather, sufficient for holding the awn, so that the cross, not having passed through to the bottom, remains fixed.

Deceptions, to be handled more cautiously, are prefaced by a question, such as, "Which woman in this assembly is of outstanding beauty?" or "Who hides a glove or playing cards?" Meanwhile, another is ordered to recite various names, and at the mention of each person, the cross is fixed in the box, first applied to the mouth, as if to cast a spell; yet it is not moved when they come to the person designated within themselves; while they apply the cross to the mouth, they touch the beard of the oat with the tip of the tongue and moisten it, and thus the cross is fixed in the box. Afterwards, it is seen to turn gently and quietly four or five times, which arises from the unfolding of the oat's beard due to the moisture secretly applied. These things will be more evident if the cross is fixed between the fingers, instead of in the box. Hence it is evident that this movement from slight moistening is more effective than that contraction of leaves, or the inclination of the head in the marigold.

*Various experiments on how herbs and fruits*
*may be adapted for medicinal uses.*

499. Vain are the things told, and equal to fictions, concerning the altering of the smell, color, or taste of fruit by infusion, mixture, or grafting into the bark or root of a tree, flower, or herb, so that its substance, imbued with this or that color, becomes aromatic or medicinal; the reason being that all these things have completed their period and do not nourish, and any such alteration of qualities in vegetables must necessarily occur from that which can serve as nourishment for the plant.
But it is true that if cows feed on wild garlic, the milk is imbued with the taste of garlic. Mutton too is more pleasing to the taste if the sheep feeds on wild thyme and other very wholesome herbs. Galen mentions cow's milk in the cure of scirrhus of the liver, when the animal's fodder consists only of certain herbs. Spanish honey smells almost of Rosemary or Orange, from where the bee collects it. From the ancients came that story of the girl nourished by Aconite (than which, among all vegetables, nothing is more immediately

[a] Experiment 462.

--- Page 339 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. V. 595
(is not more poisonous) and continuous use had made it harmless to her, while it killed others who dealt with it. Others observed that Bezoar is given, some potent and some of no efficacy, distinguishable also by a difference in appearance; and one (type) is collected from beasts accustomed to feed in mountains, where there are theriacal herbs; the other, ineffective namely, from those (beasts) which have fed in valleys, where such herbs are not found. Up to now I hold this view: that just as maceration renders wines and beers medicinal, and moreover, a certain compounding of powders imbues bread; so also foods (meat, fish, milk, eggs) can be transformed into the role of medicine and a support for diet, if the beast, bird, or fish is fed with things chosen for this purpose and suitable for the disease. However, the matter would not be without danger in secret poisonings. But doubts prevent asserting that these things can be referred to plants and herbs, inasmuch as the sap, their nourishment, is more common, and with difficulty admits a quality not assimilated by the plant.

500. But lest the prejudice of incredulity hinder most useful experiments (especially since many of the ancients have committed them to writing), we have deemed it worthwhile to briefly propose four methods from their ideas, so that plants may be made medicinal.

--- Page 340 ---
296        OF FRANCIS BACON
medicinal. The first is, a splitting of the root, and an infusion of medicine into it, such as hellebore, opium, scammony, theriac, etc. And then a binding. Probability is lacking for this opinion, because the root draws immediately from the earth, whence the nourishment is more common and less qualified. Moreover, a longer delay is required before it is insinuated into the fruits. The second is, to pierce the body of the tree, and to insert medicine into it; which is to be preferred to the former. For if any power of the medicine is received, the path to ascent is shorter and to be completed in less time. The third, is the maceration of the seed or kernel in a liquid into which medicine has been infused. This method is very suspect to me, since the seed (as I believe) does not attract parts of matter imbued with the property. But it is much more probable, if the medicine is mixed with dung; because the seed naturally imbibing moisture from the dung might likewise also receive some property. The fourth, is frequent irrigation of the plant with an infused medicine. This method seems to prevail over the others for this reason, because a frequent and repeated application of the medicine occurs, whereas others are applied only once, so that the virtue might more easily vanish. But I utterly doubt and fear,

[Large decorative initial T] The whole labor of this endeavor revolves around this
(as we frequently remind the Reader), that experiments

may be that does not yield ripe fruits there.

502. It is a curiosity to impress variously devised shapes upon fruits: this is an easy task, if you shape the tender ones in clay or wooden molds. Thus, one can have cucumbers oblong like a reed, round like a sphere, or shaped into the form of a cross. Apples also shaped like pears or citrons. Indeed, you can even give fruits the most accurate shapes, namely of a man, of beasts, of birds, from a fabricated image which you teach them to imitate as they grow. With this observation, however, that the mold which you surround [the fruit with] should fill a proper capacity, and that narrowness should not cause imperfection of the fruit, if it grows to its proper size. If the opposite happens, you will prevent the expansion of its mass from spreading throughout and filling the entire hollow, and you will be frustrated in your desire for the impression, as usually happens in shaping liquids. But someone might doubt whether the exclusion of the sun might not be harmful to the fruit? Obvious experience answers in fruits that grow covered. Let it also be inquired whether not

Various experiments concerning the degeneration of plants and the transmutation of one into another.

518. It has been proven by frequent experience that plants degenerating from lack of cultivation become inferior within the same species; so much so sometimes that a change of species follows. To this contribute: 1. A prolonged stay in the same place, not changed frequently. 2. Dryness, unless the inherent moisture of the earth is sufficient. 3. Transplantation, and removal as it were into a more unfavorable environment, or the omission of those things which relate to the composition of the soil. Thus, through neglect, curled mint is changed into garden mint, and cabbage into turnip.
519. Any fruit grafted onto a root or shoot, if its seed is planted, will depart from its former nature. The planted stones of grapes, figs, almonds, pomegranates produce degenerate and wild fruits. Again, if you expect most fruits of the grafted kind from planted kernels or stones, you will see them degenerate. It is indeed true that peaches (as the preceding [experiments] have shown) grow more successfully from planted stones than if they are grafted; but this exception from the rule

--- Page 353 ---
**SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VI. 309**
Let the rule be, that whatever plant delights in much moisture promises better growth from a pit or kernel than if it is grafted. Although indeed the nourishment from the stock may be thinner, yet it is less [abundant], with the earth nourishing more generously.

**520.** Exceedingly old seeds, yet not entirely deprived of vigor sufficient for a plant, usually degenerate. Hence industrious Gardeners test the soundness of seeds by placing them in gently simmering water; which, within the space of an hour, if they are sound, will germinate.

**521.** It is worthy of wonder what they relate about basil, namely, that if it is exposed to too much Sun, it turns into wild thyme; although those herbs acknowledge no natural affinity. But basil is a very hot plant, with rich and succulent leaves. If this oiliness is drawn out by the enticing Sun, it seems probable that a change will arise from it.

**522.** It is an old tradition that if an oak branch is buried in the earth, a wild vine will grow from it. If we are not deceived by a fiction, the oak undoubtedly does not assume the nature of a vine, but that decaying branch imbues the earth with a quality which will produce a vine.

**523.** It is possible, and I was present at their discourse-

is nourished by a scanter sap than to produce

   § 24. Among country folk, the opinion reigns, that if

--- Page 355 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VI. 311
miracles of nature; since among the pronouncements of common philosophy it is held that it cannot happen; and indeed the matter requires no light labor and a scrutiny probing the innermost recesses of nature. But the opinion of impossibility is overcome by several instances drawn from experiments, so that an examination of the causes may be entered upon. Living things generated from putrefaction demonstrate a great transmutation of one into another, such as flies from grubs, etc. And it may be plausibly said that living things not born from seed can change their species. For nature, which intimately constitutes the seed, prevents the creature from deviating, as if by imposed bonds. Thus it is permissible to conclude that, since the earth produces plants without seed, a migration of those plants from species to species can occur. Therefore, since readily apparent instances are insufficient, we will endeavor to establish a method of investigation through experiments that suggest probability. And generally, we ask all readers who approach this work of Sylva Sylvarum to set aside causes for astonishment, and not to attribute to haste, as if they were raw impulses, the fact that we give place here to particulars not yet verified by experiment. For I hold the contrary opinion, namely, that such particulars possess that dignity

--- Page 356 ---
312 FRANCIS OF BACON
dignity by which experiments have hitherto prevailed,
and which have become thoroughly known; since these, from
the latter kind, as they are offered, must be
admitted; the former, by directing the investigation of
causes, sharpen it, and aid the constitution of axioms.
	526. Above all, it must be known that if you pursue
the transmutation of plants into one another, it is
necessary that the nourishment should predominate over
the seed; which in this experiment is required, being
most contrary to the nature of the herb, lest however
the faculty of growing be hindered. Let the seed also
be very weak and of minimal vigor. Therefore, it would
be advisable to plant marsh herbs on hill ridges and
in open fields: And conversely, plants which desire
much moisture, subject them to the dryness of sandy
soil; thus, let dendromalacha and sedge be transferred
to hills; conversely, let cucumber, lettuce, and
cabbage seed be planted in a sandy plain; thorn,
heather, white hellebore, fern in a marshy place.
I also establish this, that edible and garden herbs on
hill ridges become more medicinal, but less suitable
for eating than before. Perhaps also, herbs which are
wild in nature, may be changed into salads. Let this
be the first rule for transferring, as it were, substance
into another.

527. Let the second method be to commit a small amount of the seed of that herb, whose intended conversion is sought, to the earth mixed with other seeds, so that you may learn whether the sap of other seeds imbues the earth with such a quality that the seed, towards which the intention of imitation is directed, is altered. For example, let purslane seed be sown mixed with lettuce seed, or lettuce with purslane, or basil among thyme seed. Let a change of taste or anything else be observed. But you will do best if you wrap it in a small linen cloth and exclude the foreign seed from that whose change you are preparing.

528. The third method is the preparation of the earth by mixing crushed or otherwise comminuted plants, whether in leaf or in root. For example, mix crushed cabbage leaves into the earth, into which you place tall thistles or parsnips. Thus, cast fennel into earth prepared with crushed marjoram, oregano, or wild thyme, etc. In this operation, a continuous process of nature will exist (as I indeed believe), not because the herb to be changed will be nourished by the sap of the foreign plant (for I rejected that in the preceding sections), but the matter will pass into a new confection of the composite earth [a]; from which perhaps the seed may be altered, the species of the former herb not persisting.

*Various experiments concerning the height, and the art of making dwarf trees.*

532. It is certain that cultivated trees in groves grow more upright, and with branches less luxuriant in their lower parts, than those which occupy fields. The reason is, because there is a natural movement in plants to enjoy the Sun. Moreover, they are not saturated with excessive nourishment, the forest drawing part of it to itself, repletion always being harmful to stature. Finally, they are kept warm, which is a great factor for the height of plants.
533. Trees by their nature very warm (and their inflammable gum shows their warmth), such as fir and pine, are carried upwards by spontaneous growth until they have filled the top, with no branches on the side detracting anything from this. The reason is partly in the warmth, partly in the thinness of the sap, O 2. both-

--- Page 360 ---
FRANCIS BACON'S

both prerogatives transmitting sap upwards. Juniper is only a shrub, nor of such thickness as to be able to contribute to tallness.

534. It is reported that good and strong hemp, if spread upon a tree that grows low shoots, when it begins to send out its own shoots, will render the tree dwarf and spread it out. The reason is manifest, because every plant proportions its growth to the capacity of the place.

535. The source from which trees grow are either roots or a kernel. If you place their shoots in the earth (as is permitted in some, especially the mulberry), some of them will sprout; but (as they say) the trees will be low. The reason is, because a shoot does not draw nourishment as strongly as either a root or a kernel.

Various experiments concerning the rudiments and growths of plants, or [a] superfetation in plants.
[a] superplants.

The Sacred Scriptures relate that Solomon wrote a natural history from the cedar in Lebanon to the moss growing in the valley, as the best versions have it. And it is true that moss is only the rudiment of a plant, as it were, the mould of the earth or of bark.

537. Moss is produced especially on houses covered with tiles or thatch, and on the extremities of walls, which presents a clear and pleasant greenness. It grows on slopes, because just as water and moisture generate moss, so it also desires flowing, not stagnant, water. The growth on walls or tiles is due to the dryness of the place, whose moisture, because it is not sufficient for producing a plant, germinates by pushing out moss. Although if, softened by age or other causes, they disintegrate, they sometimes produce plants, such as pellitory, and almost every moss has a tiny stem, besides the hairs and fibers in its lower part.

538. Moss grows in walks, especially those exposed to cold and facing north, as in various open pergolas. Again, if they are frequently trodden upon,

Various experiments concerning foreign plants.

574. It is reported that earth from the Indian climate and distant regions, exported for ballasting a ship to some soil in Italy, produced exotic herbs unknown to Europeans. Also, from their roots, barks, and seeds crushed together, and mixed with other earth, and thoroughly irrigated with warm water, herbs not dissimilar to others arise.
575. Plants transplanted from warm regions and transported to others struggle in pushing out their shoots at the time proper to their own climate. Therefore, so that harm may be averted, nothing more is required than that they be safe against the injury of retardation from cold. It also stands by historical record that grains from warm soil, when transferred to colder soil, surpass in precocity the common grains of colder earth. Among flowers with us, early ones are: primrose, violets, anemones, [a] marsh asphodels, spring crocus, some tulips; all of which are cold, and therefore, as it seems, they grow, perceiving the sun's heat more keenly than warm herbs; just as a cold hand perceives the slightest heat more quickly than a warm one. \*Various Experiments concerning the duration of herbs or trees.\*

583. Durability is most conspicuous in those which have the largest body, such as oaks, elms, chestnuts, [a] the lotus tree, etc. But this concerns trees; for in herbs the opposite often holds true: since borage, cabbage, melons, though of quite vast bulk, are of short duration, and hyssop, savory, germander, thyme, sage remain intact for a long time. The reason is, because the vitality of trees depends on the measure of their vigor and the quantity of their sap, being otherwise sufficiently protected by the circuit of their bark against injuries from the air. Herbs, however, are nourished by languid sap, armed with soft bark, and those which excel in longer life are of pungent odor and woody stem.
584. Nut-bearing trees surpass fruit-bearing ones in the prerogative of durability; especially those whose fruits are more moist; such as oak, beech, chestnut, walnut, almond,

a] *the Loat-Tree.*

--- Page 381 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VI. 337
almond, pine, etc., surpass
apple, pear, plum, etc. in durability. The cause is
the fatness and oiliness of the sap, which resists
consumption more than watery [sap].
585. Trees which leaf out later,
and shed their leaves later, surpass in longevity those
for which leaves sprout and fall earlier. The cause is,
because slower production indicates a more fixed moisture,
the other a more loose, and more easily dissolvable [moisture]:
the same reason holds, why wild trees

The cause is, because the sap repressed in the bark
does not burst forth at once (as in the bodies
or trunks of trees or the stalks of herbs)
until they put forth branches; and when they
burst forth, they emerge by chance, by whatever way
is given in the bark. It is true, that some
come forth with more dispersed branches, as is customary for the holm oak,
winter pear, quince apple, medlar,

and rise to a [a] boss at the end, as the pear
(whose origin critics derive from πῦρ, fire),
orange tree, fir, service trees,

as the beech, [b] hornbeam, &c.
the others behave more indifferently. The cause why they thus dis-
perse their branches, is the hurried eruption of sap,
from which they do not produce a body of proper
height, but with branches wandering about the ground.
The cause of the pyramid (shape), is the repression of sap long
before it sends out branches, and its consumption at an equal
rate as soon as they emerge.
Dispersion comes from sap abundantly carried upwards
without consumption, and is simultaneously hurried
without interruption.

**Various Experiments concerning the Principal Differences of Plants.**

591. Few plants flower before they leaf out, such as the almond, peach tree, dogwood, blackthorn, etc., but for most, the leaves precede the flowers, as shown by the apple, pear, plum, cherry, hawthorn, etc. The cause, in those where the flowers precede, is an acrid spirit (therefore they usually produce fruit earlier in springtime, but whose maturity is later, like most of the aforementioned particulars) or an oily sap, more apt for producing leaves than flowers.

*Various Experiments concerning the Method*
*of Composition and Improvement of Soils.*

595. That which first presents itself and is the most common aid, is manuring. In goodness, sheep dung surpasses others; cow dung holds second place; horse dung is held in third place, but its heat must be tempered by mixture. Pigeon dung especially benefits the garden, and is applied in moderate measure to the soil. The method of manuring that comes into use is this: that the earth accustomed to be turned by the plough should receive the scattered dung immediately before ploughing or sowing, and thus be covered by ploughing. For if it is cast long before over the fields, the Sun boils away much of the richness. If the land is pasture, scatter it somewhat later and near winter, so that it languishing
                                                               cens

--- Page 389 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VI. 345
...the languishing heat of the Sun may dry it out less. Concerning composition which specifically relates to horticulture (as concerning a heated bed, etc.) [a] we have spoken before.

596. Another method is to sprinkle various earths, such as marl, lime, sea sand, marsh earth, earth added on top of earth, and to temper them by mixing them variously. Marl is recommended by its richness and a heat that is moderate between extremes. Next is sea sand, to which, without doubt, there is some prerogative of virtue from salt, the rudiment of life. Lime somewhat burns the earth too much; so that it is more suitable for cold-loamy or wet places. But I was present at the discussions of very experienced farmers, when he said that those commonly err who think lime is beneficial to arable land, but not to pasture, since it is profitable both for grass and for grain. But that the error was occasioned by the fact that land worked with lime, with varied and uninterrupted [b] produce, they wear out and exhaust, so that afterwards, when exhausted, it provides only sparingly for grass. Furthermore, there is a suspicion among some intimately skilled in the art of agriculture, that collected ferns heaped upon stony ground (a frequent practice) do not constitute approved agriculture according to the rules of the art, because they retain the earth's heat, lest it dissipate.

--- Page 393 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VI. 349
But these things are done solely for the benefit of meadows, which have a river far distant. The other is, the derivation of water from lands where springs are found, down slopes into lower ground through channels, from which, when led across, the water may flow out more widely dispersed. And this drawing off creates hope of profit from a more fortunate yield of grain and grass; the more splendid, the more fertile the sloping land is, because it carries away with it something scraped off from the richness of the soil. But in whatever way it is finally viewed, it never lacks utility. Generally, where marshes and anything similar to them overflow as if by a flood of water, that overflowing through the winter increases of water provides fertility for the following summer. The reason may be, that it both preserves the heat of the earth and nourishes the earth itself. But those experienced in marshes affirm that ditches or channels should be managed thus, lest too long a stay of stagnant water generate marsh sedge and rushes. For then the land, like a grove, excludes the Sun, from which the lingering moisture causes the grass of that year not to be as desired. So much for irrigation. What pertains to avoiding and draining off an excessive quantity of water, and aids to the land in that kind, will not escape our diligence elsewhere.

Various experiments concerning the affinities and differences of plants and inanimate bodies.

601. [Decorative initial Q]hatever distinction there is between animate and inanimate things we will accurately consider under a heading to which we set aside a treatise on life, vital spirits, and faculties; being content here with a cursory narration. Therefore, these differences are reduced to two main points, since spirits and a pneumatic part are present in all bodies. But two things especially distinguish animate and inanimate things. The first is, that whatever spirit animates living things, flows undivided with a continuous current into veins and hidden channels, like blood; except that it does not only have its own branches, but

--- Page 395 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VII. 351
but certain ventricles or receptacles,
the seat of the principal spirit, and to which they are, as it were,
channeled. But the spirits of inanimate things are en-
closed, and cut off from the tangible parts,
impervious to each other; as air exists in snow.
Secondly, that all spirits of animated things are
more or less kindled and have something subtle of a
flame mixed in, and in substance become airy. But
inanimate bodies nourish spirits that cannot be inflamed.
Nor does this difference denote the heat or cold
of spirits; for cloves, and other aromatics, naphtha
or petroleum consist of the hottest spirits
(far exceeding the heat of oil, wax) but not kindled;
and whatever among these temperate bodies, fostering
more languid spirits, is inflamed, becomes strongly
hot beyond others where they are not inflamed,
besides light and motion, etc.
   602. Secondary differences, and which
arise from the former as from radical ones, are these.
To all plants there is a figure from a determined
conformation, not to inanimate bodies. For note,
how far the spirit can be continuously dispersed,
nor abandons its series, so far does the
configuration proceed, and its limits from the utmost

Both send forth spirits branching out, which they protrude in a continuous flow, and possess those apt for inflammation, but those (spirits) in animals have ventricles and receptacles,

_Miscellaneous experiments concerning_
_Plants._

610. The Indian Fig sends down its branches within
one year so much curved, that it spontaneously
puts forth new roots, by which again,
being multiplied from one another,
one tree exhibits the appearance of a grove. The cause
is the abundance of sap, and the softness of the trunk,
which depresses the branches, if they are too much laden, and not strongly
supported. The leaves equal the width
of a small shield, the fruit the thickness
of a pea. The reason is, that continuous
shade helps in increasing the leaves,
while the fruit, which is of the sweetest taste, is defrauded (of nourishment).
And without doubt it is from the oily
humidity and the tenderness of the sap which renders the
branches in that plant so flexible.
611. Someone among the ancients asserts,
that among the Indians there is a tree, which for a few, but
immense—

a] Bee-Flovvers.

immense leaves, three cubits in length and two cubits in width, and bears fruit of excellent taste growing from its bark. It could be that there exist plants which propel sap so vigorously that there is not enough time either to distribute it into various branches or to form a stem capable of bearing fruit. Among us, if a comparison is drawn, trees generally have small leaves. The fig tree bears the largest, then the vine, mulberry, sycamore. Of the last rank are the willow, lime, thorn. But you will find places where herbs, rather than trees, have the prerogative of large leaves, as in burdock, gourd, cucumber, cabbage. The cause coincides with that which we gave for the Indian fig: a rapid and copious expulsion of sap.

612. There are three things which popular use has made most highly commended for their sweetness: sugar, honey, and manna. The first was scarcely known to the ancients and rarely in use. It is found in reeds, but let it be inquired whether in a primary or a secondary way, or whether the bark of the reed also yields sugar. Bees make or collect honey. I remember hearing from a man whose industry in the study of agriculture excelled, that bees are occupied in preparing wax, and that at the beginning of the month of May he found beehives devoid of honey, and within

It may seem true that the sap and tears of certain trees are of a sweet taste. Also, sweet juices from certain fruits could be prepared by decoction for various uses, perhaps with the consistency of honey or sugar. But sun-dried raisins, figs, and currants would more readily promise this, though the method should still be investigated.

An experiment with a hard tree, such as a service-tree or a fir, implanted in sand, would be useful.

620. I took care to keep old cinnamon very dry at germination time, more than other plants, and everything by which others prospered, turned to its detriment. A cause embracing so many effects could equally be given: the nourishment, which that plant draws more sparingly. Let it be investigated how far Cassia, substituted for cinnamon, proves these things in itself.

622. Today's vines are of a lesser magnitude than that in which they were formerly seen, when cups and the image of Jove were fashioned from them. But they seem to have been wilder in their nature. **629.** It is an observation of the ancients that fruits, placed in jars submerged below well waters, last a long time.

**630.** Of herbs and plants, some, even raw and not having undergone the work of cooking, are used for meals, such as lettuces, endive, purslane, garden tarragon, nasturtium, cucumbers, muskmelons, radish, etc. Others only when cooked, such as celery, Roman sage, parsnip, turnip, asparagus, cultivated thistle (although even this, while it is tender and young, is not rejected from the table, and is edible even uncooked). The eating of others is not made suitable by any preparation, such as wormwood grass, wheat in the blade, centaury, hyssop, lavender, melissa, etc. The reason is, because these herbs, condemned for eating, lack two flavors containing all nutritive power, fatness and sweetness; or on the contrary, they consist of bitterness and a sharp taste, or of a juice so crude that it cannot be cooked to any maturity of nourishment. Those herbs or plants which may be eaten raw are strong in both qualities already mentioned (which is the nature of all edibles), such as onion, lettuce, etc. But in sweetness we require this (since the stomach admits what is sweet) that it not be too thick and heavy: for parsnip and garlic

      632. The seeds of most plants excel leaves or

the heat of this plant is very dissipable, which,
confined underground, gains strength, but exhales,
vanishing, at the touch of air.

   636. There are two excrescences accustomed to grow on trees and to be considered fungi. One, called "boletus" by the Romans, found on the roots of oaks, and used as a delicacy for tables. 639. Plants from which, when cut, milk spurts out, are the fig, old lettuce, [a] sow-thistle, [b] spurge, etc. The reason is perhaps a rudiment of putrefaction, since that milk betrays acrimony, although it is thought to possess a lenitive faculty. For paper written with fig milk bears invisible letters, unless it is brought near fire; by which action you may see it turn black, so that a sharp and biting juice may thereby be proven. Lettuce of such age as to contain milk is infamous for poison. Spurge also is of a poisonous nature; and although sow-thistle feeds rabbits, sheep and other livestock nevertheless shun them. Add, that their milk, by opening warts and quickly consuming them, reveals a corrosive power. You will also find that wheat and any other kind of grain, if you remove it from the earth before the sprouts emerge, abounds in milk. The beginning of germination itself is nothing but a certain putrefaction of the seeds. In spurge (Euphorbia) there is milk, though not excessively white, yet of remarkable acrimony. The milk of celandine turns yellow not without sufficiently strong acrimony, and is a remedy for eyes suffering from cloudiness, and for purging catarrhs.

662. An observation from antiquity by some, that the winds which the East sends forth, although they are cold and blow not without harm to fruits, yet the South winds sometimes reign with a damaging blast, especially while the tree is in bloom, and the sky is rainy; so that they altogether stir up excessively humid conditions. Zephyrus (the West wind) is considered most benign, and diligent investigation has also shown that green winters, not bound by frost, harm trees; so much so that if such a winter recurs two or three times, it kills almond and other trees. The cause coincides with the preceding one, because, namely, the vigor of the earth, too much consumed, fails; some of the ancients, namely, commending warm winters.

A scarcity of plants clearly reveals the leanness of barren land, especially with their color tending towards dark. 668. The grafting of vine onto vine (such as my imagination suggests to me) has today become obsolete, though used by the ancients, and indeed in three ways. The first was that which was commonly known. The second was the boring of the middle trunk, which would receive adopted shoots. The third was, of two vines growing with, as it were, conjoined growths, the cutting back to the pith, and their tight binding together.

Another disease is the production of sterile darnel and wild oats, into which grain (barley especially) often degenerates, and it arises from the weakness of the sown grain, which if it has been either too old or moldy, is accustomed to produce darnel. Another (cause is) the satiety of the earth, which by continuing the yield of the same grain (I do not mean growing there, but grains of the same species, for example, barley, wheat, etc.) falls short of its former fertility; so that it is fitting not only for the soil to rest, but also for the seed to be changed. Also there is a harmful blast of winds, which harm at two times, either while they shake off the flowers, or (when) the grain is in full maturity. Another plague of the farm is great heat when wheat pushes out ears, rare among us, frequent in hotter regions; so that the calamity (calamitas) may have originated from the stalk (calamus), when the grain could not emerge from the stem. Equally harmful is excessive moisture at the time of sowing, infamous among our countrymen for great scarcity of grain, so that the grain does not grow at all; whence they are often forced to sow summer grain in the place where winter grain had been sown. *A solitary experiment concerning the healing of wounds.*

677. I find it recorded by ancient writers that skins, especially of rams, freshly removed and applied to wounds, prevent them from swelling up and becoming ulcerated, and, once consolidated, heal them again. Egg white has the same power. The cause is a moderate agglutination, since each body is tenacious and viscous, and with the defluxion of humors repelled from the wounds, it does not compress too much.

*A solitary experiment concerning the fat which is diffused through the flesh.*

678. All flesh can generally be turned into a fatty substance, if it is cut into small pieces, and the parts are placed in a glass closed with a membrane, which is placed in boiling water for six or seven hours. This experiment may be profitable for preparing fat or grease for various uses. But it is necessary that the flesh be unsuitable for human consumption, such as horse, dog, bear, fox, beaver, etc.

  A solitary experiment concerning

  680. Beasts are hairy compared to men,

liquid, and their flesh is generally dry.

Solitary Experiment concerning the swiftness of motion in birds.

681. The swiftness of birds in motion exceeds that of beasts, whose flight for the most part no beast's running equals. The cause is the greater abundance of spirits in birds in proportion to the smallness of their body, than in beasts. The reason brought forward by some, that that motion partakes of carriage, while beasts walk, is invalid, since thus swimming ought to be swifter than running. And that carriage does have the subsidiary aid of wings to be accomplished.

   684. The bottom of a vessel full of hot water

685. It did not escape the diligence of the

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*hiccup.*

686. It is from the same workshop of antiquity
that sneezing drives away hiccup. The reason is, because the movement of hiccup is an elevation of the stomach, which sneezing somewhat depresses, and diverts the movement elsewhere. For first, we see hiccup arise from too much food ingested (especially in children), whence an extension of the stomach. Also acidic food and drink causes the same by irritating the stomach, and this movement ceases either by diverting or by holding the breath. The former happens in sneezing, the latter is clear from the fact that held breath partly removes hiccup. You will feel the same with the mind turned to serious matters, as is commonly done; and with vinegar applied to the nostrils or gargled, because it constricts and inhibits the movement of the spirits.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*sneezing.*

697. Looking at the Sun causes sneezing. The cause is not the heating of the nostrils (for otherwise, if the nostrils were merely open to the Sun, it would only excite it for a moment), but the depression of the humors of the brain, which suffuse the eyes, whence by a sympathetic movement they are drawn to the nostrils and create sneezing. Thus, conversely, internal tickling of the nostrils draws humors to the nostrils, but by sympathy to the eyes, which are moistened. But yet, observation dictates that one accustomed to sneeze frequently can overcome sneezing if he rubs his eyes until they are suffused by a flow of watery humor. The reason is the diversion of the humor, which was about to descend to the nostrils, to the eyes.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*the weakness of teeth.*

688. Teeth are more affected by cold drink or similar things than other parts. The reason is twofold: because bone resists cold more than flesh, which yields to it; whence from the resistance of the bone, the cold is intensified. Secondly, because these parts are bloodless, since blood tempers cold; therefore a strong impression on the nerves—

bloodless. Thus sharp cold renders bones fragile;

Various experiments concerning insects.

Let human industry labor worthily and profitably in examining the nature of vivification; whose ingenious workings small things usually reveal better than large ones, imperfect things than perfect ones, parts than the whole. Thus, they propose that vivification generated from putrefaction should be known more exactly, by contemplation that will be most profitable; first in explaining the vivification of

696. The material of insects is varied. Some are born from mud or dung, such as worms, eels, snakes, etc. For both kinds are from putrefaction, as they lack any means of preservation when water and the Moon are waxing. As for dung, all excrements are ejected matter of putrefying nourishment. Others [are born] in wood, either growing or cut. Let it be inquired which woods produce these offspring more, and what season of the year. We see polypod worms, accustomed to rolling themselves into balls, generated especially under logs, not in the wood itself. They are also said to be found in gardens, where there are no logs at all. But their generation requires some receptacle, against the sun, rain, dew, such as is provided in wood: therefore, being free from venom, and among

Others are born in the hair of living creatures, such as the louse, and a skin growth from sweat, more tightly confined and somewhat dried by the hairs. The excrements of living creatures are not only fertile for insects when separated from the body, but also when retained within it, as worms show, a problem most frequent for children, especially in the intestines. Recent experience of doctors has also taught that when diseases, especially pestilential ones, are often raging, worms are found in the extreme parts of the body where excrements are absent, not putrefied humors. Fleas, in particular, are produced by straw and matting somewhat moistened, or by the straw of a bed not exposed to the air; it is a received opinion that these are killed by scattering wormwood in those places. It has also been observed as true that bitter things contribute more to removing putrefaction than to promoting it; while fatty and sweet things especially contain the rudiments of putrefaction. There is a worm which flour produces, in the shape of a large white termite, a delight to the nightingale. Clothes and other woolen goods create moths, especially if you store them damp and wet, and it (the moth) delights in the flame of a candle. carrots, etc. The source of others is water, especially shaded and stagnant water, such as six-footed aquatic spiders; flies called phryganium, accustomed to be born from matter floating on the surface of the water, and usually found around lakes. Also, the dregs of spoiling wine are impregnated with a worm, which afterwards (as some among the ancients observed) changes into a gnat. And we owe to Antiquity, attesting from experience, that aging snow brings forth a worm of reddish color, slow in movement, surviving its birth for a short time. The reason why that worm, once born, perishes so suddenly, could be the sudden exhalation of its tender spirit, once it has withdrawn from the surrounding cold and the cold in which it was enclosed. For as heat animates butterflies, which are torpid in cold; so predatory heat destroys those spirits which cold protects. It is an experience confirmed by the consensus of both Ancients and Moderns, that in brass and copper furnaces, into which chalcites (commonly called vitriol) is often thrown and smelted for correcting the operation, a fly suddenly emerges, which sometimes moves as if clinging to the sides of the furnace, sometimes is seen beneath the fire, and having left the furnace, perishes. The spirit dilated in a hot furnace immediately freezes at the sensation of moderate cold. Without doubt, this action also receives aid from chalcitis, for which the spirit is eager to produce and germinate, as is established by the evidence of chemical experiments. To conclude, from most putrefied things are born insects of various names, which I need not enumerate now.

697. The ancients teach that insects are nourished by a small amount, but this escapes the diligence of observers. For cicadas devour whatever is green in the whole region; silkworms quickly consume leaves; ants gather a large supply of food for themselves. It is true that animals accustomed to indulging much in sleep live on little food, such as dormice, bats, etc., for they are bloodless. The reason perhaps is that the juice in their bodies is unique, not truly blood, flesh, skin,

bones, as in perfect animals; while there is a great

Bees, however, are found to live seven years;

To most insects (like butterflies and other

698. In insects, movement is voluntary, and therefore also imagination. But of the ancients who said that their movement is indeterminate, and their imagination indefinite, they betrayed their negligence. For ants directly seek their hiding places, and bees, not without the admiration of observers, discern the way by which they seek their hive from the flowery plain of the fields, through two or four miles. Perhaps in gnats and flies, imagination is more changeable and dizzying; just as some of the ancients attributed only touch to small birds. But they fell short of the truth; for if they tend directly somewhere, it is necessary that they be endowed with sight. Furthermore, they make a choice of the flower or herb in which they take more delight; therefore, they also possess taste. Bees are also recalled by the sound of agitated air; which argues for hearing, and, although their spirits go diffusely, that the seat of the senses is given in the head.
Furthermore, what matters pertaining to insects pressed themselves to be annexed to this topic, along with their enumeration, we relegate to the heading concerning animals in general.

***A solitary experiment concerning***
***running.***

**699.** The speed of a runner is increased by a weight held in the hands. The reason is, because a weight (namely, a proportionate one) by contracting the nerves, strengthens them. Where this contraction is not needed, the weight will be a hindrance; which is evident in a race instituted by horses. For they carefully take precautions, lest one horse be burdened more than another by even the slightest weight. In running with a weight, the arms are first pushed backwards, then forwards, with perceptibly increasing momentum; for the hands are sent back before they are moved forward. Inquire, whether a movement of the spirits contrary to the intended movement, and that immediately before we begin to move in the destined direction, causes the spirits, more vehemently impelled, to burst forth; just as a spirit drawn in and held back is expelled more vehemently. In throwing also, the arms are drawn back, so that the rotation may be stronger.

702. Not far from the bottom of the straits

When drawn onto the shore, they feign the amplitude of a mass;
when compressed, they occupy the least amount of space.

      Various Experiments concerning
                sweat.

   706. A bath of hot water does not draw out sweat
from the parts under the water. The first reason
is, because sweat is a kind of liquefaction,
which only the driest or the most humid heat
produces. For excessive moisture somewhat
extinguishes heat, just as hot water [extinguishes] fire;
and excessively dry heat closes the pores.
Therefore, someone covered in the sun or by the fire
will more easily emit sweat than [someone] naked;
and earthenware bottles filled with hot
water provoke sweat in bed more gently
than hot brick baths. Secondly, hot water causes the skin to evaporate,
so that the material is consumed first in the parts
below the water, rather than being turned into sweat.

may come forth. Then, moderately increased heat elicits sweat more copiously than heat that is at first more vehement and equally intense. The reason is that gentle heat opens the pores better than violent heat; with these opened, sweat flows out more freely. Therefore, physicians acted according to the dictates of reason, who, by applying bottles in bed, provoked sweat through sudorific herbs decocted in hot water, measuring the heat by degrees; so that a less hot bottle would take the first turn, and afterwards, a hotter one the second.
     707. The taste indicates sweat is salty. The reason is, because the fresh and sweet part of nourishment is changed into blood and flesh, but sweat is an excretory part.      708. The upper parts of the body emit sweat more than the lower parts. The reason is, because those parts swell more with spirits, which propel sweat; moreover, they are less fleshy, from which and from drier parts sweat especially comes forth. Such are the forehead and the chest.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*The Glow-worm.*

712. The nature of the Glow-worm has not hitherto been sufficiently explored. It is established that it is generated chiefly during the hottest months of summer, neither in fields, but in brambles and hedges. From this it can be understood the tenuity of the spirit within it, which cannot be attenuated except by summer heat; and furthermore, that this tenuity allows easy exhalation. Italy and warmer regions produce a fly, which is called lucciola there, shining like a glow-worm, and perhaps it is a flying glow-worm; but this fly especially frequents lakes and marshes. However, the two former observations can be referred here. For it is not visible except during summer; and sedges or whatever grows green around marshes, provide shade equally good as brambles. Perhaps the cold of other regions does not allow the glow-worm to grow to such an extent that winged ones are found.

*Various Experiments concerning impres-*

On account of the closed pores of the skin is the erection of the hairs, which, lying obliquely, must necessarily be raised. Recoil is the apprehension of terrible things, and thus it is a contractive movement, and as it were an inquiry, as to what may be the origin of the event; and for this reason it is erective. Hence he who prepares himself for sudden listening recoils, for the spirits raise themselves to attention. Horror is an appetite for expelling that which suddenly struck the spirits.   714. Pain and suffering cause sighing, hiccuping, groaning, trembling and wailing, or shouting, tears, distortion of the face, grinding of the teeth, sweat. Secondly, the cause of laughter is merely a slight contact of the spirits, nor an impression penetrating so deeply, as other passions suggest. Therefore, it is moved with no affinity to mental affections, and indeed strongly from the mere titillation of certain parts in the body; so that someone, even with a mind composed to seriousness, sometimes cannot restrain laughter.
Thirdly, it is always conjoined with some delight, whence exhilaration has an affinity with joy, although the movement is much lighter; true joy is a serious thing.
Fourthly, its object is deformity, absurdity, misfortunes, and similar things.
Now let us speak of the causes to which the mentioned effects can be referred, from which some light shines forth from these general notes. A solitary experiment concerning caterpillars.

728. The caterpillar is among the most common worms, usually produced from dew and leaves, for you may see swarms of caterpillars produced on trees and hedges, causing the greatest part of the damage to leaves on trees and hedges, because they are both born from them and nourished by them. Springtime is especially infested by this plague, because neither dew nor leaves are then lacking, and they are usually generated if the East wind has blown for a longer time. The cause is the dryness of that wind; since all vivification from putrefaction requires that the matter not be too moist. Moreover, what we see covered with spiders' webs, is a sign of slimy dryness; as in lands which spiders' webs cover, appearing from dew and sun. The inner parts of roses also produce green caterpillars, especially those that have not experienced strong winds, in which the dew becomes moldy, but cabbages produce the largest and most numerous caterpillars, with their fat leaves and suitability for putrefaction. Expiring summer shows the caterpillars to be winged, and changes them

--- Page 476 ---
432          OF FRANCIS BACON
and changes them into butterflies or another fly.
There is also a caterpillar with a woolly body, having a great affinity with silkworms.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
           *Cantharides flies.*

   729. Cantharides flies are generated
from a worm or caterpillar; but they infest certain
fruit-bearing trees more than others,
such as the fig, pine, and wild bramble;
all with sweet fruit, which proves some hidden
biting and acrimonious nature. For the fig
contains a milky sap, sweet and corrosive;
the pine nut is sharp and abstergent;
the fruit of the bramble is said to infect children
who eat it with scabies, so that it is not at all
surprising if cantharides possess a corrosive and
cauterizing power. For all other insects are generated
from coarser and duller material.
The body of cantharides shines with color; and perhaps
peacock-colored flies or [*a*] dragon-flies,
dyed with excellent color, have the same corrosive
power.

Weariness is cured by bathing, or anointing with oil, or hot water. The reason is, because all weariness is a kind of bruising and compression of the parts, but bathing and anointing relaxes and softens; and oil mixed with water is better than when applied separately; because water penetrates the parts better, and the oil afterwards softens more effectively. Experience testifies that the use of tobacco drives away weariness. The reason is, because it revives and strengthens the spirits, it opens up bruised or compressed parts, and especially because by the benefit of its opiate virtue it refreshes the spirits, and thus removes weariness; as we also see happen in sleep.

731. When ascending a hill, the knees become weary, when descending, the hips. The reason is, because while one alternates the feet to overcome the mountain, the burden of the body falls upon the knees, in descent, upon the thighs.

*A solitary experiment concerning the use of bathing and anointing.*

740. We wonder that the use of bathing, a part of the regimen, has fallen into disuse. For Romans and Greeks, it was like food and drink. Today, among the Saracens, its practice has not perished; our people only recognizing it as a part of medication. I am of the opinion that bathing, in the way the Romans used it, was harmful to health, by softening the body and making it susceptible to consumption. For the Turks, their dietary regimen is more suited to it, since the drinking of water and the rice they eat, and other food of moderate nourishment, make their bodies solid and hard, so that the fear that the use of bathing might weaken them is vain. Moreover, the Turks enjoy a sedentary life, and rare walking,

--- Page 484 ---
440      OF FRANCIS BACON
and rare walking, with the result that less expelled sweat makes the bath more recommendable to them. Nevertheless, that in the bath, and especially in anointing, when rightly applied, there is an aid to health and to prolonging life. But these things elsewhere, among medical experiments, await an opportunity for discussion.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
         *wavy [a] paper.*

   741. The Turks are excellent makers of the paper which we call wavy; a skill unknown to our countrymen. They take various colors dyed with oil, and sprinkle them, drop by drop, onto the water, and gently stir the water, with which they then moisten somewhat thick paper, which draws the lines of undulating veins, like cloth or marble.

Perhaps someone might think that the cause is from blood very much overcooked; since we see in sausages of common use that blood turns black by boiling. The cuttlefish, however, is a delicacy, and is eagerly sought after.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*the increase in the weight of earth.*

743. They report, whose credibility it is impious
to call into doubt, that earth taken from places
adjacent to the Nile, if both moistening and loss
are prevented, and if it is weighed daily,
remains constant until the seventeenth of June;
on which day the Nile swells; and its weight
increases until the river has reached its proper height. If
the truth of the account does not falter, it has its cause
from nowhere else but the air, which then
begins to condense, and thus changes into
moisture within the small amount of earth, [resulting in] an increase
of weight. It has also been discovered with
cut and weighed Tobacco, that some of its
former weight is lost if it is dried by fire;
and that after being exposed to the air, it recovers whatever
it lost. It can be seen that the swelling river
brings about some change in the entire body of air
flowing around it in the vicinity. For (which
has more significant causes for wonder) they truly report,
that on the day the Nile swells, severe plagues
usually arise in Cairo.

744. Those who are very cold, especially in their

    746. Sleep nourishes, or at least preserves

Various experiments concerning teeth and hard substances in the bodies of living creatures.

If a method of restoring teeth were available, one might boast of having discovered a mystery of nature; let men direct their thoughts to this matter. Be that as it may, the nature of teeth deserves investigation, as much as other parts of living creatures.
747. There are five solid and harder substances in the bodies of living creatures: the skull, a tooth, bones, horns, and claws/nails. The head everywhere displays many things of this solidity, as it has both the skull entirely of bone, teeth, jawbones, and that somewhat hard instrument of hearing from which horns emerge; so that the structure of living creatures is like the framework of a building,

--- Page 488 ---
444      OF FRANCIS BACON
(for they lack) an eggshell, and feathers, since a spur is nothing different from a nail/claw. But no animals which have a harder shell (such as oysters, conches, mussels, scallops, lobsters, crabs, freshwater turtles, the humpback shrimp, and especially the tortoise) have internal bones, but only cartilages.
   748. Bones, having reached the measure of their proper growth, remain in the same size; the skull also, and horns in some animals are shed and renewed; teeth, in a state as it were of growing, are not increased, except that use wears them down. Nails/claws grow continuously, also beaks, so much so that they protrude, which in eagles and parrots are changed.
   749. Most of the hard substances have withdrawn to the outermost parts of the body; such as the skull, horns, teeth, nails/claws, beaks. Bones alone are internal, covered by a mantle of flesh. All viscera lack bones; except that sometimes a bone has been found in the heart of a stag, perhaps also in other animals.
   750. The skull is the receptacle of the brain, which resembles marrow. The spine has an unformed marrow, with great affinity to the brain, and which is different from other bones of the body. The jawbones do not contain a peculiar marrow, but a little pulpy-

751. Among substances notable for their solidity, none is endowed with sensation except teeth; nor are they only sensitive to pain, but also to cold.

But other things by which the structure of a substance hardens, let us relegate to their proper place, content with the inquiry made concerning teeth.

Various experiments concerning
visible phenomena.

761. It is beyond controversy that light is augmented by refraction just as much as colored objects are. For just as the magnitude of a solid object increases at the bottom of water, so too does that of a candle, which is held placed in a lantern under water. I remember having heard of an experiment where glow-worms, inserted into glass and placed under water, were used to attract fish.

--- Page 496 ---
452 OF FRANCIS BACON
fish. But so far it is unknown to me whether a diver, carrying open eyes under the waves and floating on his back, sees things situated in the air as enlarged or diminished. For it is undoubted that if the eye is situated in a thinner medium, and the object in a thicker one, the presented image grows. Conversely, when the eye's rays pass through a denser medium, if the object is situated in a thinner one, what will happen is unknown to me.

762. It would be expedient to investigate more deeply whether reflection might not cause greater refraction than rays emitted directly. For example, take an empty basin, and place a gold coin or anything else in it; then move further away from the basin until the sight of the coin vanishes, as being out of the direct line of sight. Then let the basin be filled with water; reflection will represent it in a place not its own. Therefore, to proceed, insert a mirror into the water-filled basin; I suppose the image will not be seen directly, or at equal angles, but obliquely. I wonder if this experiment could not be arranged so that the image appears in sight, the mirror being undetected by the eyes. Here novelty vies with charm; the image, like a spirit, about to occupy the air and thus become visible. For example, opposite a cistern or marsh let there be placed

--- Page 497 ---

let a picture of the devil or whatever you wish be placed, yet so that the water is not perceived by the eyes; and let a mirror be placed. If from an oblique angle, the picture of the devil strikes the sight, not the water, you will have the likeness of the devil appear before you. Now for a long time among the Oxonians (people of Oxford) the rumor holds that the Monk Roger Bacon passed through the air between two obelisks of two temples, which was then believed to have been done by means of glasses, although he was walking on the ground.

Various experiments concerning impulse and percussion.

763. A heavy body, once moved, is more easily impelled than the first time when it was at rest. The reason is, partly because motion dispels the inertia of a solid body, which besides the motion of gravity, also has in itself a natural desire for rest; partly also, because a body at rest suffers a stronger compression of its parts from the resistance of the body in which it rests, than it would have from itself; so that a greater force must be applied to dislodge it from its state. For if a heavy body is suspended, even by a thread, the impulse will be equally easy as if it were entirely in motion.
764. A huge or very small body so

--- Page 498 ---
654          OF FRANCIS BACON
cannot be projected as far as another of me-
dium measure, so that, according to the law of pro-
portion, a force commensurate with the body
moved, which moves it, seems to be required. The cause is, because
impulsion does not occur without the virtue of the moving body
and the resistance of the moved; but if the body
is of enormous magnitude, it yields more slowly;
if of smallness, it does not resist strongly enough.
     765. It is commonly known that no weight
presses and breaks so strongly if placed upon another
body, as if it is impelled or struck from above. Perhaps
something is to be attributed to the air in promoting
percussion. But the principal cause seems to me to be, because the parts of the body moved by impul-
sion or by continuous motion of gravity have compression downwards equally
as if projected and emitted through the air, forwards.
I also conceive that the swift relaxation of this motion
prevents the resistance of the lower body; the priority of forces
everywhere proving its efficacy, as appears in infinite instances.

               *tickling.*
     766. Tickling is most perceived in

                                             parts

covers parts, also by rare contact of them. For all titillation is a slight movement of spirits, which thinness of skin, sudden and rare contact promotes. Thus a feather or reed lightly wandering over the lips or cheeks, excites titillation, not a blunter or harder contact. As for sudden contact, it is clear that no one is tickled by himself; also the palm, with skin equally thin as the parts already mentioned, does not admit titillation, due to the frequency of contact. Titillation also moves laughter. The cause perhaps, an emission of spirits and thus of the soul, by flight from titillation, in which a recoil and recession of the part is always noted so that it may avoid it. Also, when the nostrils are tickled internally by a feather or straw, they excite sneezing; which is a sudden emission of spirits, and expels humor. There is also titillation joined with pain, so that it cannot be tolerated.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*the scarcity of rain in Egypt.*

767. It is strange that, with the Nile flooding Egypt, as it is accustomed to happen, thin or no rains are felt in that region. The cause can be referred either to the nature of water, or of air, or of both. Of water, if also a longer [aspect] is considered

--- Page 500 ---
456      FRANCISCI BACONI
a course is given, that with a swift, rapid flow it exhales less than stagnant water; and its concoction, when properly concocted, does not evaporate as much as when raw, just as water boiling over a fire emits vapors more sparingly after a moderate interval from the first boiling than at the very beginning. It is also established that the waters of the Nile are found to be sweeter in taste than others, by common judgment; and are recommended for calculus and hypochondriacal melancholy; whence a soothing virtue is inferred; and are carried through a hot climate, a flat region not shaded by woods or mountains; so that it is necessary for the Sun, pressing down with great force upon the river, to remove its crudities. It can be attributed to the air (I conceive its role in this scarcity of rain to be primary) that it is thin by nature and thirsty, and eagerly absorbs watery moisture, and disperses it throughout its entire body in such a way that it does not allow it to remain in the form of vapors by which it might swell into rains.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*leafless plants.*

769. Scarcely are plants found which, deprived of leaves, have branches; unless coral is excepted. But the deserts of St. Macarius in Egypt nourish a plant, long, leafless, of black color, branched like coral, except that its top is closed. That plant, taken into houses and placed in water, unfolds in a wonderful way; and a superstition has seized the people living in the vicinity, that it helps women suffering in childbirth.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the pro-*
*hibition of putrefaction & the long pre-*
*servation of cadavers.*

771. The preservation of cadavers for many years, with the marks of their dimensions intact and not disappearing in any part, deserves no ordinary attention; as appears in Egyptian mummies, some of which are believed to have lasted three thousand years. Indeed, the method of removing the brain, and the viscera whose corruption you can scarcely prevent, is understood by them; but that is not so great as to express admiration. For we see how soft a substance flesh is, and most easily prone to putrefaction above the other parts of the body. But it could be seen from our observation and axiom, which we gave in the hundredth experiment, that putrefaction, in my conception, is a natural period of bodies, only an accident; nor is matter the cause of accelerated corruption. Whence it is established that bodies in shining amber, mercury, balsam (of which we have already spoken), wax,

wax, honey, gums, and perhaps in snow-preservers
or snow-storehouses, etc., to be preserved for a very

what was said in that experiment, to repeat
those things which pertain to annihilation.
For if the three things accustomed to causing putrefaction
are prevented, corruption can be entirely kept
away. The first is, that air be excluded, which
silently undermines the body, and as it were conspires
with its spirit towards dissolution. The second,
that what is around and adjacent to the body should
not be of the same material, but entirely heterogeneous
with respect to the body to be preserved; for thus
the one can receive nothing, and nothing can proceed
from the other. Such are Mercury, white amber
in herbs, flies, and bodies of that kind. The third,
that the body to be preserved should not be of such
a mass that it can spontaneously dissolve into corruption,
even if nothing of it exits into the adjacent body.
Therefore, it ought to be rather slender and small, than
vast. And a fourth aid is given, that if the body
to be preserved is of such a magnitude as it is usually
seen, then the containing body should be endowed
with the faculty of attracting and drying out the moisture
of the contained body, lest putrefaction, begun
internally, should gain strength, although nothing may exit.

I remember Livy relating that once two leaden caskets were found in a certain monument; and in one the body of King Numa, in the other the books of sacred rites and the discipline of the Pontiffs were enclosed. The casket containing the corpse exhibited nothing but a few light ashes at the extremities; the other [casket] the books so unharmed and entirely free from damage, as if it had been a recent Scribe's writing. A singular observation concerning the
abundance of nitre on certain shores.

772. Near the fortress of Catia, and the wells
of Assanios in Idumaea, along a long stretch of
journey, the sea, though rather distant, is perceived
as if it were near; the gleam of nitre from the sands
feigning proximity; such an abundance of nitre
overflows that shore.

A singular observation concerning
bodies which float on water.

773. The Dead Sea, yielding bitumen, is of
such a density that living creatures thrown into it
with hands and feet bound, floated on it and were
not submerged. From this we learn that sinking
under water is nothing other than the body's weight,
by which it exceeds the water's weight; so much
so that it (the liquid) can be rendered so heavy and
strong by mercury perhaps or similar substances,
that it suffices for sustaining iron. Of which thing
I see no use, but it provides an occasion for
imposture. The same principle will show that all
metals, except gold, float on mercury.

A Solitary Experiment concerning a
  fuel which consumes little or nothing.

  774. They say that at the foot of a hill near
the Dead Sea, a black stone is found (held by
Hermits as an aid in preparing fire) which,
burning like coal, knows no diminution, but
increases in splendor and brightness. If this is
true, I do not indeed wonder, since iron glows
red from heat and is not consumed; but that it
endures for some time, that is what may be
wondered at; for the redness of iron, when
removed from the fire, immediately vanishes.
It would indeed be a matter of no small
convenience and profit if a fuel were devised
which, when lit, would both give light and last
for a longer space of time. Nor do I entirely
deny that candles are made from Salamander's
wool, a kind of metal, which, when inflamed,
glows white-hot and is not consumed. The
question is, what feeds the flame, and usually it
is a tangible body consisting of weight. But it
seems possible that a spirit or vapor (both
devoid of weight) might excite it in a body;
such as the material of ignis fatuus. You might
perhaps object that this vapor, about to expire
shortly, would fade away. It will be replied that
by means of oil and wax, or other material
destined for making candles, the flame can be
nourished, without the wick being lit.

A Solitary Economic Experiment
    concerning cheap fuel.
  775. Fossil coal lasts longer than
that from wood, and coal from roots, cut into large
pieces, lasts longer than that commonly used from wood.
Common turf and that from heather are of low price,
and are long-lasting fuels. Coal from branches and
shrubs or thorns, placed on top of coals from vigorous
wood, provides fuel for a long fire.
Sedge is a cheap fuel, frequently used by brewers
and bakers, otherwise useless for other purposes. Let
earth or chalk mixed with fossil coal be investigated. This
mixture (which coal-merchants are accustomed to
use clandestinely), if applied to make the mass of
coal appear greater, is a fraud; but if only the pursuit
of knowledge is considered, it would be a matter of advantage.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning judgments about the salubrity of the air or the contrary.*

777. One ought not to apply oneself idly to this, that, whatever bodies or places you may choose, the salubrity of the air or the contrary should be explored, both as regards the seasons of the year, and the inhabited region. It is certain that in some buildings there is more, in others less, danger to stored provisions and baked goods from mold. Nor would I rashly persuade myself that meat or fish sooner feel harm in this air than in that. Excellent are the experiments which shed light on such things not yet fully understood: for they are useful for natural prognostics of weather, better than the aids of astronomical skill. Moreover, they teach men what locations are to be chosen for habitation, so that health may be safe, and better provided for.

   780. On the southern coast of the Sicilian sea many corals are collected.    *A Solitary Experiment concerning*

   781. Calabria produces the best manna and in abundant yield, which it collects from the leaves of the mulberry tree, (the mulberry trees are) far different from those which grow in the valleys. Manna, like other dews, falls onto the leaves during the night. *A solitary experiment concerning*
*the correction of wine.*

782. A method is circulated by which Greek wine is prepared so that it does not evaporate or intoxicate, by adding a little sulfur or alum; of which the former is unctuous; the latter astringent; nor is it doubted that these two very well prevent evaporation. Let that be transferred to other wines and beers of better quality, by adding substances of a similar nature while they are fermenting, so that they both evaporate less and become more potent.

*A solitary experiment concerning the matter*
*of artificial fire [a] from sulphur,*
*bitumen, and gunpowder.*

783. A not improbable reason has been devised by some, why artificial fire (which is principally bituminous) cannot be extinguished by water, because bitumen first congeals from fire and water mixed, but not sulphur. This is attested by a place near Puteoli, called Vulcan's court, which sends forth horrible thunder from water and fire mutually vexing each other in conflict, with the eruption of hot waters through siphons. Moreover, there is a great quantity of bitumen there; whereas the fires of Etna and Vesuvius, and similar mountains, which are sulphurous, belch forth smoke, ashes, pumice, not water. They also report that bitumen mixed with glue and placed in water, as it were, hardens into the substance of an artificial rock.

A singular experiment regarding a judgment
     on the healing of certain
          ulcers and wounds.

785. The ancients reported that in bodies full of humors and impure, wounds of the calves are healed with difficulty, but those of the head more easily. The reason is that ulcers and wounds in the calves require desiccation, which the downward flow of humors impedes, while ulcers and wounds of the head do not require it, but on the contrary, dryness prevents them from being conveniently consolidated. An observation of our time has found a similar difference between an Englishman and a Frenchman; the former having a humid, the latter a dry bodily constitution; so that a head wound in a Frenchman, and a calf wound in an Englishman, is more difficult to heal.

   *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
               *wounds.*

   787. The same antiquity has transmitted to us in writings,
that wounds inflicted by brass are cured more easily,
than those by iron. The cause, that brass
possesses a healing virtue, and thus brings immediate
remedy. Iron, however, has the power of corroding, not of healing;
so it would be useful, if the instruments of surgeons,
to be used for curing wounds, were made of
brass rather than iron.

seized [by cold], if they are brought near fire, they immediately putrefy. The cause is, because fire suddenly draws out the few spirits remaining in the affected parts, so that the incipient putrefaction is thus completed. From this experiment, the treatment of gangrenes could be aided, whether those arising spontaneously, or those induced by an excessive application of opiates; in which dry heat is to be avoided, and recourse should be had to refrigerants, which possess the capacity to foster internal heat and strength.
