*Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the floating of bodies.*

790. Take two ounces of aqua fortis, and as many drams of quicksilver (for aqua fortis can support that weight); if you dissolve it, it will not support a flint stone the size of a nutmeg. Nevertheless, however, water increased in weight increases its carrying power; just as brine, having enough salt, will carry an egg floating. I remember baths from a certain mineral having been used by a physician for the cure of gout, etc., where a body placed in the bath did not descend as easily as in ordinary water. But it seems the weight of the quicksilver, though greater than that of the flint, compensates for the flint's weight no more than the aqua fortis [does].

*Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the flight of an unequal body in air.*

791. A body of unequal weight (such as of wood and lead, or bone and lead), if it is thrown with its lighter end forward, will ob-

--- Page 517 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VIII. 473
facing forward, it will change its position, and the heavier end will precede, unless the excessive length of the body prevents it. The cause is, because a denser body suffers a more vehement pressure of its parts from the initial impulse; and this is the cause (although hitherto unknown, as has often been said) of all violent motion. And since the posterior part moves more quickly (because it suffers less compression of its parts) than the anterior part can yield its place, it is necessary for the body to turn: for when turned, it is able to draw the lighter part forward more easily. Galileo rightly notes that if an open trough, full of water, is impelled more strongly than the water can follow, then the water collects in a heap towards the posterior part, where the motion began. He (confidently assuming the motion of the earth) established this as the cause of the ebb and flow in the sea, because the earth moves more quickly than the water. Although this theory is false, yet the former experiment is true. The unequal pressure of parts manifestly appears if you take iron or flint, and another body is wood, of the same magnitude and form; when projected with an equal exertion of force, the wood will almost be left behind, as the stone or iron travel further.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*water as a medium for sound.*

792. It is beyond controversy (as we have
partly [a] said before) that water can
become a medium for conveying sound. The collision of two
stones under water produces sound; as does
a long pole struck by pebbles under water. If
anyone thinks sound ascends by means of the pole,
let him observe an anchor lowered by a rope
making a sound, even though the rope is not
a solid body through which the ascending
sound is communicated.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning the flight*
*of spirits from unpleasant objects.*

793. Objects that greatly offend the senses
compel the spirits to retreat, and when these
are scattered in flight, the parts are abandoned,
whence trepidation and horror. As for sounds,
it is found that by the sound of a reciprocating saw or other
sound that is harsh, the teeth are blunted, and the body
is thoroughly permeated by an insinuated horror.
As for taste, we feel the head and
neck shudder from a draught of medicinal potion or taken pills.
Unpleasant odors do the same;
but that effect is less perceived, because by stopping the nostrils, a remedy

   *A solitary experiment concerning*

   794. At Ticinum in Italy there is a temple
windowed only at its highest part, 100 feet

itself to be heard. *Note*, that every reflection of sound
occurs better towards old walls than new ones,
as being drier and more hollow.

Solitary Experiment concerning the power
    of imagination to imitate sense.

    795. Those effects which senses, when struck,
produce, and which flow from actual things,
in some way also depend on imagination.
Hence, he who observes another eating sour
and tart things, and those things by which teeth
become dull and blunted, carries an imagination
imbued with this object, so that from the
sight of another's action, he feels his own teeth
blunted. So he who sees another driven in long
circles, or wheels often going in a circle, he
himself is seized by dizziness; and placed on
high without obstructing barriers or restraints
(unless habit has made it easy), will cling,
wavering with uncertain steps. Many also, from
the sight of another's blood, torture, or strangulation,
suffer a fainting spell as if their own
blood were flowing and they themselves were
being afflicted.

   *A solitary experiment concerning*
      *the submersion of a baser metal in*
               *a more precious one.*

   798. I call that submersion of metal,
when a baser metal is so incorporated into a more precious one
that it cannot be entirely separated. This is a kind
of transmutation, but a spurious one; as if silver
were inseparably incorporated into gold; or copper
or lead into silver. Ancient electrum,
in comparison to gold, was five times the value of silver;
and a composite metal is produced,
equally suited for various uses as gold,
with greater splendor and some prerogative of qualities.
But it admitted such easy separation. If anyone secretly
works on this matter, or with the composition disguised
passes it off as a simple precious metal,
it is an imposture of adulteration. But if it is
attempted deliberately and without deceit, it would be a great
saving of the more precious metal.
I remember having heard from a man most skilled
in metallurgy, that a fifteenth part
of silver incorporated into gold cannot
be recovered by any separating liquid, unless a larger
quantity of silver is added to attract
the smaller [quantity]; which, as he used to say, the ultimate
                                             separa-

--- Page 523 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. VIII. 479
is the ultimate refuge of separation. But this method is complicated by difficulties, so that hardly anyone would undertake to explore it. More accurately, that should be investigated, and the quantity of the fifteenth part should be changed to a twentieth, with a slight addition besides, so that intrinsic incorporation may be promoted. Note, a mixture of silver with gold is detected by a weight test, if it is compared with its dimension. But lead in silver (since it is a heavier metal) cannot be detected; if the excess of weight in the lead is above the weight of the silver.

*A solitary experiment concerning the fixation of bodies.*

799. Gold is a substance that contains nothing volatile, and yet it melts without any difficulty. Melting shows that it is not empty, or devoid of spirits, so that its fixation is not a defect of spirits, causing them to exhale, but an equal distribution of tangible parts, and their tight compaction, whence they have less desire, nor any reason to escape. Therefore, it would be expedient to try whether anything of weight departs from glass after it has been re-melted, for the parts in glass are equally distributed but not so compact as they are in gold; as is evident from the fact that it readily admits

--- Page 524 ---
FRANCIS BACON'S
admits light, heat, cold, and becomes slight in weight. Other bodies are fixed, endowed with few or no spirits; so that nothing can exhale. Such is the material from which goldsmiths' [a] cupels are made, which they place in furnaces, unharmed by the force of fire. Therefore, there are three causes of fixation: equal distribution of spirits and of tangible parts, and their tightening, and the scarcity and extreme comminution of spirits; of which the two former are compatible with a nature apt to be liquefied, but the last one is not.

*A solitary experiment concerning the rest-*
   *lessness of natural things in themselves*
      *and their appetite for change.*

   800. Deep is the contemplation of nature, if one considers the need (so to speak) and dissatisfaction of various bodies, and their appetite for admitting others. Air imbibes light, sounds, odors, vapors; and it is manifest that this is done by it with a certain as it were avidity, as if it were not content with its former consistency; otherwise indeed it would never admit them so easily and suddenly. Water and liquids suddenly receive dry and more earthy bodies proportioned to themselves; dry bodies in turn imbibe waters

and liquids; so that one (which he among
the ancients said concerning terrestrial and aqueous sub-

alone does not admit any body, but either

as a conqueror, or destroys and extinguishes itself.

*Various experiments concerning perce-*
*ption in insensible bodies, ten-*
*ding towards natural divination*
*or subtle experiments.*

[Decorative initial I] t is among the most established truths that all bo-
dies, whatever their nature, even those devoid of
sense, possess some faculty of perceiving. For when
body is applied to body, something akin to choice is
observed in admitting what is agreeable, and in excluding
and rejecting what is disagreeable. Perception, always
preceding action, also distinguishes the altering body
from the altered body; for otherwise, all bodies would
be indifferent to one another. This power of perceiving
far surpasses the subtlety of sense, which comparison
demonstrates to be crude compared to it. Thus,
thermometers or the psychiologion reveal the heat or cold
of the air, even when very slightly varied, which men
would otherwise anxiously exhaust themselves trying to
detect. That perception is sometimes at a distance,
sometimes by contact; as when a magnet attracts iron;
or a flame seizes Babylonian naphtha from a great
                                                                           [end of page, "great" cut off]

--- Page 527 ---
great distance. Therefore, let investigative curiosity be occupied not without glory, which with zeal grasps the subtlety of perception; making it an alternative key for unlocking nature to that of sense, to which (sense) perception is often preferred. It is also the foundation of reason, which animates natural magic, and whatever here presents itself later becomes manifest in great effects of things. Nor does it serve so much to reveal secrets as it aids predictions of future events, as the subtlety of many experiments teaches. For example, when doubting whether seeds are old or new, the reliability of sense fails. If they are boiled in hot water, you will distinguish the new ones by their quicker germination. Of better water, taste is not the indicator, but its sudden consumption; and in other things described previously, it is more safely believed. In Physiognomics, the features of the body will reveal silent impulses which nature arouses, for concealing which dissimulation offers a pretext, or for overcoming which doctrine has been a master. Therefore, for our present undertaking, we prepare material for only a twofold perception, both of which favor natural magic or revelation; setting aside now, and to be rendered elsewhere, the treatise on perception concerning other matters. It is indeed true that other paths also lie open by which one may enter the inner chambers of divination; such as if the causes are not hidden, or if you know the accompanying circumstances, it will be possible to form a judgment about the future effect; which must also be said concerning revelation. But our work will primarily be concerned with that divination and revelation which nature and subtle perception suggest.

Air or water secretly inclining to corruption and putrefaction must undoubtedly be subjected, as it were, to the examination of the inquirer, before a manifest plague and a deadly year come upon trees and crops. So in other things. Therefore, we will propose prognostics of seasons suffering from plague and unhealthiness.

**801.** We have previously discussed the South wind blowing for a long time without rain, or worms in galls or oak-apples [a]; and how a multitude of frogs, cicadas, flies, and similar creatures born from putrefaction portends pestilential years.

**802.** Great and unseasonable heats, which spring (especially May) brings without winds, offer the same omen; and in general, years with rare winds and thunder.

**803.** Notable summer droughts, which extend until the end of August, and the moderate rains that follow them, with the sky then drying up again, presage an inauspicious summer for the following year. *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the sweet smell of the Iris.*

832. The ancients observed that wherever the Iris [rainbow], as if impending or leaning, descends, a sweet odor is exhaled. The cause is the nature of certain bodies, endowed with an inherent sweetness, which the gentle dew of the Iris elicits. Moderate showers produce the same effect, which suffuse the earth with sweetness; but none are as delicate as the dew of the Iris, falling by chance into any place, because sweetness is inherent in the water itself, since the Iris is nothing but agglomerated droplets, which cannot fall unless from a very low atmosphere, which can retain the entire fragrance of herbs and flowers, like distilled water. For rain and other dew, falling from a height, cannot preserve the odor, which exhalation dissipated and lost during ascent. I also wonder if water itself does not possess some rudiment of sweetness. It is true, indeed, that such is not found in marshes, rivers, springs; but good earth, recently tilled, [has] a pleasant and agreeable

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*Fragrance.*

833. Fragrance requires both heat for the matter to be concocted, and moisture for it to be dispersed through exhalations. As for heat, woods and spices are more fragrant in hot regions than in cold ones. As for moisture, it is manifest that things too dry lose their sweetness; and flowers, while budding, bloom more sweetly in the morning than in the evening. For some, fire applied destroys fragrance, such as violets, pellitory, carnation, veronica, and in general all flowers which consist of a cold and delicate spirit. For others, it remains unimpaired in fire and when removed from it, such as rose water, etc. The fragrance of some is scarcely elicited, or at least not so delicately, unless with the aid of fire, such as juniper, and sweet gums, etc., and all odors which lie enclosed in hard bodies. **A solitary experiment regarding foul and fragrant odors.**

835. The excrement of most animals is foul-smelling, especially to those animals which relieve themselves; for we see that pigeons and horses—man excepted—fare best if their stables and the places where they are fed are kept clean. I state the same regarding birds that live confined in cages; and the cat removes its waste, hiding it from sight. This is especially true in beasts whose nourishment comes from flesh <note>original: "ex carne nutrimentum"; referring to carnivores.</note>. Dogs are almost alone among beasts in delighting in foul odors; which suggests something peculiar in their sense of smell, differing from the smell of other living creatures. The cause of why excrement smells foul is evident: because the body itself rejects it, and even more so do the spirits <note>In Bacon’s physiology, "spirits" are the subtle, active substances that govern life and movement; they instinctively recoil from waste.</note>; nor are we ignorant that the excrement of the first digestion smells the worst, such as the waste of the abdomen; that of the second, less so; and that of the third, even less; for sweat is not of such a malignant nature as the other two; especially in men who abound in heat <note>Early modern medicine believed "heat" drove the body's ability to "concoct" or digest materials efficiently.</note>. Thus, a stench flows from most putrefied things, for they either stink or become moldy. A Solitary Experiment concerning
the causes of putrefaction.

836. Of all putrefaction, especially internal, the causes are spirits, and partly the ambient body, whether air, liquid, or whatever it may be. This last occurs in two ways: either by the ingress of substance from the ambient body into the putrefying body; or by the excitation and solicitation of the putrefying body and its parts from the ambient body. The received opinion, that putrefaction is caused by cold, or by internal and preternatural heat, is not far from nonsense. For cold is most hostile to the putrefaction of inanimate things, although it extinguishes vivification, which always consists in attenuated spirits, which cold freezes and coagulates. As for external heat, it is so far correct if adventitious heat, by excess of proportion, predominates over the natural and inherent heat, and over the spirits of the body, leading to dissolution or manifest alteration. But it arises rather from the emission, suppression, or suffocation of the native spirits; and from the confused order and perverse position of the tangible parts, and other unobserved passages which nature establishes, not from a conflict of heats.

--- Page 547 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IX. 503

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*imperfectly mixed bodies.*

837. Where nature works great changes and alterations of bodies, a body is interposed between what previously existed and what subsequently emerges; which is imperfectly mixed, transitory, and not permanent; such as clouds, smoke, vapors, chyle in the stomach, and living things at the beginning of animation. The intermediate action, by which these imperfect bodies are produced, is aptly called by some ancients "inquinatio" (defilement) or "inconcoctio" (unconcoction), which is like putrefaction; for the confused parts cling together until they settle into this or that form.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*concoction and crudity.*

838. The term "concoction" or "digestion" has been primarily transferred from living beings and their organs to liquids and fruits, etc. Thus we call food, urine, and excrement "concocted"; and we hear of four modes of concoction in the stomach, liver, arteries, and nerves, and in each part of the body, and that all indeed proceed from heat. These notions were produced by the stupidity of an intellect scarcely attentive to a few things; which nevertheless especially in

--- Page 548 ---
504      FRANCIS BACON'S
which are commonly met with in human observations. The most consistent notion of concoction is that by which it signifies the degrees of alteration of one body into another, from crudity to perfect concoction, the goal of the action and of the whole process. A body to be converted and altered, while it strongly resists the one attempting conversion or alteration, its prior form and consistency unimpaired, is throughout that time crude and unconcocted; and the process is called crudity and unconcoction; which it is true is perfected by strong heat, but not by heat alone; for all things which promote the endeavor of concoction and alteration, such as rest, mixture of the concocted body, etc., are means for accomplishing concoction. Concoction has two periods: one, which is assimilation, or absolute conversion or subaction; the other, which is called maturation. The former is most conspicuous in the bodies of living creatures, which perfectly assimilate nourishment to the body; and in plants and metals, which exhibit complete transmutation; the latter, namely maturation, is in liquids and fruits in which ultimate conversion is not required or intended, but only an alteration into that form by which the thing becomes suitable for human use; as in the clarification of drink, and the maturation of fruits, etc.
                                                              But

--- Page 549 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IX. 505
But *it must be noted* that there are two kinds of absolute and perfect conversion; the first is when one body is converted into another body, as previously mentioned; as when nourishment turns into flesh, called assimilation. The second is that which produces a completely new body, not previously existing; as if silver could be changed into gold, or iron into bronze. And this conversion, for the sake of distinction, is called transmutation.

*A solitary experiment concerning alterations which may be called major.*

439. The consistency of bodies is varied: dense, rare, tangible, pneumatic, volatile, fixed, determinate, indeterminate, hard, soft, adhesive and non-adhesive, congealable, non-congealable, apt to liquefy and not, fragile, tenacious, flexible and inflexible, tactile or ductile in length, intractable, porous, solid, even and smooth, uneven, venous, fibrous, full of grains, integral, and many others. If all these things are ascribed to heat, cold, humidity, dryness, the contemplation will be compendious but useless. But concerning these, consult our Alphabet of Nature, and throughout this forest of natural experiments. Nevertheless, here we will indulge somewhat in a varied scrutiny of them.

_A Solitary Experiment regarding_
_bodies apt to liquefy and the opposite._

840. Liquefaction results from the detention of spirits, which dwell in the body and open it up. Hence bodies most of all with spirits

--- Page 551 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. IX. 507
swollen with spirits, or where they are more strictly imprisoned, or again, where they dwell more calmly and undisturbed, are apt to liquefy; since bodies behaving in these three ways do not allow the escape of spirits. An example of both of the former properties is in metals, of the latter in tallow, pitch, sulphur, butter, wax, etc. The inclination not to liquefy is due to the easy emission of spirits, which contracts the coarser parts. Hence bodies devoid of spirit, or which lose their spirit more easily, do not liquefy, such as wood, clay, cut stone, etc. However, many of these bodies, incapable of liquefying, become thoroughly or quickly soft, such as iron on an anvil; and a rod hidden in hot ashes acquires greater flexibility. There are also those which liquefy or are dissolved by fire, such as metals, wax, etc. Others are dissolved in water, such as salt, sugar, etc. The cause in the former is the expansion of spirits from heat; in the latter, the loosening of tangible parts, admitting the liquid. There are also those in which both methods are effective for dissolving, such as gum, etc. And these either swell with abundant spirit, or have tangible parts in need of moisture; the former serves the expanding spirits to receive fire; the latter stimulates the parts to admit moisture.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*fragile and tenacious bodies.*

841. Some bodies are fragile, some tenacious and not fragile; and if you try to break some, they yield at the place where force is applied; others separate in such a way that they fly apart into various pieces. The cause of fragility is an inability to withstand extension; thus stone is more fragile than metals; and earthenware more fragile than raw earth; dry wood, than green. The cause of this inability to extend is a small quantity of spirits, which promote the extension and dilation of bodies, and it is usually conjoined with porosity and dryness in the tangible parts. Conversely, in tenacious bodies, the spirits are more abundant and the pores fewer, and the tangible parts more humid. Hence membrane or leather permits extension, paper does not; likewise, a woolen garment endures it, a linen one scarcely.

A Solitary Experiment concerning the alteration of colors in hairs and feathers.

851. In animals generally, age changes the hairs, so much so that it induces grayness, as is clear in man; although in some sooner, in others later. In horses which are distinguished by dappled [*a*] spots, they become white; and in aged squirrels which bear somewhat gray hairs, and in many others. Some birds also, like cygnets, change ash-colored for white; hawks change black ones for more whitish ones. And birds are found which, when feathers have fallen out, put on another color, like the robin, when feathers are changed, gradually reddens anew; as also the goldfinch, on the head. The cause is, because humidity especially imbues hairs and feathers with color; and dryness produces gray and white (hairs/feathers); feathers also, like hairs, drying out with age. As for feathers, when they have fallen out, new ones grow up similar to those of young birds. Thus the beard, being younger than the hair, for the most part grows gray later.    *A Solitary Experiment concerning*
      *the comparative size*

   853. Fish are found larger than any beast;
and the whale far surpasses the Elephant in size. Beasts in general

whereas motion and labor consume. That birds
are surpassed in bulk by beasts, is because these are carried longer
in the womb, and there are nourished
and grow; whereas with birds, once the egg is excluded,
nothing further regarding growth and nourishment
is provided by the mother; for incubation
vivifies, it does not nourish.

A Solitary Experiment concerning
the de-ossification of fruits.

854. In part, we have in the preceding sections described a method of producing fruits without pits and stones. To this, we add that more moisture is required, because stones are formed by drier sap; and it appears possible for the tree to produce only flowers, not fruits; as in cherries with double flowers, all the more so in fruits that lack stones. They say that an apple shoot grafted onto a cabbage stalk produces a large apple without a core. It is probable that if the internal pith of the tree is removed, so that the sap ascends only through the bark, the effect will follow. For observation has taught that in a tree with amputated branches, if water entering from above excavates the top, the yield is more abundant. I add what is reported by others as certain, that if the thinner part of a shoot is inserted inverted, it produces fruits with very small or no stones at all.

*A singular experiment concerning various heats producing the same effects.*

856. The heat of the Sun for ripening fruits, and the heat of living creatures, is represented, and where each is deficient, it is aided by the heat of fire. Thus the heat of the Sun and of life mutually resemble each other. Trees sheltered by chimneys from outside anticipate maturity; vines, admitted within the windows of a room, anticipate the vintage by a whole month. Heaters inserted into walls provide aid for ripening to citrus fruits. Eggs, as some testify, have been hatched by the heat of a furnace. It is recorded that the ostrich lays its eggs under sand, to be hatched by the heat of the Sun.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the Salamander.*

860. Tradition has carried almost all opinions concerning the Salamander, that it lives in fire, and is able to extinguish it. If we are not deceived by the account, two things are required for the effect to be produced: first, a very compact skin, which the flame, being less hot in the middle, cannot penetrate. For we see that the palm of the hand thickly anointed with egg white, with aqua vitae poured upon it and ignited, can bear the flame for some time. The other is extreme cold, and an extinguishing power in the body of that animal, which suffocates the fire. It has been found that artificial fires [a] are better extinguished by milk than by water poured on, because it penetrates more.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*

865. Water contiguous to air cools it, and

avoid mixture, imbibition cannot occur. Therefore,

or a smooth body, nor does it moisten.

Various Experiments concerning Eyes and Sight.

**\*A Solitary Experiment concerning the color of the sea and of any water.\***

874. Motion renders sea water or any other water turbid; rest makes it more transparent. The reason is, because motion does not allow rays of light to pass straight through, whence it becomes darker; while rest transmits the received rays straight through. Moreover, in brightness there is a degree of whiteness, especially if a moderate reflection is present. For a steel mirror shines more brightly than simple glass. This experiment deserves to be extended further, by testing in what way motion impedes sight.

**\*A Solitary Experiment concerning scaly fish.\***

For they are distinguished by sex like other fish, nor are they generated from putrefaction, especially those that move. It is certain that oysters, snails, mussels, devoid of motion, are not separated by that distinction. Inquire, at what time and how are they generated? Oyster shells seem to be born where none were before.

*shadows.*

879. The shadow is observed to tremble at its extremities. The cause is the continuous motion of atoms in the Sun, even when the wind is not perceptible to the senses. Therefore, that motion at the boundary of light and shadow, from light into shadow, and from shadow into light, makes the shadow appear to tremble, because motion is present in the medium.

*A solitary experiment concerning the un-*
*dulation of the sea, and shallows therein.*

880. Shallows and narrow places break waves more than the depth of the sea, extending in every direction. The cause is that the impulse is the same in both cases; except that where there is more water and space, the water moves more slowly, with less uneven rise and fall, or with less mountainous or steep undulation. But where there is less both of water and space, and the water is more dashed against the bottom, it moves more quickly and into a steep fall, which every breaking of waves generates.

A singular experiment concerning the sweet-
ening of salt water.

881. The ancients relate that salt water,
if thoroughly boiled, and when boiled, is cooled,
becomes more suitable for drinking than if it were
raw; although salt, having undergone the distilling
fire, does not rise among the exhaled vapors,
and distilled water is sweet. The reason might be
that part of the salt water rises partly in the
form of foam, partly goes into sediment,
and seeks the bottom; so that it should rather be
called separation than evaporation. But den-
sity prevents it from rising into vapors, just as
bitterness prevents it from rising; for simple waters
of wormwood and similar substances, when they
have been distilled, deposit their bitterness.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning at-*
*traction by similarity of substance.*

883. Ancient writers attest that salt thrown into salt water dissolves more quickly than in fresh water. The reason perhaps is that the salt of the former water draws to itself that which is thrown in by similarity of substance, whereby it happens that, dispersed into the liquid, it vanishes more quickly. An experiment of great value, if its truth is not doubted; for it indicates a principle which makes infusions both quicker and easier, and at the same time it is an excellent instance concerning attraction by similarity of substance. Try it with sugar thrown into water, first into water imbued with sugar, and then into water not previously mixed with sugar.

*A solitary experiment concerning*
*subterranean heat.*

885. Water in wells is warmer in winter than in summer, as is also the air in caves. The reason is, because in parts of the earth not interior, or nearer to the surface, there is a certain degree of heat (as sulfurous veins, etc., show) which winter, being more tightly confined, intensifies, while summer diminishes it, being relaxed by perspiration.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*
*the ascent of water by means of flame.*

889. An experiment commonly discussed, but the cause is hidden. Take a pot, or rather a glass, so that in it you may observe the movement, and place a lit candle in the bottom of a basin filled with water, and invert the mouth of the pot or glass over the candle, so as to cause the water to rise: those who attribute it to the attraction of heat stray from the truth, since it is clear that the movement is one of connection, which they call 'lest a vacuum be given', which proceeds thus. When the flame of the covered candle begins to be suffocated by the compressed air, it gradually diminishes, and then the water rises moderately, the flame gradually occupying a smaller space, and the rise of water corresponds to the diminution. But at the very instant when the candle is extinguished, a large part of the water suddenly rises, because the body of the flame no longer fills any space; and thus air and water take its place. The same will happen if, instead of water, you place flour or sand in the basin—

--- Page 588 ---
544          OF FRANCIS BACON
you might have placed; which argues that the cause is not the attraction of the liquid as if it were nourishment, as is supposed. For all bodies agree in this, that motion has a place in them; as I have observed a glass held in the hand to have lifted the basin and other things from their place, so strongly did the motion of connection affix the bottom of the basin. For that experiment, when the basin was lifted, oil, not water, was used; nor did the outcome disappoint expectation; when first, namely, the mouth of the glass was placed on the bottom of the basin, the water was moderately lifted, then it paused a little, until the candle was almost extinguished, as we said. That first showed attraction; to which we dedicate more extensive work among attractions from heat.

*A Solitary Experiment concerning*

898. Burnt wine is also more austere and astringent than unburnt wine. They say that citron drink made from apple juice ripens on voyages under the equator, while wine and beer turn sour. Also, small jars of verjuice should be exposed to the Sun during summer, like vinegar, so that we may learn whether it ripens and sweetens.

*A solitary experiment concerning animals that hibernate through the whole winter.*

899. There are various animals that sleep through the whole winter: the bear, the hedgehog, the dormouse, the bee, etc., which grow fat in sleep and excrete nothing. The cause of this fatness during sleep could be a defect of assimilation, since whatever is not assimilated is changed into sweat or fat. These animals have been observed for some period of sleep to move absolutely not, but at other times to move indeed, but not from their place; and they seek warm and enclosed retreats for their sleep. It was observed by the Dutch wintering in Nova Zembla that bears fall asleep around mid-November, and then foxes, previously terrified, come out. I find it mentioned by ancient writers that a pregnant bear [a] gives birth to her cubs during her period of sleep; and that a pregnant one is rarely seen.

a] See Exper. 758. & 9.

*A solitary experiment concerning the generation of animals from coitus and putrefaction.*

900. Some animals are fertile by coitus, some are born from putrefaction. And of those which putrefaction animates,

*Various experiments concerning the trans-*
*mission & influence of immaterial*
*virtues & the power of imagi-*
*nation.*

[Large decorative initial P]ythagoras's philosophy, maddened by super-
stitions, gave birth to that monster of imagination,
which the school of Plato and others
afterwards nourished; namely, that the world
is one, entire, and perfect animal endowed with life;
so much so that Apollonius of Tyana, a prophet from the Pythagorean
tripod, affirmed that the ebb and
flow of the sea is the respiration of the world, drawing in
water like breath, and expelling it again. They
proceed and build upon this statement: if the world lives,
it has a soul and spirit, which according to their opinion
is, and is called, the spirit of the world. Nor by this word
do they denote God (although the Deity was not unknown to them),
but only the soul, and the essential form of the world.
With this foundation laid, they were free to invent
whatever specious error might suggest. For in animals,
even those of vast bulk (e.g., in a whale)

--- Page 597 ---
**SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. X. 553**

whale) the sense and affection of any part in the body
is instantly diffused throughout the whole body. Nor
did they wish to imply anything else by that madness of invention,
than that magical operations could overcome any distance of place,
nor be bound by the defect of unprepared matter;
but that (e.g.) Europe could receive the sense of a thing done in China,
and an effect could be produced without and against what matter would allow, with no help
of angels or spirits, but by that unity alone which the
consent of nature produces. There were those for whom not only up to this point
error would deceive, but would drive them wandering further from the straight
path of reason, while they thus assert;
if the spirit in man (whom they call a microcosm),
about to make a suitable impression, flows into the spirit
of the world, the power and efficacy of imagination, and
firm persuasion, can dominate nature. For Paracelsus
and some ignoble authors of magic
attribute to exalted imagination the virtue of miraculous faith.
That vast triviality, compounded of putrid absurdities,
has breathed a lovely madness upon many.
    But we, constantly proceeding through the footsteps of God impressed upon His
works, nor deviating from sense, which is the
lamp of God (and this the breath of man), will soberly and
severely inquire whether nature anywhere allows such
a transmission and influx of immaterial virtue; what the power of imagination (can do),
whether in the body whence it itself arises, or in another. A labor indeed not unlike the
Herculean toils in cleansing the Augean stable, that nature,
of its own right and purged of superstitious magical
observations, may stand; if not to be received with applause,
certainly it will not be entirely condemned. And although
by ranging into this matter occasion will be given everywhere,
yet now it pleases us to open an entrance to other things.

Various cautionary experiments pertaining
to the transmission of spirits and the power
of imagination.

901. Men should be warned not to discredit
operations arising from the transmission
of spirits and the power of imagination,
because the outcome sometimes fails. For
just as contagion, diffused from body to body,
is often received, yet sometimes the strength
and good constitution of the passive body
repels it before the disease takes hold; so
also, and all the more, an impression from
soul to soul, or from spirit to spirit, often
triumphs victoriously. But it is also possible
for the patient soul and spirit to recollect
itself, and having struggled free from the
bonds of an as-yet-unsolidified dominion,
to overcome it, before the dominating plague
refuses to be dislodged. That power is
especially potent against languid minds and
spirits, such as those of women, the sick,
the superstitious, children, and animals of
tender age.

     903. Just as in those operations and their causes error is to be avoided, so also, and especially, care must be taken lest effects deceive us, rashly judging them to be such, which have not yet proceeded so far. Thus prudent judges, as if by a prescribed rule, are unwilling to give rash credence to the confessions of Witches, nor even to the proof of facts against them. For a giddiness of imagination disturbs Witches, so that they think they are doing that which they are not doing; and here credulity deceives the people, so that they attribute the works of nature to enchantment. It is worthy of observation that in ancient times and in an age nearer to our own (concerning, namely, the Thessalian witches of old and the recently reported gatherings of sorceresses, of which very many confessions make mention) the miracles that exist, handed down in writings, such as being lifted into the air, transformation of oneself into another body, etc., are not said to have been performed by incantations or magical ceremonies, but by the body with ointments

For we know that the anointing of the forehead, neck, feet, and spine is used for inducing deadly sleeps. If anyone should think that this is better done by potions taken internally, let him receive the answer that the medicines, the ingredients of the ointments, are of such efficacy that if taken internally, they could kill those who use them. Therefore they operate powerfully, but when applied externally.

The eighth and ultimate is the emission of immaterial virtue, examples of which it would be a matter of scruple to propose (so prodigious does the matter seem to us), had it not obtained the faith and assent of many, and had I not, as if by the severity of the said law, taken on the role of a careful examination, admitting or rejecting nothing whose probability had not been thoroughly investigated. 934. It is certain that odors nourish little, especially those of wine; and that a hungry person is affected by perceiving the smell of warm bread. Stone walls are unhealthy; wooden ones contribute more to health; but especially brick ones. For some, the thickness of the walls, with chalk inserted between the bricks, succeeded very well in preventing evaporation.

   938. Emissions of this kind (as we said before) are to be arranged into separate and proper headings, that is, visible and audible ones each deserve their own treatise. Here it will suffice to bring forward general points and those common to both. First, they appear incorporeal. Second, they operate swiftly. Third, their power is exerted over a great distance. Fourth, they are curious in their variety. Fifth, they accomplish nothing so as to leave a work behind them, but are mere energies. For their operations in mirrors and echo-generating places change nothing in these bodies; but the action is the same as the primary one, though reflected. As for the movement of windows from concussion; or the rarefaction of air from the impact of great sounds; and heat from burning glasses, these are rather such things as accompany audible and visible species, than their effects. Sixth, they are of a tender and weak nature, since they affect only a slender and subtle substance, such as the spirit of living beings.

This Augur is believed to have been suborned by Cleopatra, so that Antony might live in retirement in Egypt, far from Rome. Whatever the case, the opinion concerning the predominant and imperious spirit of one person over another is old and thoroughly widespread.

    945. There is also some contagion of shame and pride; the flight of one inclining others also to flight, and shame passing into others, which suffused one out of regard for him.
    Now we undertake to explain the powers of imagination on another's body; in what ways it is strengthened when exalted. I understand imagination to be a representation of individual thought; and it is threefold. The first is connected with faith in a future thing; the second with memory of a past thing; the third is of the present, or as if present, by which I embrace whatever imagination invents and fabricates for the mind's pleasure; as if someone imagines such a man clothed in pontifical ornaments or winged. I exclude and separate from this treatise that (imagination) which arises from faith in the future. The matters to be discussed here, according to the laws of our method (which consists of induction), are involved in the greatest difficulties of argument; since those things which are circulated abound in rumors and fables, and new things can scarcely be done, except most cautiously, because of a reason to be proposed by us later.
    The powers of imagination are of a threefold difference: either they act upon the body of the imaginer itself,

is conceived; or they tend towards inanimate bodies,

Then he asked, "Do you remember whether he first asked the man to prefigure some card in his thoughts, and afterwards whispered into the ear of another what he had conceived in his mind, or whether he first whispered to the man who was about to show the card that this or that person had conceived such a card, and then asked him to conceive the card?" I replied that the matter was thus, namely, that he first whispered into someone's ear that someone would think of such a card. Here that learned man was greatly pleased with himself; "as you see," he said, "I was right in my opinion: for if the other had first conceived the card, his thought would have been fixed; but the prior imagination of the other constrained his thoughts." Although that carried some weight with me, yet I replied that the matter was of lesser importance, even far below my own opinion. For I said that I held the opinion that the conjurer and two servants had done the thing by arrangement, though led to this by no reason. For to my father

for each owed his service, nor had the magician ever before been in the house: who also ordered a garter to be lifted, asserting that he knew it would be touched by this or that person at such a place, so many inches distant from the longer end, so many from the shorter: and he immediately performed it, first by suggesting to the imaginer, then by asking the actor to think.

Having dispatched this narration—not because it is of such great importance, but because it skillfully places the whole matter before our eyes—I return to what was interrupted: namely, that experiments of imagination should be performed by others, not by oneself.

For there are three ways of strengthening belief: first, experience; second, reason; third, authority: which, above the others, is of the greatest weight, when belief from reason or experience wavers.

947. Belief from authority is twofold: in the art and in the artisan. Things based on belief in the art can be practiced by ourselves; belief in the artisan depends on being demonstrated by another: as if someone has faith in Astrology and finds a prosperous figure; or in natural magic, and that a ring with such a seal, or such a part of an animal worn, is beneficial, he strengthens his imagination. But belief in the artisan is much more active.

     953. 957. It is expedient to consider in what things imagination is most powerful. The rule (if I conceive rightly) is, that it exerts its chief power in the most subtle and most easily moved things, and therefore especially in human spirits, and there in such affections as are not laboriously aroused, as in stimulating love, in arousing lust, where imagination dominates; a man struck by fear, or of wavering mind, etc. Let the inquiry be more strictly pursued through all things of this kind. These things could be tried in plants, and that diligently; as if you tell someone that this or that tree will die this year, and you instruct him to inspect at some intermediate time how it thrives. As for inanimate things, it is true that the movements of shuffling playing cards, or the throwing of dice, are very subtle. It is also a very common folly to predict the outcome of games, or fortune less than desired, from certain bystanders. Let it also be tried with a ring hanging by a thread, which is contained within a glass; and you predict to someone that the ring will strike the sides of the glass so many times and no more, or if two people hold a key with their fingers without incantation, and you say to them, he who bears such a name, it will fall from his fingers; for these two movements are very subtle. 958. It is a very common belief that a corpse, in the sight of the murderer, will emit blood anew through an inflicted wound. This could be ascribed as a miracle to the just judgment of God, who generally does not allow murders to remain hidden; but if it is referred to a natural force, it must be attributed to imagination.

Various experiments pertaining to the secret virtue of Sympathy & Antipathy.

960. Many things act upon human spirits by the forces of Sympathy and Antipathy. It is an old and universally accepted opinion that precious stones, accustomed to be worn as ornaments, possess admirable faculties, and that effects of curious vanity are attributed to them. So far, so good, that stones contain subtle spirits, which their splendor proves, so that by consent they can operate on human spirits, by refreshing and cheering them; of which the most attested virtue in this kind are the diamond, the emerald, the Oriental hyacinth,[a] the gold-stone which is also the green Topaz. But that they attribute special properties is groundless, and deserves no credit. It is manifest that light has the primary role above all else in refreshing human spirits, and it is very probable that with varied splendor of light the same effect is produced, and indeed with the added charm of novelty. And this is one of the causes why precious stones comfort. It would therefore be useful to tint lanterns or umbrellas with glass of green, blue, yellow, scarlet color.

the most celebrated virtue is that of parts from living creatures, provided their life is separated without blemish; as if a living animal would infuse into the separated parts the vigor of an immaterial virtue. So far, the truth holds, that a part of an animal recently slaughtered is more potent than from a similar animal that died spontaneously; because it abounds more in spirits.

995. It is permissible also to apply the experiment to parts from individual plants and animals; for instance, if you allow a cut part of a slip to putrefy, to see if the rest of the slip withers; or a part cut from the tail or leg of a dog or cat, whether its putrefaction hinders the healing of the remaining part.

996. They say that a ring or bracelet worn, made from the hair of a beloved, helps to feed love. Perhaps because it excites the imagination; a glove, or any other thing destined to attest favor, would possess the same power.

997. The sympathy of individuals, which were once whole, or from contact, exceeds belief above all. Therefore, it is pleasing to engage in a more thorough examination of it, according to the principle of our method. It is a commonplace that warts are removed if you allow to rot that which you have rubbed on them. My belief here wavers less, because it is wrong to contradict one's own experience, when I was quite a boy...

--- Page 649 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. X. 605
while I had a wart on my finger, around my sixteenth year of age when I was living in Paris, gradually more began to grow on both hands, at least a hundred, within the space of a month. The wife of an English orator, a woman by no means superstitious, said one day that she wished to remove whatever warts disfigured her hands. Afterwards she took a small piece of bacon, with the skin not removed, with the fat of which she anointed all the warts; and among them that one which had almost been coeval with me up to that time. Then, having affixed the piece of bacon with a nail to the post of her bedroom window, which faced south, she exposed it to the sun to be putrefied. The result was that all the warts completely vanished within seven months; even that one which surpassed the others in age. I do not wonder that those born in a short time died quickly; but the destruction of that one, which had remained clinging to my hand for so many years, still occupies my mind. The same effect is attributed to Elder, if you apply a green stick from it for rubbing warts, which afterwards, placed in dung, should rot. It could be tried on corns of the feet and scrofulous tumors and similar excrescences; also on parts of animals which are most akin to excrescences, such as the combs and spurs of cocks,
Cc 3 bestia-

--- Page 650 ---
606      OF FRANCIS BACON
of beasts' horns, etc. The method of experimentation should be twofold: either the parts are rubbed with lard or elder, as in the aforesaid; or those parts, cut into smaller pieces, you may have what is left to decay, and observe what the decay of a separated particle avails for one that was once joined.

   998. A widespread opinion has prevailed among many, that by anointing the weapon and whatever inflicted the wound, the wound is healed. From the account of a most trustworthy man (although hitherto I cannot be induced to believe the experiments) you will note the following. First, the weapon-salve consists of various ingredients, among which the most remarkable and difficult to obtain are moss from the skull of an unburied corpse, bear's grease, and a she-bear killed in parturition. In the latter two, I readily suspect that a loophole has been sought, so that, if the cure did not succeed, it could be pretended that the beasts had not been killed at the proper time. Ireland supplies a great quantity of moss from bodies killed, heaped up, and unburied. The remaining ingredients are, hematite reduced to powder, and certain other things that stop blood; which moss also does. A description of the entire salve exists in Crollius's Chymical Dispensatory. Secondly, that salve (is applied) not to the wound
                                          but

--- Page 651 ---
SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. X. 607
but applied to the weapons themselves, it exerts its power.
Thirdly (which I much approve of), for the preparation of the salve, they do not require a certain constellation; a usual refuge for ignorance in magical medicines; [whereby] if they fail, [they claim] it was not prepared under that sign which is destined in the heavens for its preparation. Fourthly, it can be applied to the weapons, even if the patient is far removed at long intervals. Fifthly, it does not seem necessary that the imagination of healing should concur; since the injured person can be cured even without any knowledge of what is intended. And so far, experience testifies that if the salve, for example, was wiped off the weapons while the wounded person was unaware, the pains flared up again, until the weapons were again anointed. Sixthly, they assert that if the weapon itself is not available, it is sufficient if an iron or wooden instrument, not dissimilar in form, is inserted into the wound so that it draws blood; the anointing of which is equally momentous for the cure. That, I believe, is an invention, so that this wonderful method of healing may be more sought after and used; since weapons are often lacking. Seventhly, the wound must first be cleansed with white wine or the urine of the injured person, then tightly bound with a thin linen cloth, which must not be removed before the healing process is completed. Eighthly, the sword must be properly covered with a sheath, lest the anointed part be exposed to the wind.

be placed. Ninth, that the salve, wiped from the sword
and preserved, can double its service; its
virtue increased rather than diminished.
Tenth, that it heals much faster than other
wound salves. Lastly, that the cure in man
and beast will be with equal success;
which pleases me above all, since the whole matter
can be more easily investigated.

   *A solitary experiment concerning*
          *hidden properties.*

   999. I would like men to know that, although
I reprehend the supine negligence in seeking
the causes of things; while these are attributed
to hidden faculties and properties (a hindrance
and a deadly slumber to the instituted
investigation for further knowledge) I do not
nevertheless establish that much should not be left
to proof by experiments
in the practical part of knowledge, where judgment
does not penetrate so exactly; and this not
only in species, but in individual cases. Thus in
Medicine, if you wish to cure the king's evil,
it is not enough to say that the medicine should not be
cooling, since it impedes deobstruction,
which the disease requires; nor should it be hot,
since it exasperates bile, so that it penetrates to the
gallbladder, for in it the obstruction
adheres, the cause of the disease, etc. But from experien-
                                                              ce

--- Page 653 ---
      SYLV. SYLVAR. Cent. X.      609
-rience is to be accepted, that powder of ground-pine or similar taken in beer cures the royal disease. Again, a prudent physician will not continuously apply the same medicine, but will vary it, if the first medicine disappoints the hope of success. For remedies for the royal disease, stones, fevers, etc., which are beneficial in one place, harmful in another; according to the suitability that intervenes between the medicine and the individual body.

   *A solitary experiment concerning*
      *the general sympathy of the human*
               *spirit.*

   1000. The pleasure which popularity, fame, honor, submission, and subjection of minds, wills, and affections generate in men (although another end may be proposed for seeking these things) seems a thing pleasing and suitable to human nature, nor does it admit further contemplation of a more widely extending consequence. But truly to one paying attention, a deeper meaning occurs, as if all human spirits and minds had proceeded from one divine source. Otherwise indeed, how would man be so greatly affected by those things which others bring forth conceived in mind? The best temperament and constitution of mind seeks solidly good fame and
               Cc 5               true-

--- Page 654 ---
610        FR. BACON'S SYLV. &c.
true honor; a lesser one seeks popular favor,
and enjoys the title and applause of a people-pleaser.
A worse one seeks subjection and
plots tyranny, as is evident in conquerors
most abundantly filled with affected glory, and
the world's agitators. Yet this is revealed more
clearly in Arch-heretics, since the introduction
of novelty in the doctrine of salvation, is a kind
of tyrannical domination over the intellect
and human faith.

A remedy for Gout devised for the Baron,
to which Experiment 60 pertains,
consists of the following.

I. Prescription for a Poultice.

Take about three ounces of fine flour bread,
only the crumb, finely shredded; let it be
cooked in milk until it thickens into a small
poultice. Add at the end a drachm and a half
of red rose powder. Ten grains of saffron.
An ounce of rose oil. Let it be spread on a
linen cloth, and applied warm, and continued
for three hours.

II. Bath or Fomentation.

℞. Half a handful of sage leaves. Six
drachms of cut hemlock root. Half an ounce
of bryony roots. Two handfuls of red rose
leaves. Let them be cooked in a pot filled
with water in which steel has been quenched,
until the liquid has been reduced to a
quarter. After per-

of black salt; let it be applied with a scarlet

in the warm liquid, the application repeated seven
times. Let these things be done in the space of a quarter
of an hour or a little more.

III. Plaster.
Recipe. Plaster of Diacalciteos,
as much as is sufficient for the part to be covered. Let it be dis-

the most honorable author conceived with this intention,
that in it he might present a certain model and description of a College,
established for the interpretation of nature, and the greatness and power of works;
and that he might distinguish it by the name of Solomon's House,
or the College of the Works of the Six Days. And he extended
the thread of his discourse thus far, until he completed this.
The model, (I confess) according to the custom of Poetics,
is grander and loftier than what, in all respects, might be open to imitation;
but nevertheless, in most things, human industry should not despair of itself.
He also had in mind, in this very fable, a book concerning
                                  a 2               legi-

--- Page 708 ---
4        TO THE READER.
laws, or concerning the best state of a Commonwealth,
to write; but since he foresaw that this work
would be lengthy; and also was carried away by the desire
of collecting Natural History, and of weaving together
other parts of the Instauration (which he considered
far more important); here he stopped.
    New Atlantis, as far as the English edition
is concerned, found its place here by my Lord's decision,
because of its great affinity, for the most part, with
    the Natural History, which precedes
        it.

We were sailing from Peru, where we had stayed for a whole year. We were seeking, however, China and Japan, carrying twelve months' provisions with us; and for the space of five months, and more, with favorable winds blowing from the East, although light-
posi-

--- Page 710 ---
6 OF FRANCIS BACON
our provisions spent, without supplies,
we plainly thought ourselves lost, and
expected death to be near. Nevertheless,
we lifted our hearts and voices to God in the Heavens;
*Who shows His wonders in the deeps;*
praying to Him for His Mercy,
that, just as in the beginning,
He commanded the *Gathering of the Waters*,
and made the *Dry Land* appear; so now
He would also show us land, lest we
perish. It happened however, that on the following
day, towards evening, within a moderate distance,
we discerned, towards the North, as
it were thick Clouds: which gave us hope of land,
being well aware that that tract
of the *South Sea* was entirely unknown:
and could contain Islands and Continents,
not yet discovered;
therefore, that whole night, we directed our course thither,
where the land, as we conjectured, had
shown itself: and at dawn on the next
day, it was manifest that what we had seen
was truly land, indeed low-lying
and woody: which had made it appear more obscure.
And after an hour and a half's
sailing, we reached the Safe Port:
the Port of a certain city, not great
indeed, but beautifully built, and
which, from the side facing the Sea, had an ele-
			gance.

N O V U S A T L A S.          7
gance displayed great elegance. But we,
finding every moment slow by which
we were away from land, hastened to the shore,
and prepared ourselves for descent onto land.
Immediately, however, we saw some of the
city's people, with staffs in their hands, who by
nod and signs forbade us to descend onto land:
yet without shouts or ferocity. Whereupon,
greatly saddened, we deliberated among ourselves
what was to be done.

Mean-
while, a boat, not very large, proceeded towards
us, carrying about eight men; one of whom
carried in his hand a staff of yellow reed,
imbued with blue color at both ends. He
confidently boarded our ship. And when he
had seen one of ours coming forward to meet
him, he drew from his bosom a certain scroll
of parchment, (but our parchment was a little
yellower, and shining like the leaves of codi-
cils, but otherwise quite soft and flexible.)
And he gave it into the hand of him who had
first offered himself from among us. In which
Scroll, in ancient Hebrew, also ancient Greek,
quite pure Latin, and Spanish, these Words
were written; *“Do not descend onto land;*
*much less any one of you. Moreover, hasten your*
*departure from these Shores,”*

humanity, it was no small consolation to us:
above all, the sign of the cross affixed to the instrument,
filled us with unique joy,
as a manifest omen of safety.
An answer was given by us in the Spanish language.
that our ship was in sufficiently good condition,

winds rather than

the servant received our answer, a boat

in a toga with wide sleeves, of most beautiful
blue camelot, much more splendid than we have in Europe:

accompanied by only men, in the same boat.
But another followed behind, in which there were about twenty men.
As soon as he had come within a spear's throw, we were warned by certain signs from the boat that we should send some of our men to him. This we did immediately, in our ship's skiff; sending the chief man among us (with one exception), and four with him. And when we were about six rods from the boat, they ordered us to stop and not to approach closer. Which we also did. Then indeed the man, whom I just described, stood up on his feet and asked in a loud voice in Spanish, "Are you Christians?" We replied that we were Christians: fearing less, because we had seen the sign of the Cross on that standard. To which reply, he raised his right hand towards Heaven, and then gently brought it to his mouth; which gesture is customary for them when they give thanks to God. Then he continued; "If you swear (each one of you) by the merits of the Savior, that you are not pirates, nor have shed human blood, whether by right or by force, within the space of the last forty days, you will obtain permission to land." We replied that we were all ready for that oath.

that many among you are unwell, he had been
warned by the health official in the city

humble servants; and that we considered it a great
honor, and attributed it to his singular humanity,
what had already been done; but we hoped
that the illness with which our sick ones
suffer was by no means contagious. So
that chief man returned. A little later
the Notary came and boarded our ship;
holding in his hand a certain fruit of that
region, not unlike an Orange, but with a color
more inclining towards scarlet, which breathed a most
sweet odor. He carried it, (as it seemed), so that
it might serve him as an antidote against contagion.

The travelers' house is a beautiful and spacious building, constructed of bricks, like ours, but a little more purple in color; with elegant windows, some of glass, but others of delicate linen cloth, dipped in oil. I make known to you, that the custom of this Kingdom requires, that after the present day, and tomorrow, (which we permit you for transferring men and your goods from the ship) you keep yourselves, within these doors, for three days.

We also offered him twenty gold pieces, but he also, smiling, said only this: What, do you want me to be a man of double salary? thus he departed.

A little later, our lunch was brought: which certainly provided a sufficiently lavish, and wholesome meal, both in respect to food, and drink: certainly better and more abundant, than according to the measure of any College, as far as I know, in Europe.

On the morrow, after those three days had passed, a new man came to us, whom we had not seen before, clothed in a blue garment, just like the previous one, except that his Turban was white, with a small red cross on the top. So he departed from us, not without tears welling up from tenderness of spirit; and he left us also confused and overwhelmed with joy and a feeling of gratitude, and we said to one another that we had come into a land of Angels, who appeared to us daily and anticipated us with consolations which we could not even have imagined, much less expected.

Thus therefore you see, that we have instituted commerce: not for gold, silver, and gems, not for silks, or spices, nor for any other crude things, but only for God's first creature, namely light: light, I say, breaking forth and germinating in whatever region of the earth.

But after it was spread among our men, that that state was accustomed to grant conditions to foreigners who wished to remain, we could scarcely persuade any of them to attend to our ship, or to prevent them from going immediately to the governor to ask for conditions. But, not without great difficulty, we at last restrained them, until we should decide by common consent what was to be done.

Among other conversations one day, I happened to say that I had been greatly delighted by that account, which I had received from some of our own people, concerning their custom in celebrating the festival they call the Family Festival; for I did not seem to myself to have ever heard of any solemnity in which nature presided so remarkably. But since the propagation of families proceeds from marital union, I desired to learn something from him, both concerning their laws and customs regarding marriages; and finally, whether polygamy was forbidden among them?       On the appointed day, the Father entered. He was a man of moderate stature and age, handsome in appearance, bearing a countenance as if compassionate. He was dressed in a gown of pure black cloth, with wide sleeves and a cape. His inner garment was of linen, certainly most elegant and whitest, reaching down to his feet, with a belt likewise white, of linen. He also wore a liripipe around his neck, of purest linen. He had sumptuous gloves, adorned with gems. Hyacinthine shoes of velvet. His neck was bare up to his shoulders. His hat was in the shape of a helmet, or a montera, as the Spanish call it: beneath which hung his curls, slightly curly, and arranged in a becoming manner. He sat alone, upon a cushion of a somewhat rougher blue velvet: but under his feet he had a rug, likewise of silk, of various colors, similar indeed to a Persian one, but more elegant. His right hand, as he went, he raised bare, blessing the people, but in silence. The streets were so arranged that a wide path lay open, nowhere obstructed: nor (I believe) was a battle line ever in an army better arranged than the people, at that time, in the streets. Moreover, even within the windows themselves, the spectators stood not improperly, but each as if placed in his own order. The celebration having finished, the Jew said to me: "For several days now, I will be detained, so that I cannot be with you, as usual, and as I desire: because a duty has been entrusted to me by the prefect of the city, to serve this eminent man." Three days later, the Jew returned to me, and said: "You have arrived here under good omens: For the Father of Salomon's House has been informed of your stay in this city: and has commanded me to announce to you that he and the entire society

your company to his presence, and also, separately, to speak with one of you, whom you shall choose for this purpose. For this matter, he appointed the day after tomorrow. He was sitting upon a low throne, magnificently adorned, and above his head he had a canopy, of blue silk, elegantly interwoven with gold. The room was empty of people, except that on either side of the throne, for honor's sake, stood a servant, clad in white garments. His inner garment was similar to that in which we had seen him clad in the street. But instead of a Toga, he was clad in a cloak, with a hood, of very fine black cloth, fastened around his shoulders. large, and deep, of various depths. The deepest of them will extend down to six hundred fathoms. And some of them have been dug out under great mountains, so that if you consider the total depth of the cavern, some of them are three miles deep. For we have found that the height of the mountain, up to the plain, and the depth of the cave from the plain, are truly the same, both being equally removed from the Sun, and celestial rays, and open air. These caves we call the lowest region. But we use them for all coagulations, indurations, refrigerations, and preservations of bodies. We also use them to imitate natural mines; and for the production of new artificial metals, from materials and cements which we prepare there, and bury for many years. We sometimes use them (which may seem strange) for the cure of certain diseases, and the prolongation of life, in some hermits who prefer to live there, well supplied with all necessary things, who are certainly very long-lived; from whom we also learn many things.

	We also have very diverse furnaces, which exhibit and maintain diverse degrees of heat, namely, of a sharp and swift kind, robust and persistent, gentle and moderate, blown, tranquil, humid, dry, and similar. We also have houses of suffumigations and odors, where we also add experiments of tastes. There we multiply and strengthen odors (which might seem strange). We imitate natural odors, making all kinds of odors emanate from other mixtures rather than from their genuine sources. Similarly, we also imitate tastes, so that they completely deceive the taste, however accurate. In this house is also contained a confectionary, where we make sweets, cakes, and other such things, both moist and dry: indeed, we even preserve them with other very pleasing sweet things, besides sugar and honey. There we make most pleasant wines, dairy products, broths, salted foods, and salads, certainly pleasing to the taste, and by no means in use among you.

We also have houses of Machines, where machines and instruments are ready for all kinds of motions. There we try to produce motions faster than any you have among you, whether from your smaller firearms or any other machine. We also try to make motions easier and more intense, by multiplying them through wheels and other methods. Then motions to produce

We have three who collect experiments of all mechanical arts; and also of the liberal sciences, moreover, and of all practical things which have not yet coalesced into an art. These we call Hunters. We have three who apply themselves to new experiments, as it shall seem expedient to them. These we call Diggers, or Miners. We have three who digest the experiments of the aforementioned others into titles and tables, so that the intellect may better operate upon them, for drawing out from them observations and axioms. These we call Dividers. We have three who are ordained for this purpose, that they may look into the experiments of their fellows, and from them extract and devise discoveries which pertain to the use of life and practice, as well as those which serve the sciences, not only as regards works, but also for clear demonstrations of causes, methods of eliciting natural predictions, or easy and manifest information as to what are the latent parts in individual bodies, what virtues? These we call Benefactors. Then indeed, after many meetings and consultations of all the fellows, who thoroughly intro-

As for our ordinances and rites, we have two spacious and beautiful galleries.     We also have certain hymns and forms of liturgies, which we daily sing and recite; with these we resound praises and jubilees, and thanksgivings to God, because of His wondrous works: likewise certain forms of prayers, with which we implore His help and blessing, that He may deign to direct and illuminate our labors, and convert them to good and holy uses.

   And when he had said these things, he raised himself to his feet: but I, as I had been instructed, fell on my knees, whereupon, placing his right hand on my head, he said: May God bless you, my son; may God likewise bless this account which I have made.
